articles.title: Federal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation - reflector.com
articles.summary: Federal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation  reflector.com
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates Wednesday even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices.
The Fed's latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation.
Yet Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won't easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
After the Fed announces its rate decision, Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed's next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed's desire for a “timelier” return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors.
If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.
On Thursday, a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.
Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy.
“Unless the Fed takes this problem more seriously and stops essentially making excuses about inflation, I think we're not going to get back to 2% until the next recession,” Bhave said.
Warsh will likely seek to keep the Wednesday press conference relatively short. It was about 30 minutes last month. Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, often held news conferences for about 45 minutes.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

articles.title: FOMC Preview: Fed Faces Tough Rate Decision as Weak Jobs and Hot Inflation Complicate Outlook - Coin Edition
articles.summary: FOMC Preview: Fed Faces Tough Rate Decision as Weak Jobs and Hot Inflation Complicate Outlook  Coin Edition
articles.full_text:
- The Fed faces a tough rate decision as weak job growth clashes with persistent inflation.
- Markets expect a pause in October, but hotter prices keep another rate hike in play.
- Bitcoin, gold and US stocks await Fed signals and fresh PCE inflation and GDP data.
The Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy decision as it prepares for its October 27–28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
Weakening US employment growth is colliding with inflation pressures that are forcing policymakers to balance slowing economic activity against the need to bring inflation back to its 2% target.
The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points in September, bringing the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4.00%. However, October’s economic data have complicated the outlook. Weaker-than-expected payroll growth has raised concerns about the labor market, while hotter consumer and producer prices have reinforced the case for restrictive monetary policy.
Economists broadly expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged at this meeting. A Reuters poll published on October 20 found that nearly all surveyed economists anticipated a pause in October, followed by another rate increase in December. Bank of America remains a notable exception, forecasting another hike this month.
For Bitcoin, gold and US stocks, the decision will be significant. The Fed’s statement and Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference will also hint at the next policy move.
US Weak Jobs Data and The Pressure on Fed
The September employment report, released on October 2, revealed the US labor market was losing momentum.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls increased by just 29,000, missing the 89,000 forecast. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, while average hourly earnings increased by 0.1% month over month, below the expected 0.3%.
Revisions further weakened the employment picture. August payroll growth was revised from 162,000 to 133,000, while July’s figure was revised from a gain of 21,000 to a loss of 10,000. Together, the revisions reduced previously reported job growth by 60,000.
The figures confirm a sharper slowdown in hiring than initially reported. Softer wage growth also points to easing inflationary pressure if the trend persists. For the Fed, weaker employment strengthens the argument against additional tightening, as higher borrowing costs further restrain business investment, household consumption and hiring.
One disappointing report does not establish that the economy is entering a recession.
Hot CPI and PPI Affect Interest Rate Outlook
US inflation accelerated in September, supporting the case for retaining restrictive monetary policy.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI), released on October 14, showed headline inflation rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year. Annual headline inflation exceeded the 3.6% forecast, while monthly inflation matched expectations.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose by 0.3% month over month, above the forecast of 0.2%. Its annual rate rose to 2.6%, up from 2.4% and above expectations of 2.5%.
Energy costs drove a substantial portion of the headline increase. Gasoline prices climbed 9.1% during September, accounting for more than half of the monthly CPI increase. Shelter costs also rose by 0.4%.
Producer prices delivered another inflation warning the following day. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand increased by 1.3% month over month, compared with a forecast of 0.6%. Core PPI, excluding food and energy, rose by 0.7%, against expectations of 0.3%.
Persistent producer-price increases raise business costs and eventually feed into household prices. The combination of accelerating inflation and weakening hiring leaves policymakers with limited room to maneuver.
Another rate increase would reinforce the fight against inflation but add pressure to economic activity, while a pause would give officials more time to assess incoming data.
Will the Fed Hold Rates or Raise Them Again?
The October FOMC meeting will assess whether September’s rate increase provides sufficient control or whether steady inflation warrants another immediate move.
The baseline expectation is for the Fed to hold its benchmark rate at 3.75%–4.00%. PIMCO also expects a pause, while maintaining the prospect of further tightening later in the year.
Bank of America’s forecast for a 25-basis-point October increase highlights the division over the appropriate policy response.
A pause would not signal the end of rate increases. Policymakers would use the meeting to assess the effects of September’s hike and determine whether inflation is becoming more persistent.
Investors will scrutinize the statement for changes in the Fed’s assessment of inflation, employment and economic activity. The voting pattern will offer additional clues: dissent from officials favoring another increase would reveal the strength of inflation concerns despite the weakening labor market.
Why Bitcoin, Gold and Stocks Are Watching the Fed
Bitcoin and other risk assets generally benefit when investors anticipate stable or declining interest rates as lower expected borrowing costs ease financial conditions.
Recent market reactions illustrate how economic data generate different outcomes across asset classes.
Following the September employment report on October 2, Bitcoin traded above $87,000 before later moving toward $85,300 in the reported intraday snapshots. Gold also gained, while major US stock indices closed higher.
The reaction reversed after the CPI report. Bitcoin fell to around $81,900 in an early post-release snapshot, while gold declined and the Nasdaq Composite finished the session down 1.88%.
The October 15 PPI release produced a different outcome. Bitcoin briefly fell below $80,000 before recovering toward $81,000, while gold rose to $4,156.52 per ounce in a reported intraday snapshot. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all closed higher that day.
The recovery coincided with lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar, while stronger retail sales also influenced the session.
These moves show how markets adjust as investors reassess rate expectations and weigh economic data.
PCE Inflation and GDP Will Shape the Next Fed Decision
The October meeting precedes two important US economic releases scheduled for October 29: September PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP.
The PCE price index is the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge. The latest available August data showed headline PCE inflation at 3.4% year over year and core PCE inflation at 3.0%. An October 26 forecast snapshot listed expected monthly core PCE inflation of 0.3%, compared with 0.2% previously. Separately, Barron’s reported expectations for annual headline and core PCE inflation of 3.6% and 3.1%, respectively.
The advance GDP estimate is forecast to show annualized quarterly growth of 3.2% for the third quarter, compared with a revised 2.2% in the second quarter. These figures remain forecasts, not actual results.
Because both releases arrive after the October meeting, they will not affect the decision announced on October 28. They will, however, shape expectations for the December meeting.
The combination of inflation and growth data will influence market sentiment:
- Cooler inflation, resilient GDP: Easing price pressures and steady growth would support risk assets.
- Hotter inflation, strong GDP: Persistent inflation and robust demand would strengthen the case for restrictive policy or another rate hike.
- Cooler inflation, weak GDP: Lower rate expectations could support Bitcoin and stocks, while growth concerns weigh on sentiment.
- Hotter inflation, weaker GDP: Persistent inflation and slowing growth would complicate the Fed’s policy decisions.
What to Watch After the October FOMC Decision
The October 28 rate decision will be the main market focus. Investors will also examine the Fed’s statement and Warsh’s press conference for clues about future policy.
Three factors will be especially important:
- Treasury yields and the US dollar movements will show how markets adjust expectations for future interest rates.
- Real yields and risk appetite will help explain gold’s performance and whether Bitcoin and stocks benefit from easier financial conditions or face pressure from economic concerns.
- The October 29 PCE and GDP reports will provide updated evidence on inflation and economic growth ahead of the December meeting.
In sum, the Fed faces a balancing act between steady inflation and a weakening labor market. While markets widely expect a pause, the statement and press conference will shape expectations for future policy. The subsequent PCE and GDP reports will influence the December outlook and set the tone for Bitcoin, gold and US stocks heading into November.

articles.summary: Dollar-yen rises into mid-157 range as markets eye US, Japan policy ahead of FOMC and BOJ meetings  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
According to the currency outlook published on the morning of the 27th by Gaitame.com Research Institute, the dollar-yen is expected to climb into the mid-157 yen range amid continued speculation over US and Japanese monetary policy carried over from the end of last week. Takuya Kanda, a senior currency analyst at the institute, set the day's expected range at 156.80-158.00 yen and said the pair is likely to hold firm in the upper-156 yen zone.
In Tokyo trading on Monday the 26th, Germany's October Ifo Business Climate Index beating market expectations lent support to European currencies. The index came in at 90.2, above the market forecast of 89.9 and the highest since May 2023. It was helped by the expectations component, which signals the outlook, rising to 91.6, its highest since February 2022. The Ifo Institute said companies assessed the current situation as somewhat worse but "a more optimistic outlook was evident," adding that "the economic recovery is continuing."
Looking at major markets, the Nikkei Stock Average fell 503.51 points to 62,189.65, while European and US equities were broadly firm. The NY Dow closed up 146.42 dollars at 52,361.58, Germany's DAX rose 229.19 points to 25,410.84, and the UK's FTSE gained 78.70 points to 10,769.06. In bond markets, the US 2-year yield rose to 4.7159% while the US 10-year yield edged down to 4.9884%, with flattening of the yield curve in focus. In commodities, NY crude fell 1.51 dollars to 101.76 dollars a barrel, while NY gold rose 30.50 dollars to 4,038.40 dollars a troy ounce.
The week's biggest focus is the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting scheduled for the 27th-28th and the Bank of Japan monetary policy meeting on the 29th-30th. As currency analyst Tsutomu Nakamura noted in the report dated the 26th of last week, both meetings are widely expected to leave policy rates unchanged, shifting market attention to hints on the timing and pace of future rate hikes in statements and press conferences. With participants wanting to see the outcome of the meetings, the overall market tone is prone to a stronger wait-and-see stance.
That said, the upside is not one-way. At the end of last week on the 23rd, the dollar-yen posted a gain of less than 0.1% on a closing basis, and during trading hours it briefly fell to around 156.08 yen. Yen-buying prompted by a sharp drop in the Nikkei Stock Average came first, and the decline was later erased amid a narrowing of equity losses and higher crude oil prices stemming from uncertainty over the Middle East situation. In a scenario where concerns about the outlook for AI investment reignite and global equities undergo a major correction, dollar-selling and yen-buying could still strengthen.
Among economic indicators released at the end of last week, Japan's September nationwide consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.1% year-on-year on a core basis excluding fresh food, matching expectations and accelerating from the previous month. Core-core CPI, which excludes fresh food and energy, came in at 2.4%, above the market forecast of 2.3%, supporting expectations for the Bank of Japan's policy normalization. In the US, the October flash manufacturing PMI hit 56.0, its highest in four years and five months, while the services PMI fell to 57.9 from the previous month, painting a mixed picture of economic strength.
In Europe, Moody's kept France's long-term sovereign credit rating at "Aa3" and maintained its outlook at "negative." However, the agency explained that the current rating assumes passage of the 2027 budget and an easing of interest rate and social tensions, leaving room for future downgrades.
Gaitame.com's published expected ranges for popular currency pairs for today are as follows.
| Currency Pair | Expected Range | 
|---|---|
| Dollar-yen | 156.800-158.000 | 
| Euro-yen | 175.100-176.600 | 
| Pound-yen | 209.300-210.900 | 
| Australian dollar-yen | 110.100-110.900 | 
Note: Expected ranges published by Gaitame.com Research Institute dated October 27, 2026.
Market participants expect that until the two major events—the FOMC and the Bank of Japan meeting—are cleared, moves to avoid building aggressive positions will continue. With both the US and Japan likely to hold rates steady, the wording of statements and Q&A at press conferences will be watched as the next market catalysts. Given that risk-averse yen-buying tends to emerge during sharp equity selloffs, the currency market looks set for a week in which it keeps a close eye on both policy events and the stock market.

articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of Japan will announce interest-rate decisions during the week of October 26, 2026, alongside Coinbase's third-quarter earnings release. The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee meets October 27–28, with its rate decision and press conference scheduled for Wednesday, October 28 at 2:00 p.m. Eastern. The ECB's Governing Council convenes in Frankfurt on October 28–29, with its decision due Thursday, October 29. The Bank of Japan's monetary policy meeting is also scheduled for late October, according to its published calendar.
This convergence of three major central bank decisions with a marquee crypto earnings report creates one of the most concentrated macro weeks for digital asset markets in 2026. Traders will be watching whether the Fed holds its target range at 3.75–4.00 percent, whether the ECB maintains its deposit rate at 2.50 percent, and whether the BOJ adjusts its policy stance after its June decision to alter its guideline for money market operations.
Three Central Banks Set Rate Decisions In Same Week As Coinbase Reports Q3 Earnings
The Federal Reserve's October FOMC meeting is confirmed for October 27–28, 2026, according to the official meeting calendar published by the Federal Reserve Board. The rate decision will be announced on Wednesday, October 28 at 2:00 p.m. Eastern, followed by Chair Jerome Powell's press conference. The September 15–16 FOMC meeting minutes, released October 7, confirmed the October dates and noted the committee adjourned at 10:15 a.m. on the second day of that prior session.
The ECB's Governing Council monetary policy meeting is scheduled for October 28–29, 2026, in Frankfurt, with the rate decision expected Thursday, October 29. The ECB calendar lists Day 1 on October 28 and Day 2 on October 29. This meeting will include updated macroeconomic projections, according to the ECB's published schedule.
The Bank of Japan's October monetary policy meeting is also on the calendar for late October 2026. Central bank tracking services list the BOJ meeting around October 28–30, though the BOJ's official English-language schedule for the full month has not been published. The BOJ's most recent confirmed policy action came on June 16, 2026, when the Policy Board voted 7-1 to change its guideline for money market operations.
Coinbase's Q3 2026 earnings release date falls within the same week. The company has not published a specific date or time, but the earnings report is expected during the week starting October 26. Coinbase typically reports after U.S. market close, and its results will land against the backdrop of the Fed decision on October 28 and the ECB decision on October 29.
The concentration is unusual. The Fed's decision day on October 28 overlaps with the first day of the ECB's meeting, and the BOJ's decision window sits within the same 72-hour period. For crypto traders, this means three separate monetary policy signals—each with the potential to move dollar liquidity conditions, euro-area risk appetite, and yen carry dynamics—will hit markets in rapid succession.
Market Expectations For Fed, ECB, And BOJ Rate Moves Heading Into Late October 2026
The Federal Reserve is expected to hold its target range at 3.75–4.00 percent at the October 28 decision, according to market pricing cited by Rio Times Online in its week-ahead preview. The guidance accompanying the decision is considered the main event, with traders parsing the statement and Powell's press conference for signals about the December 8–9 meeting. BofA Global Research has projected three rate increases of 0.25 percent each in 2026, starting in September, according to a private bank research note.
The ECB is overwhelmingly expected to hold its deposit rate at 2.50 percent on October 29. A Reuters poll of 73 economists conducted October 5–8 found that all but three expected the ECB to hold, matching market pricing. The ECB Watch Tool shows a 97.0 percent probability of rates staying at 2.50 percent at the October meeting. The central bank raised its key rate to 2.50 percent on September 10, its second hike of the year, responding to an energy-driven inflation rise after oil prices surged above $100 a barrel following U.S.-Iran attacks on military, shipping, and energy assets across the Middle East.
The IMF said on October 16 that it expects at least one more 25-basis-point ECB hike in 2026, but the Reuters poll suggests that move is more likely in December than October. The October 8 Reuters poll found economists expect a December hike as inflation approaches double the ECB's 2 percent target. ECB policymakers and accounts released October 8 dampened near-term rate hike bets, with longer-term price expectations remaining anchored.
For the BOJ, no specific market-implied probability is available for the October decision. The BOJ's June 16 action changed its guideline for money market operations by a 7-1 vote, and the central bank's policy rate stood at 1.25 percent according to central bank tracking services. The BOJ's October meeting will be watched for any adjustment to that stance, though no specific forecast is available.
The Fed's September minutes, released October 7, noted that market-implied policy rates through the end of 2026 increased more for the U.S. than for other jurisdictions. That suggests markets have been pricing a relatively hawkish Fed path into year-end, which would make a hold-and-signal decision on October 28 consistent with current positioning.
Coinbase Q3 2026 Earnings Preview And Crypto Market Positioning Before The Macro Week
Coinbase's Q3 2026 earnings will land in the middle of the central bank convergence, but no specific analyst estimates for revenue, trading volume, or earnings per share are available. Coinbase is identified as a key entity in the week's calendar, but no consensus figures are available. This is a material gap: traders will need to wait for the company's release or for analyst previews published closer to the date.

The absence of live crypto market data means the article cannot state where bitcoin is trading or how positioning looks heading into the macro week. What is clear from the macro side is that oil prices above $100 a barrel have revived inflation concerns in the euro zone, which is why the ECB hiked in September and why markets are pricing a December move.
The crypto market's positioning ahead of the week is therefore best framed through the macro lens. The Fed holding at 3.75–4.00 percent with hawkish guidance would keep dollar liquidity tight, which historically pressures risk assets including crypto. An ECB hold on October 29 with a December hike signal would reinforce the global tightening bias. The BOJ's decision adds a third variable: any adjustment to its 1.25 percent policy rate or its money market operations guideline could shift yen carry dynamics that have historically influenced global risk appetite.
Coinbase's earnings will provide a read on crypto trading activity in Q3 2026. The quarter included the September ECB hike, the Fed's September 15–16 meeting, and the oil-driven inflation shock. If Coinbase reports strong trading volumes, it would suggest retail and institutional activity remained robust despite the macro headwinds. If volumes disappointed, it would confirm that macro tightening is suppressing crypto market participation.

The minutes from that meeting, released October 7, showed the committee reviewing international developments and noting that market-implied policy rates through end-2026 increased more for the U.S. That hawkish repricing is the backdrop against which crypto has been trading.
The ECB's September 10 hike to 2.50 percent was driven by oil prices above $100 a barrel after Middle East escalation. That energy shock is a supply-side inflation impulse that central banks cannot easily offset, and it has forced the ECB into a tightening posture that markets expect to continue into December. For crypto, the relevant transmission channel is the euro-area risk appetite and the dollar-euro exchange rate, both of which feed into global liquidity conditions.
The BOJ's June 16 decision to change its money market operations guideline by a 7-1 vote marked a shift in the central bank's approach. The BOJ's policy rate at 1.25 percent remains the lowest among the three central banks, but the direction of travel matters. Any further adjustment in October would signal continued normalization, which has historically been associated with yen strength and potential unwinding of carry trades that have supported risk assets including crypto.

articles.summary: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes  CNBCThe Fed Is Expected to Hold Rates Steady. Warsh Will Have to Explain Why.  The New York TimesFederal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation  The Boston GlobeFederal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections  Fox BusinessFederal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate move this week. Here's what economists ex...
articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials enter this week’s policy meeting amid a critical debate over what the central bank can, should and will do to address an inflation problem that shows no immediate sign of going away.
When the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee does release its decision Wednesday, markets overwhelmingly expect no change in benchmark interest rates following September’s quarter percentage point rate increase.
Investors will be looking closely, though, for clues about future moves from policymakers, and Chairman Kevin Warsh in particular.
Brett Ryan, senior U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank, said he’ll be watching what Warsh will signal about future policy moves — something the Fed chairman has said he is highly reluctant to do as he seeks to move the central bank away from the “forward guidance” practice of most of the 21st century.
The chairman “is likely to signal that recent inflation data reinforce expectations from the September meeting that further tightening will likely be needed over time,” Ryan wrote in a note to clients. “However, skipping October allows officials more time to assess trends in the data.”
Recent inflation data has offered little respite from the price pressures that intensified earlier this year.
The consumer price index, a widely cited inflation barometer, showed the annual rate at 3.7% in September, driven largely by soaring energy prices. Even stripping out volatile gas and groceries costs, the core CPI pointed to a 2.6% rate — still well above the Fed’s 2% mandate and heading in the wrong direction after climbing 0.3 percentage point from August.
At the same time, recent economic data has shown the housing market struggling further under the pressure of mortgage rates above 7%. The labor market, meanwhile, has settled into a low-fire, low-hire pattern where layoffs are around their lowest levels since the late 1960s, while people out of work struggle to find jobs.
Calibrating policy under current conditions is complicated by Warsh’s push for a more mercurial Fed that avoids signaling where policy is heading, preferring for markets to take their own signals from incoming data.
A pause this month could give the Fed more time to assess what impact the prior rate hike had on the economy and financial conditions. However, signaling tighter policy could put more strain on the housing and labor markets. Warsh and his colleagues must show they are prepared to contain inflation while avoiding a premature commitment to how far or how fast rates will rise.
Essentially, the Fed can use its interest rate to influence inflation. It almost certainly will hold off doing so as it evaluates current conditions. Markets and economists, though, are at odds over what it should do.
The chance of a mistake under those circumstances is significant, according to Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI.
“It ought to be possible for Warsh – who is alert to market risks even though he professes not to like mollycoddling investors – to show a calming steady hand,” Guha said Monday in a note. “But there is material execution risk.”
For instance, the Fed’s lack of detail on how it sees the risks to its dual mandate of low inflation and full employment as well as how it views both the pace and tightening of monetary policy poses substantial challenges.
While inflation data has been hot, the unemployment rate has been fairly steady.
The Fed also weighs financial conditions when figuring policy. The Chicago Fed’s index of financial conditions has shown a slight tightening since the September hike, a product of stock market volatility, among other factors.
Recent chatter out of key Fed officials, such as Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, points to the likelihood of hikes at every other meeting. But how far the Fed will need to go remains a mystery.
Guha interprets remarks Warsh gave to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok recently as aligning “with the central view” on the FOMC. In practice, that’s a Fed moving “at a deliberative and methodical baseline pace of once per quarter without prejudice to what it learns along the way and how far it might ultimately have to go and whether at some point later down the line it might need to speed up.”
“If inflation continues to disappoint and/or growth momentum fails to moderate, the Fed will add more hikes,” he added.
Trading in the fed funds futures market points to about a 10% chance that the FOMC will raise rates this week, but a better than 80% probability of an increase in December, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The market sees the likelihood of another hike in March 2027, then about a 50-50 chance of a final move before the end of next year.
To be sure, there’s considerable debate among economists on whether the Fed should be tightening policy at all. Citigroup economists, for instance, think easing inflation data in the months ahead will give the Fed reason to stay on hold and perhaps begin cutting next year, though the firm is forecasting a hike this December.
Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic advisor at Allianz, said he expects further increases but believes that’s a mistake as they will hurt vulnerable areas such as housing and worsen economic disparities.
“My sense is that the market is right in saying that they’ll do nothing. [Warsh] will have to package it in quite a hawkish language because the [inflation] data all [have] come hotter than expected,” El-Erian said Monday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” “My problem is that it’s the wrong policy measure right now.”
The solution to worries about inflation and higher Treasury yields should be “fiscal containment, not monetary tightening,” he added.
“But we’re going to get monetary tightening, and it’s going to be what I call the one minus ‘X’ problem. ‘X’ is tech; it won’t be impacted that much,” El-Erian said. “It’s going to be the rest of the economy: housing, consumer car loans, consumer loans. That’s what’s going to be hit.”
Correction: Warsh gave remarks to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok. An earlier version misstated the name of one of the organizations.

articles.title: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (157.86) Rises as the Yen Lags Ahead of the Fed and BoJ — 158.50 Target, 160 Intervention Cap - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (157.86) Rises as the Yen Lags Ahead of the Fed and BoJ — 158.50 Target, 160 Intervention Cap  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- USD/JPY rose 0.22% to 157.86 on Tuesday, recovering from Friday’s five-week low near 156 on AI stock selling.
- The U.S.-Japan two-year yield spread stood at 2.792 percentage points, keeping carry demand for dollars strong.
- The Bank of Japan is expected to hold at 1.25% on Friday, with a December hike to 1.50% the market’s base case.
USD/JPY traded at 157.86 in European hours on Tuesday, up 0.22% on the day, after opening at 157.50 and setting an early range of 157.41 to 157.77. The pair extended Monday’s 0.41% gain, when it rose from 156.81 to 157.45, and it now sits 1.9 yen above Friday’s five-week low near 156. The yen gave back half of last week’s rally in two sessions, and it underperformed every major currency on Tuesday: it lost 0.19% to the dollar, 0.37% to the New Zealand dollar, 0.19% to the Australian dollar, 0.15% to the Swiss franc and 0.13% to the Canadian dollar.
The broader picture shows a pair pinned near multi-decade highs. USD/JPY sits 3.7% above its level of 12 months ago and within a 52-week range of 151.54 to 164.00. It touched 158.95 on October 14 after a hot U.S. inflation reading and traded near 158.5 around October 20 on reports that the Bank of Japan was leaning against an October rate hike. Last Friday, a global selloff in technology and AI stocks sent haven flows into the yen and pushed USD/JPY down toward 156, its lowest in five weeks. Tuesday’s move reverses that haven rally as risk appetite returns.
The dollar side is firm. The U.S. Dollar Index traded at 102.20, near a two-week high, after durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September and consumer confidence jumped to 91.7. U.S. equities rallied, with the Nasdaq up 1.33% on AI optimism, a risk-on backdrop that typically weakens the yen as investors unwind safe-haven positions and return to carry trades.
The week holds two central bank decisions. The Federal Reserve announces at 2:00 p.m. ET Wednesday, with a hold at 3.75%-4.00% priced above 90% and a December hike close to fully priced. The Bank of Japan concludes its two-day meeting on Friday, October 30, with a hold at 1.25% expected and a December hike to 1.50% the market’s base case. Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference follows at 06:30 GMT Friday.
The yield gap remains the dominant force. The U.S.-Japan two-year yield spread stood at 2.792 percentage points on Monday, after narrowing 14.7 basis points. Investors earn nearly 2.8 percentage points a year to hold dollars over yen at the two-year tenor, a carry advantage that keeps steady demand for USD/JPY even as the BoJ tightens.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. USD/JPY is caught between carry and intervention. The rate differential favors the dollar and keeps buyers active on every dip toward 156. But Tokyo’s finance ministry has warned repeatedly that it stands ready to act, and the 160 level, where Japan intervened earlier this year, caps the upside. Both central banks are likely to hold this week, which leaves the pair in a 156 to 159 range until either the BoJ accelerates or Tokyo steps into the market.
How Tuesday’s Session Unfolded: Asia Bid, Europe Extends, Carry Resumes
The session followed the pattern of a market rebuilding carry positions after last week’s haven scare. USD/JPY opened in Asia at 157.50, near Monday’s close, and held a tight range through the Tokyo morning as Japanese markets digested data showing services producer prices rising 3.7%, a reading that supports the case for further BoJ tightening.
The Asian session saw little movement despite the hawkish data. Traders who expect a hold on Friday saw no reason to buy the yen on a single price index, and the pair traded between 157.41 and 157.67 into the European open. Japanese equities rallied with the Kospi and other regional markets on AI optimism after Anthropic’s IPO filing in the U.S., and risk-on sentiment in Asia weighs on the yen.
Europe extended the move. USD/JPY broke above 157.77, the Asian high, and climbed to 157.86 by 07:22 GMT, up 0.22%. The pair was trying to return above its 20-day exponential moving average on the daily chart, a level it lost during Friday’s haven rally. The dollar index firmed to 102.20, adding support.
The U.S. data added fuel. Durable goods orders rose 1.8% to $345.4 billion in September, and orders excluding transportation rose 0.5%. Consumer confidence jumped 7.5 points to 91.7, the highest since June and far above the 81.0 forecast. Strong U.S. data supports the Fed’s hawkish stance, which keeps the yield gap wide.
The cross-asset tone was risk-on. U.S. technology stocks rallied, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 3% and bitcoin held near $80,000. In that environment, the yen’s haven appeal fades and carry traders, who borrow in yen to buy higher-yielding assets, return to the market.
Tuesday’s move reversed most of Friday’s flight to safety. On Friday, the AI stock selloff drove investors into the yen, and USD/JPY dropped toward 156. Monday and Tuesday saw that haven demand unwind as equities recovered, taking the pair back toward 158.
For the forecast, the session confirms that the yen remains a funding currency in calm markets and a haven only in stress. Without a risk-off shock or a hawkish BoJ surprise, carry flows push USD/JPY higher toward the 158 to 158.50 resistance zone.
The Bank of Japan: A Hawkish Hold at 1.25% With December in Sight
The Bank of Japan is the force that should be strengthening the yen, and it is tightening at its fastest pace in decades. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September from 1.0%, in a 7-2 vote, three months after a hike in June. The September move took the rate to its highest level in 31 years and accelerated the hiking pace from roughly once every six months to once every three months.
Governor Ueda has shifted the bank’s focus. After nearly 14 years of trying to push inflation up to 2%, the BoJ now sees the risk running the other way. Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, Ueda said that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and its main goal is to stabilize inflation around that level. At the October policy meeting, the BoJ is expected to declare victory over deflation and emphasize the risk that prices could overshoot.
This week’s decision is set up as a hawkish pause. The BoJ is expected to hold at 1.25% at the meeting ending Friday, October 30, by a majority vote. Ueda has said there is no need for back-to-back hikes, and that oversized or consecutive increases are reserved for situations where inflation rises rapidly beyond target. Market pricing gives a hold roughly 86% odds. Two board members, Takata and Tamura, may dissent in favor of a hike, which would signal the committee is leaning toward December.
December is the base case for the next move. Economists expect the BoJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December and maintain a quarterly pace. The policy rate at 1.25% now sits within the range of 1.1% to 2.5% that BoJ staff estimate as Japan’s neutral rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. The bank is expected to stress that financial conditions remain loose, signaling room for further hikes before the rate reaches neutral.
Thursday’s data will shape expectations. Japan releases October CPI data and September unemployment before the decision, giving the BoJ a final read on inflation and labor conditions.
For USD/JPY, three outcomes matter. A hawkish hold with clear December guidance and two dissents would lift the yen modestly, pushing the pair toward 156.50. A hold with cautious language that lets hike expectations drift toward January would weaken the yen and send the pair toward 158.50. A surprise hike to 1.50%, priced near 14%, would trigger a yen rally toward 155.
The Fed on Wednesday: Hold at 3.75%-4.00%, December Hike Priced
The Federal Reserve decision lands two days before the BoJ, and it will set the dollar side of USD/JPY for the week. The FOMC began its two-day meeting Tuesday and announces its decision Wednesday at 2:00 p.m. ET, with Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET. Fed funds futures price a hold at 3.75%-4.00% above 90% probability, with a December hike to 4.00%-4.25% close to fully priced. Markets see no Fed rate cuts in 2026.
The Fed is still tightening. It raised rates in September as the U.S.-Iran war’s energy shock pushed CPI to 3.7% year over year and the Fed’s preferred PCE gauge to 3.4% in August. The October 14 CPI release, which beat forecasts, sent USD/JPY to 158.95, its high for the month, as traders priced a more aggressive Fed.
The U.S. data gives Warsh no reason to soften. Jobless claims fell to 194,000 in the week ended October 17, the lowest since late July. The U.S. flash composite PMI sits near a five-year high at 57.6, with selling prices rising at the sharpest rate since August 2022. Durable goods and consumer confidence beat forecasts Tuesday.
The two central banks are tightening in parallel, which keeps the yield gap wide. The Fed is at 3.75%-4.00%, the BoJ at 1.25%, a policy gap of 250 to 275 basis points. If both hike in December as priced, the Fed would move to 4.00%-4.25% and the BoJ to 1.50%, leaving the gap unchanged. That parallel tightening explains why the yen has not strengthened despite the BoJ’s fastest hiking pace in decades.
The three Fed outcomes matter for USD/JPY. A hold with neutral language that stresses data dependence and declines to commit to December would weaken the dollar and push the pair toward 156.50. A hold with explicit December guidance, the base case, would keep the dollar firm and support a test of 158.50. A surprise hike, priced below 10%, would send USD/JPY toward 159 to 160 and into Tokyo’s intervention zone.

articles.title: How FOMC and CPI Move Bitcoin: A 2026 Macro Calendar - FinanceFeeds
articles.summary: How FOMC and CPI Move Bitcoin: A 2026 Macro Calendar  FinanceFeeds
articles.full_text:
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Bitcoin rallied after only one of eight FOMC meetings in 2025, according to CoinGecko, suggesting a sell-the-news pattern around Fed decisions.
- Block Scholes research found CPI surprises explained 25% of Bitcoin’s first-hour returns across a six-year sample, with peak sensitivity reaching 52% R-squared.
- The FOMC holds eight scheduled meetings in 2026, with the current federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00% following a 25 basis point hike on September 16.
- Bitcoin’s 52-week correlation with the US dollar index measured approximately negative 0.85 through the first half of 2026 according to CoinDesk data.
- Spot Bitcoin ETF flows shifted sharply with June 2026 outflows totaling approximately $4.5 billion before a $221.7 million single-day inflow on July 3.
Crypto markets no longer trade in isolation from the traditional financial calendar. Federal Reserve rate decisions, inflation reports, and employment data now produce measurable, documented effects on Bitcoin and the broader digital asset market.
CoinGecko’s analysis of the 2025 FOMC cycle showed Bitcoin falling after seven of eight meetings, a pattern that contradicted expectations of bullish responses to rate cuts.
This article maps the specific macro events that move crypto prices and quantifies their documented impact using institutional research.
The FOMC Cycle and Bitcoin’s Sell the News Pattern
The Federal Open Market Committee holds eight scheduled meetings per year, with rate decisions announced at 2:00 PM Eastern Time on the final meeting day. In 2025, the Fed cut rates three times by 25 basis points each, in September, October and December, for a cumulative reduction of 75 basis points. It held rates steady at the other five meetings, including May.
According to CoinGecko, Bitcoin rallied after only one of the eight FOMC meetings in 2025. This pattern suggests that markets often priced in expectations ahead of Fed announcements, leaving prices vulnerable to sell-the-news reactions.
The single positive 48-hour period followed the May rate decision, when the Fed held rates steady and Bitcoin gained approximately 15%. The broader pattern suggests that Bitcoin’s response to monetary policy announcements depends on how decisions compare with market expectations, rather than on rate cuts alone.
The 2026 FOMC schedule runs through eight meetings from January 28 to December 9. The most recent meeting on September 16 delivered a 25 basis point hike, bringing the federal funds rate to 3.75% to 4.00%, The Right Trader confirmed.
The next scheduled meeting falls on October 28, followed by December 9. Four of the eight meetings include an updated Summary of Economic Projections and the dot plot, which add another layer of market-moving information beyond the rate decision itself.
At the June 17, 2026 meeting, 9 of 18 FOMC officials projected at least one additional 25 basis point hike within the year. The dot plot median shifted from March’s projection of two cuts to one hike, marking a significant hawkish repricing that affected both equity and crypto markets.
Forward guidance was removed from the statement and replaced with language stating the FOMC “will deliver price stability,” a phrase that traders interpreted as leaving all options open for subsequent meetings.
CPI Releases and Bitcoin’s Documented Price Sensitivity
Consumer Price Index data, released monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), has become the second most significant macro event for crypto prices. Block Scholes research analyst Thahbib Rahman published a study showing that CPI surprises explained approximately 25% of Bitcoin’s first-hour return variation across a six-year sample starting in 2020, the firm reported.
A one percentage point upside CPI surprise corresponded to roughly a 5.5% decline in Bitcoin’s price during the following 60 minutes. The sensitivity was not constant across the sample period. During the peak window from December 2021 to November 2023, the R-squared value reached 52% and the one-hour rolling beta measured negative 13% per percentage point of surprise.
This means a CPI reading that exceeded consensus by just 0.16 percentage points, one standard deviation of surprise, triggered an average Bitcoin decline of approximately 1.3% in the first hour alone.
After fading to near zero through late 2024 and 2025, the sensitivity re-emerged in 2026. By June 2026, the 24 release rolling R squared recovered to approximately 22%, while the narrower 12 release window showed an R squared near 80%, exceeding even the 2022 to 2023 peak.
The most recent data point came from the June CPI release on July 14, 2026, when headline inflation printed at 3.5% against a 3.8% consensus. Bitcoin jumped toward $65,000 and closed the session up 2.9%.
The practical implication is that CPI releases create a documented window of elevated volatility concentrated in the first hour after publication. Block Scholes found no comparable effect at the 4 to 24 hour horizons, suggesting the market digests the information quickly, and subsequent price action reflects broader positioning rather than the data surprise itself.
Dollar Correlation, ETF Flows and the Macro Transmission Mechanism
The channel through which macro events reach crypto prices has shifted since spot Bitcoin exchange traded funds (ETFs) launched in January 2024. Before ETFs, crypto’s macro sensitivity operated primarily through sentiment and speculative positioning. After ETFs, institutional capital flows create a direct mechanical link between macro expectations and Bitcoin’s spot price.
Bitcoin’s 52-week correlation with the US dollar index measured approximately negative 0.85 through the first half of 2026, IG reported, citing CoinDesk data.
This near inverse relationship means that events strengthening the dollar, such as hawkish FOMC statements or above consensus CPI prints, tend to produce concurrent Bitcoin declines. The correlation intensified after ETF approval because institutional investors now treat Bitcoin as part of a broader risk asset allocation framework.
ETF flow data illustrates the mechanism in action. June 2026 saw approximately $4.5 billion in cumulative outflows from spot Bitcoin ETFs as the FOMC’s hawkish pivot repriced rate expectations.
That streak broke on July 3 when a weak nonfarm payrolls report of 57,000 jobs against 110,000 expected triggered a $221.7 million single-day inflow. Bitcoin rallied from approximately $57,750 to $62,000 in under 48 hours following that data release, demonstrating how macro disappointments can reverse institutional positioning.
The Fear and Greed Index fell to 10 in late June 2026, when Bitcoin traded near $58,411, according to IG. The realized profit-to-loss ratio also touched 2022 lows during the same period. These sentiment extremes create conditions where a single positive macro data point can trigger outsized reversals as short sellers cover positions and sidelined capital re-enters.
Building a Calendar-Based Framework for Crypto Trading
The data supports a structured approach to positioning around macro events. The FOMC schedule provides eight fixed dates per year, with the remaining 2026 meetings on October 28 and December 9.
Each announcement arrives at 2:00 PM Eastern Time, followed by the Chair’s press conference at 2:30 PM. Meetings with the dot plot carry additional significance because they update the market’s baseline expectations for the rate path.
CPI releases follow a monthly schedule, typically landing on the second or third Tuesday of the month at 8:30 AM Eastern Time. The Block Scholes research indicates the impact window is concentrated in the first hour, which means traders using daily or swing timeframes can either reduce exposure before the release or position for the expected reaction based on consensus deviation.
US headline inflation rose from 2.4% in January 2026 to above 4% by May, driven by an energy supply shock linked to geopolitical tensions.
Nonfarm payrolls, released on the first Friday of each month, showed significant Bitcoin sensitivity in mid 2024 when the R squared reached approximately 60% in June of that year, coinciding with unemployment peaking at 4.3%.
That sensitivity has since faded to near zero in 2026, making payrolls a lower priority event for crypto traders compared to CPI and FOMC decisions. However, the July 3 episode demonstrated that extreme payroll misses can still produce sharp moves.
Additional events worth monitoring include quarterly GDP releases, the Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcements, and geopolitical developments that affect energy prices and inflation expectations.
Fed Governor Lisa Cook stated she is prepared to act if inflation does not soon slow, while Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan argued that modestly higher rates would better balance the dual mandate. These public statements between scheduled meetings can shift rate expectations and produce intraday crypto volatility.
What Comes Next?
The October 28, 2026 FOMC meeting is the next scheduled decision point, with markets pricing the probability of a hold against a second consecutive hike. The October CPI report, due in mid-November, will provide the next inflation data point after US headline inflation peaked above 4% in mid-2026.
Bitcoin’s renewed sensitivity to CPI surprises, documented by Block Scholes at an R-squared near 22% on a rolling basis, means each release carries measurable positioning risk for traders holding leveraged crypto exposure.
FAQs
How do FOMC meetings affect Bitcoin prices?
Bitcoin rallied after only one of eight FOMC meetings in 2025, according to CoinGecko, suggesting a sell-the-news pattern in which expectations were priced in before announcements. The Fed cut rates three times that year, by a total of 75 basis points.
What is the FOMC meeting schedule for 2026?
The FOMC meets eight times in 2026, with the remaining meetings on October 28 and December 9, each announcing decisions at 2:00 PM Eastern.

articles.title: Fed rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey - CNBC
articles.summary: Fed rate hikes are coming, but not this week: CNBC survey  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve has considerable work to do. But it’s not going to do it in October.
That’s the key finding in CNBC’s latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, which showed that 93% expect a pause at the Fed meeting taking place this week and 76% anticipate a rate hike at its next meeting in December. And more than half say the Fed will hike next year by an average of about two rate hikes.
“Their hesitancy to raise rates is unfathomable after an extended period of monetary and fiscal generosity, with nominal GDP running 6-8%, and when the leading indicators of inflation are uniformly warm to hot,″ said Richard Bernstein, global head of macro investing at Janus Henderson Investors.
A plurality of 40% say the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem. That compares with 27% who say the Fed does not need to slow the economy and 23% who say the Fed has to slow the economy only somewhat.
The survey, which CNBC conducts before every Fed meeting, found that 70% see the inflation problem as broader than just the rising price of energy. The U.S. crude oil benchmark is forecast to be at $88 a barrel six months from now, up from $82 in the September survey, but below the current level of $101.
Asked what the Fed should do at the current meeting, 30% said it should hike rates now. At least two Fed voters are expected by survey respondents to dissent from the decision to keep rates unchanged.
“The aggregate demand data (probably north of 7%...) and the inflation data point to the strong need to hike rates,″ wrote John Ryding, chief economic advisor for Brean Capital, LLC.
Not all agree. Some are concerned with a weakening economy.
“The Iran War is intensifying, real wages are falling, interest rates are rising, and the AI-fueled stock market looks shaky,” wrote Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “Inflation is high, but there’s little sign it is becoming entrenched. This isn’t the time for more Fed rate hikes.
Amid numerous shocks and challenges — including high inflation, expected Fed rate hikes and a continuation of high oil prices — respondents still see economic growth remaining above potential, or the level of growth that doesn’t lead to inflation or deflation. Forecasts of GDP for this year rose to 2.4%. They ticked down slightly since the last survey but still hover above potential at 2.2% for 2027. Growth in 2025 came in at 2.05%.
Respondents in aggregate put the risk of the U.S. entering a recession in the next year at 26%, down from 29% in the last survey.
The outlook for the S&P 500 stayed stable for this year at around 7,600 but moved down to 8,033 for next year from 8,274 in the prior survey. The index closed at 7,676 Monday.
Unemployment is forecast to remain steady at 4.2% through the remainder of the year but rise to 4.4% in 2027. The Consumer Price Index is seen ticking down to 3.6% from the current pace of 3.7% in September but fall meaningfully next year to 2.6%.
The biggest risks: a continuation of the Iran war and the bursting of the artificial-intelligence bubble.
“Fed Chair Warsh, in all of his future conversations with President Trump, need to repeat this mantra: the quickest way to bring down inflation in the U.S. is to end tariffs and end the war in Iran,” said Rob Morgan, senior vice president and market strategist at MOSAIC.
When it comes to high bond yields, respondents in almost equal percentages say the culprits are high inflation, high growth, large amounts of debt issuance and expectations for a higher Fed funds rate. Asked specifically about which supply was the bigger source of the problem, 50% said government debt and 13% said debt to fund the AI buildout. But a third said both had contributed equally to the rise in yields.
On average, respondents see the 10-year yield remaining above 5% this year and dropping slightly to 4.8% in 2027
“With stubborn inflation amid energy and trade pressures… benchmark U.S. Treasury bond yields above 5% represent a new band, not an anomaly,” wrote Subodh Kumar, president, Subodh Kumar & Associates.
The congressional election is also seen as a market risk: 63% say there is some market risk from legal challenges that could extend uncertainty over which party controls congress.
“The potential for prolonged election uncertainty is one of the largest near-term risks to the markets, and we all know how much markets hate uncertainty,” said John Donaldson, director of fixed income at Haverford Trust Co.
More than half of respondents say the most likely outcome of next week’s congressional election is Democratic control of both houses, up from 29% in the last survey. Forty percent believe the Democrats will end up with control of the House but not the Senate.
Most see little change coming to individual or corporate taxes as a result of the election, but 41% expect higher deficits. However, that worry is not linked to which party is expected to control Congress. Individual growth forecasts also differed little based on which party the respondents thought would control Congress.

Brent crude futures climbed $1.48, or 1.3 percent, to $115.36 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate rose $1.22, or 1.22 percent, to $101.12 a barrel.
The US Federal Reserve's policy decision later on Wednesday will be a key event for global financial markets. The central bank is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, with investors focusing on policymakers' guidance regarding the future trajectory of borrowing costs. Inflation remains a central concern for the Fed, particularly as the prolonged Middle East conflict and elevated energy prices threaten to keep price pressures high.
Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, said Indian equities are likely to remain cautious ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy decision, with investors also tracking global market movements and energy prices. He expects sentiment to remain guarded ahead of the announcement, despite the recovery in global equity markets.
According to Ponmudi, the near-term direction of Indian equities will depend largely on the Fed's policy signals, movements in crude oil prices and foreign portfolio investor flows. He also expects volatility to persist as investors assess the implications of monetary policy developments and geopolitical uncertainty.

articles.full_text:
EUR/USD (1.1144) Nears Its 52-Week Low as French Debt Stress Meets a Hawkish Fed — Break of 1.1113 Opens 1.1000
Key Points
- EUR/USD fell 0.26% to 1.1144 on Tuesday, its fifth straight loss, sitting 22 pips above the 1.1113 low.
- France’s 10-year spread over Germany hit 178 basis points on October 22, the widest level since 2011.
- The Fed’s 3.75%-4.00% range sits 125 to 150 basis points above the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate.
EUR/USD traded at 1.1144 at 16:02 UTC on Tuesday, down 0.26% from Monday’s close at 1.1174, as the euro extended its losing run to a fifth straight session. The pair’s daily range ran from 1.1181 in the Asian session to a low of 1.1135 in the New York morning, a 46-pip band that pushed the euro to within 22 pips of its 52-week low at 1.1113. Nothing about the tape suggests buyers are preparing a defense: every attempt to hold 1.1175 to 1.1190 during the European session failed, and the pair broke lower after the U.S. data at 12:30 UTC.
The broader picture is bleak for the single currency. EUR/USD is down 5.12% year to date and 4.18% over the past 12 months, and it sits 7.8% below its 52-week high of 1.2083. The pair averaged 1.1610 from January through September, which means current spot is 466 pips below its own 2026 average. October has been a one-way slide: the month’s high came at 1.1267, the weekly range last week ran from 1.1175 to 1.1255, and the pair closed Friday at 1.1202 after France’s 10-year borrowing premium over Germany hit its widest since the 2011 sovereign debt crisis.
The euro is losing across the board, not just against the dollar. On Tuesday it fell 0.54% against the Australian dollar, 0.60% against the New Zealand dollar, 0.15% against the Swiss franc and 0.09% against both sterling and the yen. A currency that underperforms every major counterpart at once is pricing a domestic problem, and in this case the problem has a name: France.
The dollar side of the trade is adding weight. The U.S. Dollar Index traded at 102.20 on Tuesday, near a two-week high, after dropping to 101.45 last week, its lowest since October 1. Durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September, consumer confidence jumped to 91.7, and the U.S. economy keeps outperforming Europe on every high-frequency measure.
This is a week with two central bank decisions back to back. The Federal Reserve announces Wednesday at 18:00 UTC, with a hold at 3.75%-4.00% priced above 90% and a December hike close to fully priced. The European Central Bank follows Thursday at 13:15 UTC, with a hold at a 2.50% deposit rate expected by every major forecaster. The thesis for this article is direct: the policy gap between a Fed still hiking toward 4.25% and an ECB on pause at 2.50%, combined with a French risk premium at 2011 levels, leaves EUR/USD with one path of least resistance, and that path runs through 1.1113 toward 1.1000.
How Tuesday’s Session Built: Asia Bounce, Europe Fade, U.S. Data Break
The session followed a pattern that has repeated all week. EUR/USD opened the Asian session near 1.1174 and briefly tested 1.1181, its high of the day, as Asian equity markets rallied on AI optimism and risk appetite lifted commodity currencies. That move ran out of buyers before the European open.
European trading delivered the first leg lower. By 07:00 UTC, the pair had slipped to 1.1166, down 0.39% from Monday’s late close, and it spent the next three hours oscillating between 1.1160 and 1.1180. French government bond yields stayed elevated after a turbulent week, and the CAC 40 underperformed regional indices, keeping a political risk premium attached to every euro bid. Without fresh eurozone data, traders held positions flat into the U.S. session rather than buying the dip.
The break came at 12:30 UTC. The U.S. Census Bureau’s advance durable goods report showed new orders up 1.8% in September to $345.4 billion, the largest monthly gain in five months, after a 0.1% rise in August. The headline came in slightly below the 2.0% forecast, but the details were firm. Orders excluding transportation rose 0.5% to $225.6 billion, and nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft, the cleanest proxy for business investment, rose 0.5% to $88.04 billion. Orders for computers and related equipment jumped 3.9% on the month and are up 20.3% year to date on AI investment. Nondefense aircraft orders climbed 28.4%.
The dollar caught a bid immediately, and EUR/USD slipped through 1.1175 to 1.1190 support. At 14:00 UTC, the Conference Board’s consumer confidence index printed 91.7 against an 81.0 forecast, its highest since June. That second upside surprise extended the dollar’s gains, and EUR/USD dropped to 1.1135, its low of the day.
By 15:50 UTC, the pair was trading at 1.1145, down 0.26%, and by 16:02 UTC at 1.1144. The U.S. session confirmed what Europe had hinted at: no buyer was willing to step in front of a strengthening dollar two days before back-to-back central bank decisions.
The intraday structure matters for the forecast. The pair failed at 1.1181 in Asia, failed again at 1.1180 in Europe, and broke support on U.S. data. That is a sequence of lower highs into a falling floor, and it has repeated on four of the last five sessions.
The Fed Sits at 3.75%-4.00% and Points to 4.25% in December
The dollar side of EUR/USD is anchored by a Fed that is still in tightening mode. The FOMC raised its target range by 25 basis points in September to 3.75%-4.00%, and it opened its two-day meeting Tuesday with fed funds futures pricing a hold at well above 90% probability. The decision lands Wednesday at 18:00 UTC, with Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference at 18:30 UTC. There is no Summary of Economic Projections at this meeting, so the statement language and Warsh’s answers will carry the full weight.
The market is already looking past October. A December hike to 4.00%-4.25% is close to fully priced, and every economist in one widely followed survey expects it. Markets price no rate cuts for 2026 and see the first easing no earlier than spring 2027. For the euro, that means the dollar’s yield advantage is not peaking; it is still widening.
The U.S. data flow gives Warsh no reason to soften. September CPI rose 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% forecast, with core CPI at 2.6%. The Fed’s preferred PCE gauge rose 3.4% in August. Initial jobless claims dropped to 194,000 in the week ended October 17, the lowest since late July. The U.S. flash composite PMI for October held near a five-year high, with selling prices rising at the sharpest rate since August 2022. Durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September, and consumer confidence jumped 7.5 points to 91.7.
The energy shock from the U.S.-Iran war drives the inflation story. Brent crude traded below $114 on Tuesday after settling at $116.72 on Monday, and the national average gasoline price stood at $4.27 a gallon against $3.05 a year ago. Higher oil prices hit Europe harder than the U.S. as a net energy importer, but they push U.S. inflation higher too, and the Fed has answered with hikes rather than patience.
The scenarios for EUR/USD are clear. A hold with neutral language that stresses data dependence would ease pressure on the euro and could trigger a short-covering bounce toward 1.1190 to 1.1215. A hold with explicit guidance toward December would extend the dollar’s gains and push the pair through 1.1113. A surprise hike, priced at under 10%, would send EUR/USD toward 1.1050 within hours.
The bias in the room is hawkish. Warsh has spent the fall warning that inflation needs further action, and the data since the September hike has validated that stance. EUR/USD bulls should not expect a dovish offset from Washington on Wednesday.
The ECB Holds at 2.50% and Leaves December Open
Thursday’s ECB decision is the second leg of the week, and it is set up to disappoint euro bulls. The Governing Council meets in Frankfurt on October 28 and 29 and announces its decision at 13:15 UTC Thursday, with President Christine Lagarde’s press conference at 13:45 UTC. Every major research house expects a hold, with the deposit rate staying at 2.50% and the main refinancing rate at 2.65%. Swaps price almost no chance of a move. There are no new staff projections at this meeting.
The ECB has tightened twice since June, lifting the deposit rate from 2.00% to 2.50% in 25-basis-point steps in June and September. The September hike was the bank’s first since 2023, delivered after eurozone inflation hit 3.3% in August with energy inflation at 14.3%. Lagarde said at the time that the conflict in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine would keep headline inflation well above target for an extended period, and she refused to pre-commit to a rate path.
Inflation has since moved higher. Euro-area inflation rose to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% to 3.3% in August and 2.2% a year earlier, with energy contributing 1.71 percentage points. Core inflation rose to 2.5%. On the surface, that argues for another hike. But Governing Council members have talked in a softer tone than Lagarde since September, pointing to demand destruction and the absence of second-round effects. Energy costs have not yet fed into wages or services prices in a meaningful way, and firms’ selling-price expectations in services and retail have declined.
That shift explains why forecasters who expected an October hike dropped the call. The ECB now wants to wait for December, when it gets fresh projections and a longer run of data. Markets price roughly 20 basis points of tightening for December, and some forecasters see a terminal deposit rate of 3.00%, which would require two more quarter-point moves.
The French bond market is the wild card. Lagarde is expected to face pointed questions on whether the ECB stands ready to contain contagion from France, and on her own future amid speculation about an early departure before her mandate expires in October 2027. Fed Rate Decision: Weakest Job Growth Before Any of 52 Fed Hikes Since 1994
The Fed decides Wednesday with its rate at 3.75% to 4%, after most officials signaled in September that another hike was likely this year, and inflation has since risen to 3.7%. Hiring points the other way, since on today’s revised data job growth before September’s hike was the weakest before any of the Fed’s 52 increases since 1994.
What we calculated
- Job growth before the September hike, 0.34%: total nonfarm payroll growth over the 12 months to August 2026 on today’s revised data, against at least 1.15% before each of the Fed’s 51 earlier increases since February 1994.
- Jobs added in the year before the hike, 543,000: the same 12-month change in jobs, against 1.5 million before the slowest earlier case, June 2004.
- PCE inflation below the Fed’s estimates, by 0.2 point on both measures: BEA published August inflation of 3.4% and core inflation of 3.0%, against the September estimates of 3.6% and 3.2%.
- Rate cushion over inflation, about 0.2 point: the range midpoint (3.875%) minus September CPI inflation of 3.7%; against August core PCE it is about 0.9 point.
- Cushion in July 2023, about 2 points on CPI and 1.1 on core PCE: the midpoint then (5.375%) minus each 12-month rate; since then the midpoint fell 1.5 points and CPI inflation rose about 0.4 point.
What is the current Fed interest rate before the Fed meeting?
The Fed’s target for its benchmark rate is a range of 3.75% to 4%. It got there on September 16, when the Fed raised rates for the first time since July 2023.
The September move was a quarter point, approved 12 to 0, according to the Fed’s September 16 statement. It put the federal funds rate back where it stood after the October 2025 cut, as the Fed’s target range history on FRED shows.
The year did not start that way. In January two officials voted for a cut, and by July three voted to raise rates while the rest held. Kevin Warsh chaired his first meeting in June, and the September hike was the first rate change under him.
Show the data
| Date | Event | 
|---|---|
| 2026-01-28 | Hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, vote 10-2. | 
| 2026-03-18 | Hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, vote 11-1. | 
| 2026-04-29 | Hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, vote 8-4. | 
| 2026-06-17 | Hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, vote 12-0. First meeting under Chairman Warsh. | 
| 2026-07-29 | Hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, vote 9-3. Three preferred a hike. | 
| 2026-09-16 | Raise to 3.75%-4.00%, vote 12-0. | 
| 2026-10-28 | Decision due at 2:00 p.m. ET. | 
Wednesday’s statement is due at 2:00 p.m. ET and the press conference at 2:30 p.m., both on the Fed’s October calendar. This meeting brings no new set of officials’ projections; the meeting calendar attaches those to the December 8-9 meeting. We do not predict Wednesday’s decision here. What follows is what the Fed said and what the data since then show.
What did the Fed say after its September rate hike?
The Fed’s statement said inflation “remains elevated,” and the minutes say most officials expected one more increase before the end of 2026. None of the 18 officials projected a lower rate this year.
The September statement was three short paragraphs, ending with “The Committee will deliver price stability.” In our reading, that line tells readers the Fed is ready to raise again if inflation does not come down. The minutes released October 7 said it in plain terms: “most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end.” The next sentence adds that participants “approached each meeting with an open mind,” which leaves them room to wait.
The officials’ own projections say the same thing in numbers. In the September projections, 12 of the 18 put the rate one quarter point higher by the end of 2026. Four put it two steps higher and two left it where it is.
Show the data
| Category | Value | 
|---|---|
| A cut | 0 | 
| No change | 2 | 
| One more hike | 12 | 
| Two more hikes | 4 | 
The two meetings left in 2026 are this one and December’s. The projections only show where each official expects the rate to end the year, so they do not say which meeting. Warsh would not say either. “My business is to not give forward guidance,” he told reporters on September 16, according to the press conference transcript. He added that “Trends matter. Data points are noisy,” which in our reading means no single report since September is meant to settle the timing on its own.
Since then, officials have spoken about what comes next. Governor Christopher Waller said on October 8 that further increases “do not need to come at consecutive meetings,” in a speech in Istanbul. Governor Michael Barr said on September 29 that “further policy adjustments are likely to be needed” to bring inflation down in time, in a speech in Detroit. In our reading, that points to more increases. Our coverage of the September hike and the minutes has the full detail.
How does inflation compare with the Fed’s interest rate?
Inflation is above the Fed’s 2% goal on every measure. September’s consumer price reading of 3.7% sits just under the middle of the Fed’s range. August PCE inflation, the measure used for the Fed’s goal, came in below its September estimate.
The September consumer price index rose 3.7% over the year, up from 3.4% in August. The Bureau of Labor Statistics said gasoline accounted for over half of the monthly increase.
Because the Fed sets a range, we compare inflation with its midpoint, 3.875%. Against September’s CPI the gap is about 0.2 point. Against core PCE inflation it is about 0.9 point; core PCE is the Commerce Department gauge that leaves out food and energy. Neither gap is a Fed threshold; each only describes where the rate sits.
The CPI gap was about 2 points when the last hiking cycle ended in July 2023. Most of the narrowing came from the Fed’s cuts since then, more than from higher inflation, and on core PCE the change is much smaller.
Show the data

What worries officials is less the gap than how long inflation lasts. The minutes say many of them saw that the longer energy prices stayed high, “the greater the risk that cost increases in certain sectors could lead to broader price pressures.” Several also called the rate “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive,” meaning it does little to hold back spending.
The other side of the inflation story is the Fed’s own target measure. At the September 16 press conference Warsh said August PCE inflation “likely was around 3.6 percent,” with core about 3.2%. Those were the staff’s estimates under the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s new method, an annual update that changed how some prices, such as software and portfolio management fees, are measured.
BEA then published August PCE inflation at 3.4% and core PCE at 3.0%, about 0.2 point below those estimates. Prices further up the supply chain ran hotter, as the producer price index and our PPI breakdown show.
Show the data
| Inflation measure | Latest 12-month rate | Range midpoint minus inflation | 
|---|---|---|
| CPI, all items (September) | 3.7% | about 0.2 point | 
| CPI excluding food and energy (September) | 2.6% | about 1.3 points | 
| PCE price index (August) | 3.4% | about 0.5 point | 
| PCE excluding food and energy (August) | 3.0% | about 0.9 point | 
| Producer prices, final demand (September) | 6.3% | not comparable | 
Since July 2023 the range midpoint fell 1.5 points, from 5.375% to 3.875%, while 12-month CPI inflation rose about 0.4 point. The core PCE gap went from about 1.1 points to 0.9. On the old method the September minutes put August PCE inflation at 3.8% and core at 3.4%.
Source: BLS CPI and PPI for September 2026; BEA PCE for August 2026, published September 30; FRED CPIAUCSL and PCEPILFE for July 2023; Fed target range 3.75% to 4%, midpoint 3.875%; differences are our calculation.
How weak was hiring before the September Fed hike?
On today’s revised data, job growth in the year before September’s hike was the weakest before any Fed rate increase since 1994. In September itself, employers added only 29,000 jobs.
The September jobs report put unemployment at 4.2%, and it cut July and August by a combined 60,000 jobs. The minutes show the rate was 4.1% in July and August.
We lined up every Fed increase since February 1994, when the Fed first announced a rate increase on the day it made it. For each, we took 12-month payroll growth before the decision from today’s revis

The benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose 1.5 basis points to 2.795%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
According to Reuters, Japanese and US equities rallied sharply as optimism returned to the AI sector ahead of quarterly results from major technology companies, including Alphabet and Microsoft. The gains came as investors positioned themselves ahead of the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcement on Wednesday.
