US Treasury yields declined overnight, reflecting investor positioning ahead of the Fed's decision.
In Japan, attention is focused on the Bank of Japan's October 29-30 policy meeting. The central bank is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged after raising its policy rate to 1.25% in September. However, many market participants anticipate another increase to 1.5% in December, while some see January as an alternative timeline.
Read more: Global Market: South Korean shares jump over 4% as AI chip rally lifts Samsung, SK Hynix
In a separate book, former BOJ Deputy Governor Masazumi Wakatabe argued that the central bank would face questions if it raised rates while real economic growth remained negative and inflation was driven largely by rising costs, Reuters reported.
Across the JGB yield curve, the 20-year yield rose 1 basis point to 3.595%, while the 30-year yield remained unchanged at 3.805%.
The two-year JGB yield, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for BOJ policy rates, increased for a second consecutive session, rising 1 basis point to 1.885%. The five-year yield climbed 1.5 basis points to 2.240%.
Investors are expected to closely monitor this week's central bank decisions and corporate earnings for clues about the outlook for interest rates, inflation and risk appetite. The BOJ's guidance on the timing of further rate increases will remain a key factor for Japanese government bonds in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Gold climbs above $4,050 as Wall Street rallies ahead of Fed decision - Kitco PM Report - Kitco
articles.summary: Gold climbs above $4,050 as Wall Street rallies ahead of Fed decision - Kitco PM Report  KitcoGold Clings to Gains Above $4,000 as Markets Await Fed  WSJGold rises ahead of Fed decision as decline in oil offsets stronger dollar By Investing.com  Investing.com IndiaGold prices have plunged: Should you buy yellow metal this Diwali?  The Times of IndiaGold edges higher ahead of Fed policy decision  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were higher in late U.S. trading Tuesday, recovering from early-session losses as declining crude oil prices eased inflation concerns and supported renewed buying interest in precious metals ahead of Wednesday's Federal Reserve monetary policy decision. Diplomatic efforts involving Iran and several regional powers helped reduce some of the immediate geopolitical risk premium in energy markets, while stronger U.S. economic data and a firmer dollar limited bullion's advance. At the latest verified afternoon price reading, spot gold was trading near $4,058.20 an ounce, up $42.00, or 1.05%, while spot silver was trading near $54.200, up $0.353, or 0.66%, on the session.
Tuesday's U.S. economic reports pointed to resilient consumer demand and business investment despite elevated borrowing costs. September durable goods orders rose 1.8%, following a modest increase in August, supported by stronger transportation equipment demand. Orders excluding transportation increased 0.5%, while nondefense capital goods orders excluding aircraft, a closely watched measure of business investment, also advanced 0.5%. October consumer confidence increased sharply to 91.7 from an upwardly revised 84.2 in September, exceeding market expectations. The present situation index climbed to 120.4, while the expectations index improved to 72.6, partially reversing three consecutive monthly declines. September new-home sales slipped to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 units from a revised 680,000 in August, although the result exceeded expectations of approximately 650,000. The Richmond Fed manufacturing index remained at minus 2 in October, indicating continued modest contraction in regional factory activity.
Market positioning remains focused on an October Federal Reserve pause, followed by the possibility of additional tightening before year-end. September consumer inflation increased 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while producer prices rose 1.3% and 6.3%, respectively. Friday's preliminary October business activity surveys showed continued expansion and accelerating selling-price inflation, while consumer inflation expectations remained elevated. Fed funds futures indicated approximately a 90.6% probability that the central bank would leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% when its Oct. 27-28 meeting concludes Wednesday. However, expectations for another increase in December remain substantial, with recent market positioning indicating approximately a 73% probability of additional tightening by year-end. Treasury yields were little changed to slightly higher Tuesday, with the benchmark 10-year yield trading near 4.99%. The stronger dollar limited some of the benefit to gold from falling energy prices, although reduced oil-driven inflation concerns helped the metal recover from earlier losses.
The Federal Reserve's two-day monetary policy meeting began Tuesday, with the interest rate decision scheduled for Wednesday at 2 p.m. EDT, followed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT. Market attention will focus on whether policymakers signal that the expected October pause represents a temporary interruption or a more durable end to the tightening cycle. Thursday brings the advance third-quarter gross domestic product estimate, September personal consumption expenditures inflation figures and weekly initial jobless claims, all scheduled for 8:30 a.m. EDT. The European Central Bank is also scheduled to announce its policy decision Thursday, while the Bank of Japan meets later in the week. Softer inflation readings or less restrictive Fed guidance could reduce December rate hike expectations and support gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar. Conversely, stronger economic activity, persistent inflation and hawkish policy guidance would reinforce expectations for additional tightening and maintain pressure on non-yielding bullion.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a significant source of uncertainty Tuesday, although renewed diplomatic activity helped ease immediate concerns about another major escalation. Iranian security officials met senior government leaders following talks in Tehran with representatives from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan aimed at restoring regional stability and reducing the threat of renewed hostilities. The participating countries agreed to continue discussions on regional peace and security, although no agreement between Washington and Tehran has been confirmed. Iran continues to insist on its conditions for ending the conflict, while renewed Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and the possibility of additional U.S.-Israeli military operations remain obstacles to a lasting settlement. Maritime security risks and uncertainty about the restoration of normal commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continue to support an elevated geopolitical premium in energy prices.
Crude oil prices declined as traders assessed the prospect of renewed diplomatic negotiations against continuing threats to Gulf energy infrastructure and commercial shipping. Brent crude retreated toward $114.00 a barrel, while WTI moved closer to $100.00, reversing part of the previous week's sharp advance. For gold, the decline in energy prices reduced immediate concerns about oil-driven inflation and additional Fed tightening, allowing bullion to recover despite a stronger dollar. The absence of a confirmed settlement, however, leaves the risk of renewed disruptions to Middle Eastern petroleum supplies. Silver also benefited from improving precious metals sentiment, although its industrial exposure leaves it vulnerable to any renewed deterioration in economic activity or further increases in borrowing costs.
North American equity markets finished higher Tuesday as technology and semiconductor shares led a recovery ahead of major corporate earnings and the Federal Reserve's policy announcement. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 15.99 points, or 0.03%, to close at 52,377.57, while the S&P 500 gained 45.83 points, or 0.60%, to finish at 7,722.60. The Nasdaq Composite advanced 308.43 points, or 1.18%, to close at 26,477.81, outperforming as renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence-related stocks supported the broader technology sector. Semiconductor shares benefited from improving sentiment surrounding the prospective Anthropic public offering, while investors continued to assess the financing requirements and profitability of major artificial intelligence investments. Meta Platforms declined approximately 1.6% amid concerns about its expanded equity fundraising, while Boeing fell 10.7% following a larger-than-expected quarterly loss. United Parcel Service gained 5.8% after raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also advanced, supported by stronger base metals, financial and selected technology shares, although declining crude oil prices weighed on energy producers.
European equity markets closed mostly higher Tuesday as stronger corporate earnings and declining crude oil prices helped major benchmarks recover from early losses. The pan-European Stoxx 600 advanced 0.47% to 643.68, reversing an intraday decline of approximately 0.4%. Germany's DAX gained approximately 0.8%, while France's CAC 40 rose around 0.6%. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 underperformed, falling approximately 0.7% as disappointing quarterly results from HSBC pressured banking shares. Austrian circuit board manufacturer AT&S and Dutch semiconductor equipment supplier Besi were among the strongest performers, advancing 11.5% and 11.4%, respectively. Investors also remained focused on France's fiscal uncertainty and Thursday's European Central Bank decision, with policymakers widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged while assessing persistent energy-related inflation risks.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices lower and trading near $100.00 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $114.00. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 4.99% area. The U.S. dollar index was firmer near 102.23 during the session, reflecting stronger economic data and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive despite Wednesday's anticipated pause. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Technically, spot gold bulls' next upside price objective is to push prices back above the $4,079.00 to $4,100.00 resistance zone, with a sustained move targeting $4,160.00 and then $4,180.00. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is a break below $4,015.00, with deeper downside targets at $3,975.00 and then $3,959.00. First resistance is seen at $4,079.00 and then at $4,100.00. First support is seen at $4,039.00 and then at $4,015.00.

The next downside price objective for the bears is a break below $53.000, with deeper downside targets at $52.410 and then $51.390. First resistance is seen at $54.460 and then at $55.770. articles.title: Oil Markets Brace for a New Iran Escalation After U.S. Midterms - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Oil Markets Brace for a New Iran Escalation After U.S. Midterms  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comOil prices rise after attack on Saudi Arabian refinery reignites supply concerns  ReutersOil Prices Climb as Houthi Attacks Reignite Saudi Supply Fears  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comOil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy  WSJOil price today: Brent crude holds firm at $115 per barrel, WTI trades at $100  The Ti...
articles.full_text:
Brent holds near $115 as Iran war tensions and escalating Saudi-Houthi hostilities keep oil markets on edge ahead of U.S. midterms.
Hormuz Becomes Even More Dangerous — and More Expensive
- October has seen the most acute escalation in maritime attacks since the US-Iran war started eight months ago, with already more than 30 incidents recorded in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways, up from 14 in September.
- The most recent addition to the list of maritime targets is a crude tanker in Iraq’s exclusive economic zone, signaling that it is not only tankers seeking to surreptitiously transit the Hormuz that get targeted by Iran.
- VLCCs, the largest crude tankers available, account for 28% of all drone and missile attacks in the Persian Gulf, with the 32 impacted ships representing almost 4% of the global VLCC fleet.
- Freight rates from the Gulf remain elevated with a Saudi Arabia-China voyage still costing around $33 per barrel, whilst regional demurrage rates have been rising since mid-August to their current level of $1,000,000/day.
- UKMTO, a provider of maritime security alerts, recently admitted that it is becoming increasingly more difficult to report on strikes as transiting ships prefer to sail unnoticed and charterers are wary of pushing freight rates even higher.
Market Movers
- US gas producer EQT (NYSE:EQT) has agreed to buy Range Resources (NYSE:RRC) in a $13 billion all-stock deal to create the largest US gas company, with the combined Appalachian-focused company having a net output of more than 9 bcf/d.
- US energy firm Ovintiv (NYSE:OVV) will acquire Canada’s Logan Energy in an all-cash deal valued at $0.9 billion, adding around 20,000 boe/d of production and 266,000 net acres across the Montney shale play.
- UK oil major BP (NYSE:BP) has started the second phase of exploration in Venezuela’s offshore Loran gas field, using the research and survey vessel Fugro Brasilis to perform final seabed studies.
- US oil giant ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) reported a commercial discovery with its Rockhead-1 exploration well offshore Guyana, its first drilling success since the 2024 Hatchetfish find with a resource estimate of 500-600 million barrels.
- Italian oil major ENI (BIT:ENI) has launched the construction of its 3 TCf Cronos project offshore Cyprus, aiming for first gas in the first half of 2028, to be exported via Egypt’s Damietta LNG terminal. 
Tuesday, October 27, 2026
The oil markets are counting down the days until the November 3 midterm elections in the US, with expectations of impending hostilities rising into next month. Last-minute efforts to negotiate some form of de-escalation are ongoing, with both Qatar and Pakistan seeking to mediate between the Trump administration and Tehran, temporarily capping the upside for ICE Brent at $115 per barrel. Simultaneously to Hormuz tensions, the Saudi-Houthi conflict appears to be gaining self-sustaining momentum.
OPEC+ Holds the Fort on Supply Hikes. OPEC+ is expected to hold December output targets steady at its Sunday's meeting, with seven core members focusing on 2027 production quotas instead after they’ve completed the roll-back of 1.65 million b/d voluntary cuts, disrupted by the Hormuz crisis.
US Moves China Shipping Fees into 2027. The US is considering extending its truce with China on port charges for Chinese-linked ships by two months to January 9, preserving a suspension of tit-for-tat fees that previously imposed millions of dollars per port call and raised freight costs.
Houthis Hit Saudi Arabia’s Largest Refinery. Yemen's Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike hit Saudi Arabia's 550,000 b/d Ras Tanura refinery, causing a fire and disrupting operations at the Middle Eastern kingdom’s largest plant, with an earlier March attack shutting it for three months.
Refining Boom Derails Galp–Moeve Merger. Portugal’s Galp and Spain’s Moeve have abandoned plans for a potential downstream merger that would’ve combined 700,000 b/d of refining capacity and 3,500 service stations, claiming that 2026 bumper profits made it harder to agree M&A terms.
Brussels Builds a European Wall Against China. The European Union may introduce quotas or tariffs on Chinese chemicals, furniture and machinery from early 2027, seeking to replicate its recent import caps on hybrid vehicles as it struggles to narrow its €360 billion trade deficit.
Singapore Launches First LNG Term Tender. Singapore’s state gas buyer GasCo launched its first ever LNG term supply tender after neighbouring Indonesia had announced it would slash pipeline gas exports by 15% to 31 MMCf/d, just as the government plans to add 5 new gas-powered plants.
East Timor Buys Out Its Untapped Offshore Gem. Australia’s major Woodside (ASX:WDS) has agreed to sell its stakes in the Greater Sunrise fields offshore East Timor for $200 million to the island nation, leaving state oil firm Timor gap as the only stakeholder of the untapped 5.3 TCf field.
Alberta Pushes for Scrapping of Tanker Ban. The province of Alberta called on the Carney government to repeal Canada's 2019 West Coast tanker ban that bars vessels carrying over 12,500 tonnes from loading at British Columbia ports, backing a proposed 250,000 b/d crude-by-rail route.
Indonesia Gives Up on Market-Based Imports. Indonesia plans to replace tender-based crude oil and refined product imports with government-to-government (G2G) and government-to-business (G2B) agreements to secure supplies, courting India and China for long-term supply deals.
Dangote Considers Third African Refinery. Nigeria’s Dangote conglomerate is considering building a third 700,000 b/d refinery in Africa, alongside the existing plant in Lekki and the upcoming Kenyan refinery in Lamu, whilst simultaneously investing into refined product pipelines in West Africa.
Malaysia Doubles Down on Coal. The Malaysia government has proposed extending the lifespan of its existing coal-fuelled power plants despite an earlier pledge to retire coal by 2044, with coal accounting for 56% of current generation as JKM prices jumped to $33 per MMBtu this week.
Iron Ore Plunges Again on China Demand Fears. Iron ore prices fell to their lowest since September 2024 as weak Chinese demand and wafer-thin margins are expected to curb Q4 steel consumption, sending the Dalian iron ore futures to ¥662 per tonne, below the $100 per tonne threshold. 
White House to Ease Methane Emission Rules. The Trump administration is planning to relax rules on methane emissions from oil and gas operations, including exemptions for wells producing up to 15 boe/d, projecting incremental output of 210 million barrels for older and depleted wells.
Bahri Orders Three New VLCCs to Expand Tanker Fleet. Saudi national shipping company Bahri has ordered three VLCCs from domestic shipbuilder International Maritime Industries for $451 million, with deliveries scheduled in 2029-30 and marking the first attempt at exclusively Saudi shipbuilding.
UK Considers Fast-Track Approvals for Tiebacks. The UK’s Burnham government is considering the fast-tracking of a small number of oil and gas tiebacks before pending legislation creates Transitional Energy Certificates that extend existing fields but preserve the country’s exploration ban.

articles.summary: Morgan Stanley declares the U.S. stock market correction is nearing its end! It maintains its year-end S&P 500 target of 8,000 points and identifies three key catalysts for a rebound.  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
As Morgan Stanley continues to maintain a bullish outlook on equities, recent market performance has precisely demonstrated the strong momentum behind the rebound in semiconductor-led technology stocks. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose by 0.44% on October 23 and further increased by 2.82% on October 26.
Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Michael Wilson, Chief U.S. Equity Strategist at Morgan Stanley, emphasized in his latest research report that the firm’s current assessment is that the internal correction in the U.S. stock market, which began in June, has entered its final tail-end phase. However, indices may still undergo one last downward probe. As the pressure from AI financing costs eases, the outlook for the midterm elections becomes clearer, and the Federal Reserve’s monetary liquidity policy clarifies, the market is expected to see a significant year-end rebound.
According to top strategists at Wall Street financial giants such as Morgan Stanley, the logic for contrarian accumulation and buying on dips is forming for global AI computing power themes and broader technology stocks, which have recently suffered heavy selling pressure. However, whether technology stocks can achieve a bottoming-out rebound and sustain an upward trend thereafter will depend on a dual verification period before year-end: the earnings disclosure season and the evolution of AI financing conditions.
Just as Morgan Stanley maintains its bullish stance on the stock market, recent market performance has precisely demonstrated the tension behind the major rebound in semiconductor-led technology stocks, alongside the fragmentation and divergence in funding conditions revealed by the corporate credit bond market.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 0.44% on October 23 and further gained 2.82% on October 26, but its closing level of 11,083.5 points remains approximately 24.27% below the closing high recorded on June 22. The Nasdaq-100 Index, known as the "bellwether for tech stocks," and the broader Nasdaq Composite Index, which includes more technology constituents, rose 1.09% and approximately 0.83% respectively on October 26. They remain about 6.25% and 5.18% below their closing highs from October 6. While a short-term strong rebound has emerged in U.S. tech stocks, the deep corrections previously accumulated in the semiconductor sector, which accounts for a significant share of tech market capitalization, are far from being fully repaired.
The credit market reveals another side of negative constraints facing the AI computing power trade theme. The yield on CoreWeave’s bonds maturing in 2031 reached 15.76% in the secondary market on October 22, indicating that investors are demanding higher risk premiums and compensation for the financing dependence and debt repayment risks associated with its AI computing infrastructure.
During intraday trading on October 26, the five-year Credit Default Swap (CDS) spread for CoreWeave (CRWV.US)—the core stock target at the heart of the "AI computing power sell-off storm" and "AI bubble burst" narratives—was approximately 1,148 basis points. Assuming a 40% recovery rate, model estimates imply a cumulative five-year default probability of approximately 62%. It is important to note that this indicator includes a credit risk premium and cannot be directly equated to the company’s actual default probability over the next five years. During the same period, the five-year CDS spreads for Meta, Alphabet, and Microsoft were approximately 121, 83, and 55 basis points, respectively, up from 98, 73, and 52 basis points on September 25. This highlights a general rise in the risk compensation required by the credit market for corporate bonds, though the pressure borne by different companies varies significantly.
The five-year CDS for Japanese investment giant SoftBank, which has nearly fully bet on AI in recent years, rose to 432 basis points on October 20, reaching a four-year high. Its three tranches of U.S. dollar bonds issued in September carried coupons of 8.625%, 9.25%, and 9.75%, respectively. These data collectively indicate that whether the surge in demand for AI computing resources can translate into revenue across the industrial chain increasingly depends on customers' ability to secure continuous funding and whether project cash returns can cover financing costs. High-rated tech giants mainly face pressures from more expensive new financing and valuation discounting, while new cloud providers relying on external capital face direct constraints from narrowing financing channels.
Morgan Stanley's Wilson outlines three core catalysts for the year-end stock market rebound
Michael Wilson of Morgan Stanley stated that the bearish and negative sentiment adjustment in the U.S. stock market, which began in June, is entering its final concluding stage. The digestion of three key uncertainties—AI-related capital issues (AIQ, AIEQ), midterm election uncertainty, and changes in Federal Reserve liquidity—is expected to help form a market bottom, laying a significant foundation for the S&P 500 Index to rebound to near-record levels of around 8,000 points by year-end.
This transition of the economic cycle to the mid-cycle phase coincides with the peaking speed of change in the breadth of earnings forecast revisions. Previously, the "rolling recessions" experienced sequentially across various industries bottomed out around last year's "Liberation Day." The cycle transition has had a significant impact on individual stocks beneath the surface of the indices. As investors shift towards large-cap stocks with higher fundamental quality, early-cycle sectors such as new cloud providers, financials, cyclical consumer themes, and automobiles have clearly underperformed.
In a report released on Monday, Wilson wrote that since the onset of this rotation, approximately 60% of the constituents of the Russell 3000 Index (IWV.US), which focuses on small- and mid-cap stocks in the U.S. equity market, have declined by more than 20%. The semiconductor sector has been hit hardest, with 96% of its stocks experiencing drawdowns exceeding 20%.
The Quality Factor (QUAL) has continued to lead during this rotation and is currently breaking out. Wilson noted that although the S&P 500 Index has shown resilience and market breadth has begun to improve, indicating that index performance and internal market conditions are "converging toward the middle" as investors gradually digest the mid-cycle rotation.
Wilson stated that the tactical downside target remains at 7,100–7,200 points, implying that the index could dip slightly below its 200-day moving average. At the time of writing, the S&P 500 Index was trading around 7,688 points, less than 2% below the historical high reached in early October.
The strategist identified three catalysts that could signal the end of the correction. First, investor concerns and panic selling related to AI capital returns, cost and availability of funding, security issues, and NIMBYism (local community opposition to nearby data center construction) are expected to come to a head over the next three to four weeks.
Second, while midterm elections typically create initial headwinds for the market, strong returns often follow in the six to twelve months after the election concludes. Historically, the S&P 500 Index has averaged a gain of approximately 17% in the twelve months following midterm elections.
Third, and most critically, Wilson believes liquidity poses the greatest risk and serves as the primary catalyst for forming the market's final bottom. Federal Reserve Chair Walsh has slowed the pace of balance sheet expansion by about half, but interest rate policy remains behind the curve given that inflation is still above target. Financial conditions have tightened significantly, reaching levels comparable to those in 2018 and approaching those seen during the active tightening period in 2022.
The Morgan Stanley Composite Sentiment Indicator is currently at neutral levels, with third-quarter earnings projected to grow by 27% year-on-year. Based on this, Wilson maintains his view that attractive buying opportunities should emerge in the coming weeks as these key uncertainties gradually resolve.
Before the S&P 500 Index can break above 8,000 points, it must clear three hurdles: whether funding can be sustained, whether the election outcome will bring clarity, and whether liquidity conditions will shift.
Based on the S&P 500 Index closing at 7,676.77 points on October 26, the 7,100–7,200 point range implies a potential downside of approximately 6.2%–7.5%, while 8,000 points represents an upside potential of about 4.2%. If the index first retreats to this support zone and then recovers to 8,000 points, the gain would amount to approximately 11.1%–12.7%. This disparity suggests that the investment opportunity identified by Wilson is highly dependent on entry positioning and whether the earnings base remains stable after risks are released.
The first hurdle is whether the market can smoothly absorb the supply of AI financing. The Morgan Stanley analyst team, led by Wilson, has long monitored capital returns, the cost and availability of funding, as well as security controversies and community opposition to data center construction. In a media podcast on October 26, he further pointed out that additional financing needs to be absorbed by the market in the coming weeks; companies with weaker credentials may continue to face widening credit spreads and declining stock prices. He also expects the semiconductor index could decline another 10%–15% by mid-November. This indicates that his bullish year-end outlook still incorporates a difficult period of risk digestion.

articles.title: Fed expected to hold rates steady this week despite hot inflation — but signal they're not done hiking - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Fed expected to hold rates steady this week despite hot inflation — but signal they're not done hiking  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections.
Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause."
Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity.
"This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike."
Inflation heated up in September, as the Consumer Price Index accelerated to 3.7% from a year earlier. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, ticked up to 2.6%, while wholesale prices jumped more than 6%, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index — is projected to top 3%.
In his last remarks before this week's policy meeting, many observers think Warsh underscored what Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams previously said: that despite hot inflation reports, they would like to take time to review the data as they consider the prospect of further rate hikes.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Warsh neither endorsed nor pushed back on his colleagues' recent signals that they'd like to wait for more data, but he noted that the world had "broadly conformed to our expectations" since the Fed's September meeting.
After raising rates for the first time in more than three years in September, minutes from that meeting read that most participants assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end.
Ken Rogoff, Harvard University professor and former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund, told Yahoo Finance he thinks the Fed will hold rates steady next week because of the proximity to the midterm elections less than a week later.
"The fundamentals call for raising the rate," Rogoff said. "If you didn't have an election, they should hike … But they are going to hold rates steady and talk about how they're probably going to increase it once or twice at least in the near future."
Blinder agrees that the midterms are part of the consideration. "When it's that close to an election there's something to be said for keeping your head down," he said, noting that while it is far from the only factor, election proximity serves as a "minus" in the mental basket for raising rates.

articles.title: Japan Inflation Accelerates: ETFs to Watch Amid Rate Uncertainty - TradingView
articles.summary: Japan Inflation Accelerates: ETFs to Watch Amid Rate Uncertainty  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Japan’s core consumer price index (CPI), which excludes fresh food but includes energy, increased 2.1% year over year in September 2026 from 1.7% in August, per Investing.com, as quoted on Yahoo Finance.
Underlying price pressures were more pronounced. The index, excluding fresh food and energy, rose 2.4% year over year compared with 1.9% in August, according to the figures provided, per Reuters.
Accelerating Inflation Strengthens the Case for Rate Hikes
The data indicates that inflationary pressures are extending beyond energy and food. Higher import costs associated with energy, rising utility charges, durable-goods prices and the pass-through of labor costs are contributing to broader price increases.
Although government subsidies have helped limit the direct impact of higher energy prices on households, businesses continue to face elevated input costs.
Japan’s exposure to imported energy adds another layer of risk. The prolonged Middle East conflict has increased oil procurement costs, while a weaker yen has made dollar-denominated imports more expensive.
If companies continue passing these costs on to consumers, inflation could remain elevated even as government subsidies soften the immediate impact.
This combination of broadening inflation and currency-driven import costs gives the BOJ a stronger reason to continue normalizing monetary policy after years of exceptionally low interest rates.
BOJ’s Current Interest Rate Policy & Expected Move
The BOJ raised its benchmark interest rate to 1.25% in September 2026, which was the highest level in 31 years, per Reuters, marking another step away from its long-standing accommodative monetary policy. The decision reflected growing concerns that inflation could remain persistently above the central bank’s 2% target.
However, the BOJ is widely expected to keep rates unchanged at its Oct. 29-Oct. 30 policy meeting, following September’s increase. Instead, the central bank may raise its inflation forecasts and signal that further monetary tightening is possible if underlying price pressures persist.
What’s Upcoming in October?
Even if the BOJ holds rates steady in October, a hawkish statement or upward inflation revision could influence bond yields, currency markets and Japanese equity valuations before the next policy decision.
The developments will be particularly important for Japanese ETFs in the coming weeks. A more hawkish outlook could influence the yen even if rates remain unchanged.
ETFs in Focus
Yen ETFs
The yen is a key transmission channel for BOJ policy. Japan's currency has faced pressure from imported energy costs and the interest rate differential between Japan and other major economies.
If the BOJ signals further rate increases while overseas interest rates remain stable or decline, the yen could receive support. This could benefit investors using yen-focused ETFs.
Invesco Currencyshares Japanese Yen Trust FXY is poised to benefit from the likely rate hike.
FXY has assets under management worth $432 million and an expense ratio of 0.40%. The fund trades at a three-month average volume of 265,000 shares.
Japanese Equity ETFs
Japanese equity ETFs could face short-term volatility if markets begin pricing in additional BOJ rate hikes. Higher borrowing costs may reduce corporate investment and consumer spending, while higher discount rates can lower the present value of future corporate earnings.
However, Japanese banks may benefit from improved lending margins if loan rates rise faster than deposit costs.
The yen presents another important consideration. If monetary tightening strengthens the currency, Japanese exporters could face pressure from a potential spike in the yen because overseas earnings translate into fewer yen, and their products may become less price-competitive abroad.
Consequently, the performance of broad Japanese equity ETFs such as iShares MSCI Japan ETF EWJ will depend on the balance between financial-sector gains, exporter headwinds and the broader effect of higher interest rates on economic growth.
EWJ is the largest and one of the oldest U.S.-listed ETFs focused exclusively on Japanese equities. It gives investors broad exposure to large and mid-cap Japanese companies.
EWJ has assets under management worth $23.75 billion and an expense ratio of 0.49%. The fund trades at a three-month average volume of 3.8 million shares.
Currency-Hedged Japan ETFs
A stronger yen could benefit dollar-based investors holding unhedged Japanese equity ETFs because their yen-denominated holdings would translate into more dollars.
Hence, currency-hedged Japan ETFs are likely to underperform unhedged Japanese equity ETFs if the BOJ hikes rates over the medium term.
WisdomTree Japan Hedged Equity Fund DXJ invests in Japanese dividend-paying companies with an emphasis on businesses that generate a substantial share of their revenue internationally.
DXJ has assets under management worth $7.16 billion and an expense ratio of 0.48%. The fund trades at a three-month average volume of about 777,000 shares.

articles.title: With the Federal Reserve's decision and tech sector earnings reports approaching, the calm in the bond market may merely be "the calm before the storm." - Moomoo
articles.summary: With the Federal Reserve's decision and tech sector earnings reports approaching, the calm in the bond market may merely be "the calm before the storm."  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
At the start of the new week, global bond markets saw a welcome temporary easing, particularly after Moody's maintained France's Aa3 credit rating, which significantly boosted sentiment in the European bond market.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields have also eased markedly after the sharp volatility earlier this month, bringing a brief respite to the market.
However, despite the apparent easing, a significant undercurrent of tension continues to simmer beneath the surface of the market.
The rating agencies' reaffirmation of France's sovereign credit rating has temporarily eased market concerns about fiscal risks in the eurozone, while the pullback in U.S. Treasury yields has also reduced upward pressure on global financing costs. However, this relief reflects more a restoration of sentiment than a substantive dissipation of underlying fundamental risks.
While investors are enjoying a brief respite, they must remain vigilant, as potential sources of disruption could resurface at any time, pushing the bond market back into a volatile phase.
Underlying Concerns Remain: U.S. Treasury yields near 5%, while the France–Germany yield spread remains elevated.
Despite a slight easing in market sentiment, underlying concerns remain palpable. On the one hand, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond currently remains just below the critical 5% threshold and could once again approach or even breach that level at any time.
On the European front, the yield spread between French and German 10-year government bonds remains at levels that would have triggered heightened market alarm just a few months ago, underscoring that investors' concerns about France's fiscal trajectory have yet to be fully allayed.
Accordingly, while selling pressure in the bond market has eased for now, underlying structural concerns have hardly shifted. This dynamic has afforded some breathing room to broader risk assets, yet it also serves as a reminder that investors must remain highly cautious.
Once U.S. Treasury yields resume their upward move to test 5%, or the France–Germany yield spread widens again, the vulnerability of global bond markets could quickly come to the fore and spill over into equity markets and other asset classes.
Federal Reserve Decision: Tomorrow's Meeting Is an Obvious Catalyst
The Federal Reserve's policy decision, set to be announced Thursday at Beijing time, is the most obvious catalyst currently driving market activity. Even though markets widely expect policymakers to hold interest rates steady, the meeting itself could still spark significant volatility.
The market pays close attention not only to the interest-rate decision itself but also to shifts in the policy statement's wording, revisions to economic projections, and the nuances of the chair's remarks at the press conference. Even the slightest changes in how inflation persistence, the labor market, or the future policy trajectory are described can swiftly alter investors' expectations regarding the peak level of interest rates and how long they will remain elevated.
Against the backdrop of an already sensitive bond market, the Federal Reserve's communication will serve as a critical test of whether the current period of easing can endure. Even in the absence of rate hikes, hawkish or dovish signals could trigger a new round of volatility in U.S. Treasury yields and further weigh on global risk appetite.
Tech Earnings: Concerns Over the Return on AI Spending Could Spark a New Wave of Volatility
In addition to the Federal Reserve's decision, this week's earnings reports from major tech stocks are also worth close watch. Market participants are growing increasingly concerned about whether the massive capital expenditures underpinning the AI boom can truly justify their long-term returns.
If the earnings reports of companies such as Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon confirm these concerns, it could once again trigger significant market volatility. Particularly at a time when investors are beginning to turn back to government bonds as safe-haven assets while remaining more cautious about higher-risk assets like corporate bonds, a correction in tech stocks could quickly spread to the broader credit markets.
Under these circumstances, a decline in U.S. Treasury yields may not translate into the bullish catalyst the stock market has been hoping for; instead, it could coincide with simultaneous pressure on risk assets, creating a dynamic of "rising risk aversion and falling risk appetite." Meanwhile, the process of validating AI-driven investment returns is emerging as a potential key source of volatility this week.
Summary
At the start of the new week, global bond markets saw some easing, with Moody's maintaining France's Aa3 rating providing relief to European bonds, and U.S. Treasury yields falling sharply after volatile swings. However, underlying concerns remain: the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is still hovering near 5%, and although the France-Germany 10-year yield spread has retreated from its 2011 highs to around 153 basis points, it remains above the critical 150-basis-point threshold.
The Fed's decision on Thursday, earnings reports from major tech stocks, and France's fiscal challenges all remain in the spotlight. If concerns about the return on AI‑related spending are confirmed by corporate results, they could spark a new wave of volatility—prompting investors to seek refuge in Treasury bonds while shunning corporate debt. A decline in U.S. Treasury yields may not be welcome news for the stock market. The market may enjoy a brief respite, but it should not be mistaken for signs of underlying health.

articles.full_text:
Investing.com --Asian currencies traded mixed on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar strengthened ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy decision later this week, while the Japanese yen weakened and the Indonesian rupiah remained under pressure near record lows.
The euro and sterling also slipped as investors positioned ahead of key central-bank decisions this week.
The U.S. dollar index rose 0.2%, while the USD/JPY pair gained 0.2% extending the yen's retreat from last week's safe-haven rally. The EUR/USD pair and the GBP/USD pair slipped 0.1% to 1.3331.The USD/IDR pair rose 0.19% to 18,129.1, leaving the rupiah close to its weakest levels on record.
The yen was among the strongest-performing major currencies last week as concerns over AI-related equity valuations prompted investors to seek safer assets. That demand has since eased, leaving the currency vulnerable ahead of a busy week of central-bank decisions that could reshape the global interest-rate outlook.
Yen retreats as BOJ prepares to hold rates
The yen was last reported 0.2% weaker at 157.73 per dollar, further retreating from a one-month high reached last week. The USD/JPY pair was around 157.70.
The Bank of Japan is widely expected to keep its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at its two-day meeting concluding Friday, while signaling that further increases remain possible as inflation pressures build.
The BOJ meeting follows the Federal Reserve's policy decision, due Wednesday, with the U.S. central bank expected to leave rates unchanged at its two-day meeting. Four other major central banks are also scheduled to announce policy decisions this week.
Rupiah near record lows as BI weighs stronger measures
The USD/IDR pair rose 0.2% to 18,129.1, extending pressure on the rupiah after the currency fell 0.4% on Monday and approached the historic low recorded in early June. The rupiah has lost around 8% against the dollar this year, putting it alongside the Philippine peso among Asia's weakest performers.
Elevated global bond yields, higher oil prices and concerns that Indonesia could lose its emerging-market classification under MSCI have contributed to foreign outflows and renewed selling pressure on the currency. MSCI's proposed reclassification has also raised concerns about reduced foreign investment in Indonesian equities, adding to the challenges facing the rupiah.
Bank Indonesia pledged last week to make "necessary adjustments" to its policy tools to maintain rupiah stability. It kept its benchmark rate at 5.75%, opting for currency intervention and stronger hedging incentives rather than a benchmark-rate increase that could weigh on the domestic economy.

articles.title: FSS warns of weak controls on leveraged stock trading as firms review rules - 머니투데이
articles.summary: FSS warns of weak controls on leveraged stock trading as firms review rules  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) has determined that the securities industry's response to so-called margin investing remains inadequate, hinting at the possibility of reviewing additional regulations.
On Tuesday, the FSS held a "Roundtable on Strengthening Self-Management of Credit Loans in the Securities Industry" with the Korea Financial Investment Association and risk management executives (CROs) from 10 comprehensive financial investment businesses, including Mirae Asset Securities and Korea Investment & Securities, announcing this.
FSS deputy director Seo Jae-wan urged the securities industry to strengthen risk management and investor protection through proactive credit loan management.
While it is encouraging that the securities industry has recently formulated a "Plan to Strengthen Self-Management of Credit Loans," he emphasized the importance of responding promptly to market conditions. Seo stated, "Even before the completion of computer system construction and the reflection of internal regulations, proactive management must be prioritized with investor protection as the top priority."
The plan to strengthen self-management of credit loans proposed by the securities industry centers on limiting the scale of credit lending operations from 100% to 90% of a brokerage's own capital and managing the proportion of credit loans for specific stocks within 15%.
It was pointed out that there are still shortcomings in credit loan management even after the CRO roundtable held by the securities industry last June. It was explained that mechanical and uniform risk management, which was criticized at the time, persists. Therefore, he re-emphasized the need to actively manage credit loans.
As best practices for credit loan management, it introduced a brokerage that reduced credit loan limits for all domestic stocks or lowered the basic limit for stocks with high credit loan concentration from 300 million won to 200 million won and restricted increases in extensions. It also cited cases where RPA (Robotic Process Automation) was used to monitor credit loan status and stocks with sharp intraday fluctuations in real time, implementing measures such as downgrading stock ratings and restricting credit loans, and cases where a three-stage monitoring system of "before market open, during trading, twice a day" was established.
Additional regulations were also foreshadowed. Seo stated, "If self-management is insufficient, additional regulatory measures may be activated," and urged, "Please faithfully implement the self-management plan."
The reason the FSS is urging strengthened credit loan management is that the scale of credit loans still reaches the 30th trillion won range. According to the Korea Financial Investment Association, the monthly credit loan scale peaked at 38 trillion won at the end of last May and recorded over 33 trillion won at the end of last month. As of the 23rd, it stands at 30.1521 trillion won, still maintaining the 30th trillion won range.
If credit loan balances expand excessively, a sharp drop in stock prices can lead to large-scale forced liquidations, spreading market shocks and raising concerns about declining market confidence. Credit loans are transactions where investors provide stocks purchased with borrowed money as collateral. If stock prices fall and the collateral value drops below a certain level, brokerages initiate forced liquidation by forcibly selling the collateral stocks to recover the loan amount. In a sharp decline, forced liquidation volumes can flood the market all at once, pushing stock prices down further and leading to additional forced liquidations in a vicious cycle.
The securities industry expressed its recognition of the need for strengthened credit loan management and its intention to actively cooperate.
An FSS official stated, "We will support the effective implementation of the securities industry's plan to strengthen self-management of credit loans and continuously communicate to ensure that a healthy investment culture is established early."

articles.full_text:
Dollar Drifts as Five Central Banks Prepare to Decide
Currencies started the week in tight ranges ahead of a rare cluster of central bank decisions. Below the surface, the drivers are pulling in different directions: France won a reprieve from a credit downgrade, while UK shoppers are losing momentum just as the Bank of England prepares to raise rates.
Dollar Index: All Eyes on Wednesday
A pullback in oil prices and Treasury yields weighed on the dollar on Monday, Reuters reported, though the dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, was little changed near 101.65. Traders are waiting for decisions from the Fed, ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand. The first three are expected to hold rates, while Canada and New Zealand are expected to raise them.
In a Reuters poll, 94 of 100 economists expect the Fed to hold on Wednesday. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said further hikes are likely needed to bring inflation down, but they do not have to come at back-to-back meetings. That is why traders will focus on how many policymakers vote for a hike and on any hint about December, rather than on the decision itself.
Euro: France Avoids a Downgrade
Moody's kept France's credit rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook on Friday, meaning a downgrade is still possible later. That spared the government a cut during a week of unrest and rising bond yields, and the euro edged up 0.15% to 1.1218 on the relief. Moody's said the rating assumes France adopts a 2027 budget that reduces the deficit and that borrowing costs and social tensions ease somewhat. The next test comes from S&P, which is scheduled to review France on November 27.
The ECB meets on Thursday and is expected to hold. Traders had already cut their bets on further ECB hikes after euro zone bond spreads blew out earlier this month, Bloomberg reported. Higher rates would make France's debt even more expensive to finance.
Pound: Spending Slips Before the Budget
UK retail sales volumes, which strip out price changes, fell 0.4% in September, worse than the 0.1% drop economists expected. Shoppers bought less food, and unusually warm weather held back clothing sales. GfK consumer confidence fell 11 points to minus 24, its steepest one-month fall since the 2020 pandemic.
The data land just before Chancellor John Healey's Autumn Budget on October 28. That adds a growth risk to a pound that has leaned on expectations of a November rate hike, since weaker spending could give the Bank of England a reason to move more carefully.

articles.title: Middle Market Debt Weekly: A Hawkish Fed & AI-Driven Equity Rout Reprice the Rate Backdrop - ABF Journal
articles.summary: Middle Market Debt Weekly: A Hawkish Fed & AI-Driven Equity Rout Reprice the Rate Backdrop  ABF Journal
articles.full_text:
Asset-based lending supplied the week’s marquee transaction: Belk closed $1.275 billion of new senior secured facilities—a $900 million asset-based revolver and a $375 million first-in, last-out (FILO) term loan—with Wells Fargo as administrative and collateral agent and Pathlight Capital as term loan managing agent, replacing the retailer’s existing ABL, FILO and securitization facilities.1 Around it, secured refinancings spanned the risk spectrum: Enerpac priced a new secured revolver and term loan at an initial SOFR plus 112.5 basis points,2 while Teamshares replaced a $150 million legacy facility with a $130 million Sound Point term loan at SOFR plus 950 basis points,3 and Newegg closed a $100 million East West Bank–led senior facility two months after its prior arrangements matured.4 On the restructuring side, Getty Images’ prepackaged Chapter 11 offered secured and revolver lenders full projected recoveries.5
The macro backdrop tightened the context for every floating-rate borrower. The Federal Reserve lifted the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4% on September 16,6 and ahead of the October 27–28 meeting, CME FedWatch put the probability of an October hike at just 7.2% but roughly 78% for a December increase.7 The 10-year Treasury yield fell 19.3 basis points to 4.953% on Thursday as investors fled AI-linked equities,7 and the S&P 500 ended Friday at 7,629.92.8 For asset-based lenders, the message is that SOFR-based pricing is unlikely to relax soon, which raises the premium on borrowing-base discipline and on structures that move borrowers toward cheaper, collateral-backed capital.
Belk Consolidates Into a $1.275 Billion Wells Fargo–Pathlight ABL-and-FILO Package
Belk announced on October 20 that it closed $1.275 billion in new five-year senior secured credit facilities, comprising a $900 million ABL revolver and a $375 million FILO term loan. Wells Fargo serves as administrative agent and collateral agent on both, and Pathlight Capital is term loan managing agent on the FILO.1,9 The package replaces Belk’s existing ABL, FILO and securitization facilities, and the collateral pool spans inventory, receivables, real estate, equipment, intellectual property and the private-label credit card program.1 Pricing, fees and exact maturity were not disclosed.1
Two structural points stand out. First, folding a securitization into the ABL collateral package—with the credit card program now in the pool—simplifies the capital stack but concentrates more asset classes under a single borrowing-base framework, which raises the importance of field-exam scope and eligibility definitions on each collateral type. Second, the FILO represents roughly 29 percent of the total commitments ($375 million of $1.275 billion), a meaningful slice of last-out capacity layered beneath the revolver. CFO Vince Phelan called it an “opportunistic financing” that reflects “continued strength in Belk’s business,” while Wells Fargo’s Keith Vercauteren said the bank “look[s] forward to supporting the Company in its next phase.”1
For middle market ABL lenders, the transaction is a template for how large borrowers are consolidating fragmented working-capital facilities into one agented structure with a FILO tranche absorbing incremental advance-rate risk—a structure that can be scaled down to smaller retail and consumer credits.
Secured Refinancings Price From SOFR+112.5 to SOFR+950 as Enerpac, RealReal and Teamshares Reset Their Capital Structures
At the tightest end of the week’s secured deals, Enerpac Tool Group entered a new agreement dated October 16 with a $550 million revolver (including a $200 million foreign-currency sublimit) and a $300 million term loan, both maturing October 16, 2031, with PNC Bank as administrative agent.10 Initial pricing is term SOFR plus 1.125% on a leverage-based grid of 1.125%–1.875%, and the facilities replace a $625 million revolver and $200 million term loan due September 2027. The loans are secured by substantially all personal property of the company and its domestic guarantors, carry a 3.75x maximum net leverage covenant, and include a $425 million accordion.2 Notably, the sources describe a secured revolver and term loan with leverage and coverage covenants, not an asset-based borrowing-base facility.10
Further along the risk curve, The RealReal announced on October 15—with funding expected on or about October 19—a $150 million senior secured term loan from Fortress-managed funds at an initial SOFR plus 5.75%, paid entirely in cash, plus an undrawn $25 million revolver, maturing October 2033. The proceeds redeem 2029 secured notes that carried a 13.00% all-in rate (8.75% cash plus 4.25% PIK), and the company projects roughly $4 million of first-year interest savings.11,12 At the far end, Teamshares used a $130 million four-year Sound Point term loan at SOFR plus 9.5%—which the company described as a 150 basis point improvement—together with cash on hand to retire a $150 million legacy facility, targeting about $5 million of annual interest savings. CFO Brian Gaebe said the company “prioritized speed and certainty of execution to address a near-term maturity.”3
The spread between Enerpac’s opening margin and Teamshares’ is roughly 838 basis points, a reminder of how much borrowers pay to move from collateral-light credit to opportunistic capital. For asset-based lenders, that gap defines the competitive opportunity: borrowers refinancing from high-coupon term debt into borrowing-base structures can capture meaningful interest savings if their receivables and inventory support the availability.
Newegg’s East West Bank Facility and Belk’s FILO Show Where Lender Capacity Is Coming From
Newegg Commerce closed a $100 million senior credit facility on October 20, led and arranged by East West Bank with a syndicate of participant lenders. The facility replaces and expands prior credit arrangements that matured in August 2026.4,13 The release does not disclose pricing, maturity or whether the facility is asset-based, and the accompanying filing likewise omits a borrowing base, collateral description and rate.13 CFO Christina Ching called the closing “an important step for Newegg in further strengthening our financial position,” and East West Bank said the deal “reflects the strength of our relationship, our confidence in their business model.”4
Read alongside Belk, the week’s supply-side picture is mixed by lender type: a money-center bank agenting the senior ABL, an independent specialty lender (Pathlight) managing the FILO,1 a regional bank leading a mid-sized syndicate,4 and credit managers Sound Point and Fortress providing term capital to Teamshares and RealReal.3,11 Newegg’s case also illustrates timing risk: its prior arrangements matured in August, and the replacement facility closed in late October.
For ABL originators, the practical implication is that bank and non-bank capital are being deployed side by side rather than in competition, and borrowers with approaching maturities are running processes late enough that speed and certainty of execution—Teamshares’ explicit priority—are winning mandates.
Getty Images’ Prepackaged Chapter 11 Keeps Secured and Revolver Lenders Whole While Unsecured Noteholders Take a Haircut
Getty Images filed prepackaged Chapter 11 petitions in Delaware on October 21 after its planned merger with Shutterstock was terminated following an adverse determination by the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority; the filing also cites more than $200 million of warrant-litigation judgments and about $239 million of annual debt service as drivers of the distress.14 Getty family members and Koch Equity Development affiliates committed up to $533 million of new equity and would own 100% of the reorganized company, with an affiliate of Koch providing up to $143 million of DIP financing.15,14 The Form 8-K lists accelerated debt including $150.0 million of revolving loans, $539.9 million of 11.250% senior secured notes due 2030 and $264.7 million of 14.000% senior notes due 2028;14 a secondary summary of the court papers puts the roughly $1.46 billion funded debt stack in total.5
The plan’s treatment, as summarized from the disclosure statement by PPC Land (the recovery percentages are not in the 8-K excerpt reviewed), follows lien priority closely. Secured noteholders and U.S. term loan lenders convert dollar-for-dollar into new notes with a projected 100% recovery, and revolving lenders roll into a new $150 million revolving facility that would be repaid to a zero balance at emergence, also at 100%. Unsecured noteholders share about $170.2 million in cash against $270 million of principal plus accrued interest—a projected recovery of roughly 63%.5 Consenting stakeholders hold about 100% of revolving loan claims, about 90% of secured funded debt claims and about 83% of unsecured notes claims and have agreed to vote for the plan; ballots are due November 30.14 Co-founder Mark Getty said the transaction “is underpinned by the strength of the business.”16
The lesson for secured and ABL lenders is that senior position, liens and a revolving exposure that can be rolled into a post-emergence facility determined who was made whole here; the unsecured class absorbed the loss. Lenders should note, too, that the insider-funded DIP converts to equity, reinforcing the sponsors’ control of the outcome.
Fed Heads Into October 27–28 Meeting With Hike Odds Collapsing for October but Firm for December
Under Chair Kevin Warsh,17 the Fed raised the federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4% on September 16 in a reported 12–0 vote, with Warsh stating that “inflation is too high and has been for too long.”6 Minutes released October 7 showed most participants expecting another hike by year-end.18 This week, CME FedWatch probabilities for a hike at the October 27–28 meeting fell to 7.2% from 27.7% a week earlier and 55.4% a month earlier, while odds of a December increase eased from about 86% to

articles.title: GBP/USD Price Forecast — GBP/USD (1.3310) Falls for a Fourth Day Before the UK Budget and Fed — 1.3200 Target Below 1.3274 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: GBP/USD Price Forecast — GBP/USD (1.3310) Falls for a Fourth Day Before the UK Budget and Fed — 1.3200 Target Below 1.3274  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- GBP/USD fell 0.25% to 1.3310 on Tuesday, its fourth straight loss, after topping out at 1.3400 last week.
- UK CPI rose to 3.5% in September, and markets price a Bank of England hike to 4% on November 5 above 90%.
- The 10-year gilt yield sits at 5.43%, after hitting 5.53% on October 8, its highest level since July 2007.
GBP/USD traded at 1.3310 on Tuesday afternoon, down 0.25% from Monday’s close at 1.3342, extending its losing streak to four sessions. The pair opened at 1.3343, touched a session high of 1.3349 in the European morning and slid to a low of 1.3307 after the U.S. data at 12:30 GMT. The 42-pip range is narrow for cable, and the price action inside it has been one-directional: every bounce toward 1.3340 met sellers.
The four-day slide has erased the gains from last week’s rally. GBP/USD climbed from 1.3304 on October 19 to 1.3379 on October 20 after the UK jobs report, then to 1.3400 on October 22, its strongest level in five weeks. It closed at 1.3368 on October 23 and 1.3348 on Monday, a six-day low, before Tuesday’s break toward 1.3300. The pair has lost 0.44% over five sessions and now sits in the lower third of its recent trading band.
The broader picture shows a pair under pressure for months. GBP/USD peaked at 1.3676 in August and has made a series of lower highs since. It tested its 2026 low at 1.3140 in the week of October 12 before rebounding. The 52-week range runs from 1.3012 to 1.3847, and spot sits 3.9% below the high. A falling 100-day moving average caps every recovery attempt.
Sterling is not weak everywhere. EUR/GBP traded at 0.8368, down 4.69% year over year, with the pound near its strongest against the euro in 16 months as UK growth outpaces the eurozone’s. GBP/JPY held at 210.04 and GBP/CHF at 1.1033. The pound’s problem is the dollar, not a broad sterling selloff.
The dollar side is firm. The U.S. Dollar Index traded at 102.20 on Tuesday, near a two-week high, after durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September and consumer confidence jumped to 91.7 against an 81.0 forecast. EUR/USD fell for a fifth straight day to 1.1144.
Wednesday is the day that matters. Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Autumn Budget, with the Office for Budget Responsibility’s fiscal outlook published the same day. Hours later, at 18:00 GMT, the Federal Reserve announces its rate decision. Cable faces two major event risks within the same session, and traders are reducing exposure into both.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. The pound has every reason to rally on rates: UK inflation at 3.5%, a Bank of England hike on November 5 priced above 90%, the strongest UK PMI since February and a 10-year gilt yield 43 basis points above Treasuries. But a fiscal risk premium, built on an eroded budget buffer and gilt yields near 18-year highs, prevents sterling from capturing that yield. Until the Budget clears without a credibility shock, cable trades between 1.3274 and 1.3400, with the bias lower while the dollar holds above 102.
How Tuesday’s Session Unfolded: London Fades, U.S. Data Breaks the Floor
The session followed the same rhythm that has defined the past four days. GBP/USD opened in Asia at 1.3343, near Monday’s close, and spent the Asian session in a tight 1.3335 to 1.3345 band as Asian equity markets rallied on AI sentiment.
London delivered the first leg. Sterling ticked up to 1.3349, the session high, shortly after the European open, as UK equity futures firmed on the strong PMI backdrop. The move had no follow-through. Traders who might have bought on the UK growth story stepped back ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, and the pair drifted back toward 1.3330 by midday London time. There was no UK data on the calendar, which left sterling trading on positioning and the dollar’s direction.
The break came at 12:30 GMT. The U.S. Census Bureau reported durable goods orders up 1.8% in September to $345.4 billion, the largest monthly gain in five months, with orders excluding transportation up 0.5% and core capital goods orders up 0.5%. The dollar caught a bid, and GBP/USD slipped through 1.3320.
At 14:00 GMT, the Conference Board’s consumer confidence index printed 91.7, the highest since June and 10.7 points above the consensus. That second upside surprise extended the dollar’s gains and pushed cable to 1.3307, the low of the day. By 15:28 GMT, the pair traded at 1.3321, down 0.14%, and it settled near 1.3310 into the late London session, down 0.25%.
The structure of the day tells traders where the pressure sits. Sterling failed to hold gains during the London session when UK factors drive the market, and it broke lower during the U.S. session when dollar factors drive it. That pattern has repeated on each of the last four days: weak London bids followed by dollar-led selling in New York.
Market sentiment was broadly positive outside currencies. The Nasdaq rose 1.33% by midday on an AI-led rally and the S&P 500 traded at 7,728.90, even as Middle East hostilities continued. In a risk-on equity environment, the pound would normally firm against the dollar. Its failure to do so on Tuesday confirms that Budget caution is overriding the usual risk relationship.
The close near 1.3310 leaves cable eight pips above the 1.3302 support zone and 36 pips above 1.3274, the line that marks the next leg lower.
The UK Budget: Healey’s First Test With a Shrunken Buffer
Wednesday’s Autumn Budget is the single largest sterling-specific risk this week. Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget on October 28, and the Office for Budget Responsibility publishes its Economic and Fiscal Outlook the same day. The stakes are set by the bond market rather than by politics.
The fiscal buffer has collapsed. The government’s headroom against its fiscal rules stood at £24 billion in March. A global bond selloff since then, which briefly pushed the 30-year gilt yield above 6% in October, has raised projected debt interest costs and eroded that cushion to an estimated £8.5 billion to £16 billion. Every 1 percentage point rise in yields across the UK curve adds £8.4 billion to borrowing costs by 2029-30, and every 100 basis points of Bank of England tightening adds £5.8 billion. Rising rates and rising yields are eating the Chancellor’s room from both directions.
Tax rises are widely expected. With limited headroom and fiscal rules that the government has committed to meeting, the Budget is likely to include revenue measures, and banks are bracing for a possible tax raid. The government has also pre-announced a “Your First Home” housing scheme, whose cost will add to the financing requirement without affecting the fiscal rules directly.
The gilt supply matters for markets. The Net Financing Requirement for 2026-27 was forecast at £251.2 billion in April, with planned gilt sales of £246.2 billion, split 38.6% short-dated, 30.9% medium-dated and 9.1% long-dated. The remit is expected to rise by up to £10 billion. A larger-than-expected increase, or a shift toward longer maturities, would push long-dated gilt yields higher and weigh on sterling.
History offers a guide. Budgets where the fiscal rules are met and the main measures have leaked in advance have historically produced muted gilt reactions on the day. The damage in past UK fiscal events, most famously in September 2022, came from surprises on credibility rather than from the arithmetic itself. The market’s base case is an uneventful Budget, but the reaction risks are skewed negative.
For GBP/USD, three outcomes matter. A Budget that meets the rules through credible tax measures and keeps gilt issuance in line would remove the fiscal premium and could lift cable 50 to 80 pips toward 1.3400. A Budget that leans on optimistic forecasts or raises borrowing would push gilt yields higher and send cable through 1.3274. A Budget that raises inflation through indirect taxes would boost Bank of England hike expectations, a mixed outcome that could support the pound short term while hurting gilts.
Gilt Yields at 5.43%: High Yields, No Currency Support
The UK bond market is the reason sterling cannot capture its yield advantage. The 10-year gilt yield stood at 5.43% on October 21, after touching 5.53% on October 8, its highest since July 2007. The 30-year gilt traded at 5.89% on October 20 and briefly rose above 6% earlier in the month. The 10-year has climbed more than 100 basis points from 4.40% before the March Spring Forecast.
On paper, those yields should support the pound. The UK 10-year at 5.43% sits 43 basis points above the U.S. 10-year at 5.00%. Investors earn more holding gilts than Treasuries, a carry advantage that would normally attract capital into sterling. Instead, GBP/USD has fallen from 1.3676 in August to 1.3310.
The explanation is the risk premium. Part of the rise in gilt yields reflects expectations for Bank of England hikes, which should support the currency. But part reflects investors demanding extra compensation for UK fiscal risk, which does not. When yields rise because investors fear fiscal slippage, the currency tends to fall alongside bond prices, the pattern of a country risk premium rather than a rate-differential rally.
The global context amplifies the problem. Gilt yields have tracked a worldwide selloff driven by the U.S.-Iran war’s energy shock. Brent crude traded below $114 on Tuesday, up 80% this year, and higher oil has sustained inflation expectations across developed markets. The UK, as a net energy importer with a large current account deficit, is more exposed to that shock than the United States, which is a net petroleum exporter.
The yield curve shows the stress. The gap between 30-year and 10-year gilts, near 46 basis points in late October, reflects investor reluctance to hold long-dated UK debt. Pension fund demand for long gilts has fallen since the 2022 crisis, leaving the long end more dependent on price-sensitive buyers. The Bank of England’s decision in September to reduce its stock of gilt holdings from quantitati

Buy Tesla. A Fed pause should ease borrowing costs and improve auto-loan affordability, reducing the need for Tesla to subsidize financing. Lower Treasury yields also lift the valuation of long-dated growth bets like autonomy/robotics, and TSLA’s $1.53B Q3 free cash flow gives it cushion to ride out demand softness.
Key Risk: Fed signals a December hike or sticky inflation, pushing yields back up and worsening affordability fast.
Buy Meta. If the Fed message is less aggressive, falling yields boost the present value of Meta’s future profits, and a steadier rate outlook supports advertiser confidence to keep marketing budgets on Facebook/Instagram. Q3 revenue growth ($64.6B, +26% YoY) provides the operating base for a valuation-driven rebound.
Key Risk: Advertisers cut budgets anyway due to a real slowdown, and AI spending fails to translate into faster profit growth.
- US Fed is expected to leave interest rates unchanged this week.
- The decision could trigger a rally in TSLA, META, and NFLX stocks.
- Here's what Tesla, Meta, and Netflix have in store for investors.
The US Federal Reserve announces its next interest-rate decision on Wednesday at 2 p.m. Eastern, following its two-day policy meeting.
Expectations favour a pause: 94 of 100 economists in Reuters’ latest poll forecast an “unchanged” federal funds target of 3.75% - 4.00%, although all expected a December increase.
For stocks, the opportunity lies in the accompanying message – a less aggressive outlook may ease Treasury yields and revive demand for growth companies.
Tesla, Meta Platforms, and Netflix stand out as potential beneficiaries in that scenario.
Tesla stock: a pause could ease pressure on affordability
Tesla shares offer a relatively “direct” connection between monetary policy and consumer demand.
Vehicle purchases often depend on financing, making borrowing costs a key part of affordability.
Holding rates steady would avoid another immediate increase in the benchmark rate.
Importantly, reassuring guidance could lower market borrowing costs – potentially improving the economics of auto loans and reducing pressure on Tesla to subsidize financing.
There is also a valuation channel.
Investors assign value to TSLA’s future autonomous-driving and robotics opportunities; lower discount rates can increase the “present value” of those prospective earnings.
Note that Tesla reported $1.53 billion in third-quarter free cash flow, providing a financial cushion.
Still, the bullish Fed scenario requires improving financing conditions – and a pause would leave existing affordability challenges unresolved.
Meta stock: advertising resilience meets a valuation boost
Meta shares could benefit through both advertising expectations and the valuation investors place on the company’s future profits.
The giant posted Q3 revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26% year-over-year.
That provides an operating foundation for a “potential recovery” if investors become more comfortable with the interest-rate outlook.
The economic link runs through advertisers.
If a patient Fed strengthens confidence that consumer spending can remain resilient, businesses may feel more comfortable maintaining their marketing budgets across Facebook and Instagram.
Crucially, falling Treasury yields could make Meta Platforms’ prospective earnings more attractive relative to bonds.
That said, its substantial AI spending remains a complication.
A favourable policy message could ease valuation pressure, but investors will still demand evidence that infrastructure investment can generate adequate returns.
Netflix: lower yields could support a post-earnings recovery
Netflix shares enter the Fed decision with investors weighing profitable growth against a “softer” outlook.
Q3 revenue reached $12.87 billion, while earnings of $0.87 a share exceeded the $0.82 consensus.
However, current-quarter guidance of $13.44 billion fell below analysts’ $13.53 billion estimate.
A reassuring Fed message could help by lowering the return investors demand on future earnings, potentially supporting Netflix’s valuation after its disappointing outlook.
There is an operating argument as well: steadier household finances and business confidence could support subscription retention and advertising demand over time.
For NFLX, the strongest rally setup would combine falling yields with confidence in economic growth.
