articles.title: What to expect from the Federal Reserve's next rate decision - Euronews.com
articles.summary: What to expect from the Federal Reserve's next rate decision  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates on hold on Wednesday, six days before the US midterm elections, but with inflation at 3.7% and oil prices still elevated, investors see another hike in December as likely and will scour Chair Kevin Warsh's words for clues.
When the Federal Reserve announces its decision at 19:00 CET on Wednesday, it is widely expected to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, less than a week before Americans vote in the midterms.
However, with inflation at 3.7%, energy prices at the highs and another hike in December seen as likely, investors will be watching Fed Chair Kevin Warsh closely for clues about what comes next.
Markets put the chance of a hold at over 90%, but see a 73% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's 8-9 December meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, which tracks interest rate futures.
That would follow September's increase, the Fed's first in three years. Since then, several senior officials have played down the urgency of moving again.
Vice Chair Philip Jefferson pointed in a speech to the jump in longer-term borrowing costs, adding that "my colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time".
New York Fed President John Williams reiterated the same sentiment in a speech at the University at Buffalo stating that "there is no need for urgency".
Politics looms too.
"The Fed doesn’t want to poke the White House in the eye six days before an election,” said Joseph LaVorgna, chief economist at Japanese bank SMBC's US arm and a former Trump administration official.
Not everyone may go along.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who both say rates are not yet high enough to cool inflation, could vote for a hike, and as many as three officials could dissent.
Inflation runs hot as growth holds up
The case for tighter policy remains. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, while core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.6%. Wholesale prices jumped 6.3%.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee stated the reading was "discouraging", saying underlying inflation at today's level was "not acceptable".
Petrol, which has topped $4 a gallon for the past three months, accounted for over half of September's price increase, according to the US Labor Department. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon in late September, raising the cost of shipping almost everything.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell over 6% on Monday, from about $117.4 a barrel, its highest close since 19 March, as diplomacy over the Iran war seemingly gathered pace.
At the time of writing on Tuesday, it traded at roughly $110.8 a barrel, still far above the $72 it fetched before the Iran war began in late February.
Borrowing costs are biting too.
The average 30-year US mortgage rate hit 7.4% in early October, a three-year peak, before easing to 7.32% last week, against just under 6.2% a year ago. Research firm Oxford Economics estimates this year’s rise has priced 5 million more American households out of buying a home.
Expectations of further hikes have also kept the US dollar close to an 18-month high against major currencies.
The economy, meanwhile, is bending rather than breaking.
Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September and unemployment rose to 4.2%, yet the US economy grew at an annualised 2.2% in the second quarter, and the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow tracker points to 3.5% for the third.
The next test comes straight after the decision.
On Thursday at 13:30 CET, the US publishes its first estimate of third-quarter growth and September data for the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index.
"Fed officials still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in a note.
All eyes on Warsh
Warsh, who will speak to reporters at 19:30 CET, has offered few hints.
Speaking in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings this month, he said the world had "broadly conformed to our expectations" since September.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," Warsh said while stressing that "at the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability."
He has long expressed opposition to forward guidance, the practice of signalling future moves to the markets, and has avoided it.
Aditya Bhave, head of US economics research at Bank of America, said a surprise hike could "end forward guidance by showing markets that they can't listen to the guidance anymore," though most economists doubt it.
The Fed Chair's independence is also under scrutiny.
Warsh defied US President Donald Trump's calls for lower rates in September, but Trump later said he had told Warsh he "might as well" vote for a hike, and has since stepped up his push to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook.
Trump created a three-person committee to recommend whether he has cause to fire Cook over mortgage fraud allegations she denies. Cook is expected to appear before the committee next week.
As for Warsh, if his speech focuses on the fact that inflation must return to the Fed's 2% target faster, investors will likely read it as the confirmation for a December hike.

articles.title: Euro-Dollar Risks Fresh 2026 Low if Warsh Sounds Hawkish: UniCredit - Pound Sterling Live
articles.summary: Euro-Dollar Risks Fresh 2026 Low if Warsh Sounds Hawkish: UniCredit  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Image © Adobe Images
Euro's next move against the dollar rests on the tone the Federal Reserve Chair strikes on Wednesday, with strategists warning a hawkish message would drive it to fresh lows.
The euro risks a fresh 2026 low against the dollar should Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reaffirm a hawkish stance at Wednesday's policy meeting, investment bank analysts warn.
The Euro to Dollar exchange rate is exposed to Warsh's message through US Treasury yields, which UniCredit says move in tight step with the dollar: a hawkish Fed lifts the yields that draw capital into dollar assets, while a softer tone eases them and weighs on the US currency.
EUR/USD's direction hinges on the Fed Chair's tone more than the decision itself, with strategists at UniCredit expecting a hold at 3.75-4.00% and a hike in December, "however, what will matter is how hawkish Warsh will sound in his overall assessment of the economic outlook," says Roberto Mialich, FX Strategist at UniCredit.
EUR/USD trades at 1.1145, down for a fourth session and 0.3% above the 1.1114 low it set on 14 October, extending the downtrend we flagged at the start of the week.
EUR/USD goes into the meeting with the dollar already carrying less hawkish Fed pricing, "markets have already begun to adjust to their expectations following less aggressive remarks from influential Fed officials such as John Williams and Michelle Bowman," says Mialich.
EUR/USD would be dragged to fresh lows by a hawkish Warsh, UniCredit warns, "a reaffirmation of the Fed's hawkish stance would push the 10Y UST yield back towards its recent 24-year peak of 5.3475%, reinvigorate the US unit and drag EUR-USD towards or even below its recent low of 1.1114," says Mialich.
The euro also faces rising energy costs, with CIBC's Jeremy Stretch expecting the selling to continue, "given the rapid acceleration in the benchmark natural gas future across H2 to date, approximately 125%, we can expect EUR negativity to persist and or shorts to extend," says Stretch.
EUR/USD would then test the 2026 low and 1.1111, the 50% retracement of the rally from 2025's low to January's high, according to Stretch.
The euro would struggle against a dollar that ING says higher energy prices and a hawkish Fed "can keep… supported this week".
Above: The dollar index is heavily influenced by Fed policy-linked U.S. two-year bond yields.
What a Softer Warsh Would Mean for EUR/USD
EUR/USD would recover should Warsh sound less hawkish, with Mialich expecting the yield support behind the dollar to fade, "less hawkish signals would likely keep the 10Y UST yield below 5% and put further downward pressure on the USD," he says.
EUR/USD stands to gain more from a softer hold than it would lose to a hawkish one, according to strategists at Bank of America, who stand out in expecting a hike this week, "hawkish messaging is broadly neutral, while a dovish hold risks outsized USD weakness," says a BofA Global Research report.
The euro also has room for a sharp rebound because so many investors are betting against it, with CIBC noting that combined real money and leveraged short positions are close to early-2020 extremes, leaving those investors to buy back euros if the Fed disappoints the dollar bulls.
EUR/USD rallies towards 1.13 would meet sellers at J.P. Morgan's London desk, which expects Warsh to stick to his policy of offering no forward guidance, making the meeting "unlikely to be too market moving".
What It Means for GBP/EUR
The euro faces a double test against sterling on Wednesday, with Chancellor John Healey's Budget landing hours before the Fed decision, as Crédit Agricole turns seller of the pound-to-euro rate.
The euro has support against the pound at 0.8333 in EUR/GBP according to J.P. Morgan, equivalent to 1.20 in the Pound to Euro rate.
The euro then meets its own central bank on Thursday, when investment bank analysts expect the European Central Bank to hold rates.
EUR/USD would open a recovery towards the 21-day average at 1.1216 on a softer Warsh; a hawkish one targets a daily close below 1.1114 and a test of 1.1111.

articles.title: Precious metals weaken as Hormuz uncertainty keeps oil elevated ahead of Fed decision - Kitco AM Report - Kitco
articles.summary: Precious metals weaken as Hormuz uncertainty keeps oil elevated ahead of Fed decision - Kitco AM Report  Kitco
articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot gold and silver prices were lower in early U.S. trading Tuesday, as persistent expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening and uncertainty surrounding Middle East energy supplies continued to weigh on precious metals. Gold slipped below the $4,000.00 level during the morning session, while silver suffered heavier losses as concerns about industrial demand compounded the impact of restrictive interest rate expectations. Renewed diplomatic efforts involving Iran helped ease some immediate fears of another major escalation, although crude oil prices remained elevated. At the time of writing, spot gold was trading near $3,994.60 an ounce, down $21.60, or 0.54%, while spot silver was trading near $52.750, down $1.090, or 2.03%.
Market positioning remains focused on a likely Federal Reserve pause Wednesday, followed by the possibility of additional tightening before year-end. September consumer prices increased 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while producer prices climbed 1.3% and 6.3%, respectively. Interest rate futures indicate that the Fed is widely expected to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% when its Oct. 27-28 meeting concludes. However, traders continue to assign approximately a 73% probability to at least one additional increase by December, reflecting persistent inflation concerns despite evidence of slowing housing activity. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near 4.98% Tuesday morning, below recent highs, as softer crude prices and demand for government bonds provided some relief. Gold nevertheless remained under pressure, reflecting the influence of restrictive monetary policy expectations and continued weakness in precious metals positioning.
U.S. durable goods orders increased 1.8% in September to $345.4 billion, exceeding expectations for a 1.5% gain and following an upwardly revised 0.1% increase in August. Excluding transportation, orders rose 0.5%, slightly below expectations for a 0.6% increase, while transportation equipment orders climbed 4.6%. Tuesday's remaining economic calendar includes August home-price indexes at 9 a.m. EDT, followed by October consumer confidence, September new-home sales and the Richmond Fed manufacturing survey at 10 a.m. EDT. The Federal Open Market Committee announces its interest rate decision Wednesday at 2 p.m. EDT, followed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT. Thursday brings the advance third-quarter gross domestic product report, September personal consumption expenditures inflation figures and weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT. Softer activity and inflation readings could temper December rate hike expectations and support gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar, while stronger data would reinforce the prospect of restrictive monetary policy.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a significant source of uncertainty in global energy markets, although renewed diplomatic engagement has reduced some immediate concerns about another military escalation. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran Monday aimed at easing regional tensions and preventing renewed hostilities. The parties agreed to continue discussions on strengthening cooperation and regional security, although no settlement between Washington and Tehran has been announced. The broader confrontation remains unresolved, with continuing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabian targets and persistent threats to commercial shipping complicating efforts to restore normal energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The risk of renewed military operations and disruptions to Gulf oil exports continues to support an elevated geopolitical premium in crude prices despite the latest diplomatic contacts.
Oil prices initially declined Tuesday as hopes for continued negotiations reduced immediate supply fears, before recovering as renewed Houthi activity reinforced concerns about the security of regional energy infrastructure. Brent crude futures were trading near $116.24 a barrel in the latest verified European morning reading, while WTI was near $102.07. For gold, diplomatic efforts and the prospect of lower crude prices offer some relief from energy-driven inflation concerns, but the absence of a confirmed U.S.-Iran settlement leaves geopolitical risks elevated. Higher oil prices continue to complicate the Federal Reserve's inflation outlook, potentially offsetting safe-haven demand for bullion. Silver remains more vulnerable to concerns about manufacturing activity and industrial consumption, particularly if elevated energy costs and restrictive monetary policy further weaken economic growth.
Global equity markets were generally firmer before the U.S. open as investors assessed corporate earnings and positioned for Wednesday's Federal Reserve announcement. Dow and S&P 500 futures gained approximately 0.2%, while Nasdaq futures advanced around 0.4%, supported by renewed interest in selected technology and artificial intelligence-related shares. Better-than-expected corporate results helped offset continuing concerns about elevated financing costs and technology-sector valuations. European markets remained sensitive to corporate earnings, energy prices and regional monetary policy developments, while Asian trading reflected mixed sentiment toward technology shares and global economic growth. Investors are also preparing for policy announcements from the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan later this week, adding to uncertainty about the direction of global interest rates and currencies.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and trading near $102.07 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $116.24. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 4.98% area. The U.S. dollar remains supported by expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve monetary policy, although the direction of Treasury yields and the dollar will remain sensitive to Wednesday's interest rate decision and Thursday's inflation figures. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)

articles.title: USD/CAD reversal risk builds as central bank showdown looms - StoneX
articles.summary: USD/CAD reversal risk builds as central bank showdown looms  StoneX
articles.full_text:
USD/CAD has delivered a bullish reversal signal from established support, just as traders prepare for Fed and BoC decisions. Aggressive Canadian rate hike expectations and conflicting momentum signals make the coming session important.
- USD/CAD flashes bullish reversal signal ahead of Fed, BoC
- BoC hike expectations contrast with weakening Canadian economic data
- US Treasury yields track AI-related market sentiment
- Hedge funds remain heavily short CAD despite hawkish BoC pricing
It's going to be a big week for USD/CAD traders, with not only the Federal Reserve and Bank of Canada delivering interest rate decisions on Wednesday, but also major US tech earnings midweek, along with renewed uncertainty surrounding trade negotiations between the two nations.
When it comes to central banks, markets heavily favour the Bank of Canada delivering the first hike of its tightening cycle, while the Fed is expected to leave rates unchanged despite persistently elevated US inflationary pressures.
Ahead of this blockbuster week, USD/CAD delivered a bullish reversal signal on the daily chart on Friday, suggesting the recent downtrend may have run its course, placing greater emphasis on Monday's price action for confirmation.
BoC and Fed face very different inflation signals
Markets are heavily favouring a 25-basis-point rate hike from the Bank of Canada on Wednesday following hawkish comments from Governor Tiff Macklem that saw the implied probability surge from around 36% to more than 80% last week.
Source: LSEG
But the economic data hardly screams out for tighter monetary policy. Canadian employment fell by 68,000 in September, while the BoC's preferred trimmed-mean and median inflation measures averaged just 1.85%, below the central bank's 2% target.
Macklem's argument is that persistently elevated energy prices may spill over into broader inflationary pressures, particularly as businesses pass higher costs on to consumers. That's a legitimate risk, and one we've seen materialise elsewhere, but it's not what the latest Canadian inflation figures are showing.
That raises questions about whether the BoC needs to tighten this week. It also suggests there may be an underappreciated risk of the central bank leaving rates unchanged while delivering a hawkish message about the outlook.
Source: TradingView
Realistically, you could argue that it should be the Fed considering a rate hike this week, rather than the Bank of Canada. US inflation remains persistently elevated, with the latest CPI data for September coming in much hotter than expected, while the labour market remains tight.
Yet despite that hawkish backdrop, several senior Fed officials went out of their way to signal to markets that the October meeting was likely to be a placeholder. As a result, markets are positioned for a hawkish hold, with expectations centred on the Fed gradually raising rates at every second meeting, with the next hike heavily favoured for December.
AI sentiment drives US yields, but not USD/CAD
While both central bank meetings create the potential for knee-jerk market reactions, a look at the relationship between USD/CAD and US-Canada interest rate differentials suggests the latter haven't been an overwhelmingly strong driver of the pair over short and medium-term windows.
Source: LSEG
AI-related sentiment has clearly been influencing US Treasury yields and broader risk appetite, with yields increasingly moving in line with Nasdaq futures and inversely to volatility measures. However, that relationship hasn't flowed through directly to USD/CAD, much as it hasn't for the broader US dollar complex, as discussed in separate analysis published late last week.
It seems traders are using fluctuations in AI-linked markets as a proxy for the longer-term US nominal growth outlook.
CAD shorts extreme despite hawkish BoC pricing
Despite markets heavily favouring multiple Bank of Canada rate hikes in the months ahead, hedge funds remain overwhelmingly short the Canadian dollar. CFTC futures and options data released last Friday, covering positions as of Tuesday, October 20, showed net speculative shorts rising to 92,789 contracts, the 11th most bearish reading in a series dating back to 2007.
While this is only a snapshot of leveraged fund positioning rather than the broader market, it suggests expectations for tighter Canadian monetary policy have yet to translate into a meaningful reduction in bearish CAD bets among this group of traders.
Adding another layer of uncertainty for traders to navigate this week are US-Canada trade negotiations, with White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett suggesting on Sunday that the two countries were close to reaching an agreement. His comments followed Friday's decision to remove 50% tariffs on selected Canadian products, even as new tariffs were imposed on others.
On the surface, that's a positive development that would normally be expected to benefit the loonie rather than the US dollar. However, in early Asian trade on Monday, that hasn't been the case so far.
USD/CAD bullish reversal signal requires confirmation
Source: TradingView
USD/CAD delivered a bullish pin bar on Friday after finding buyers around 1.3967, the swing high set on March 31 this year. The subsequent reclaim of 1.4000 suggests upside reversal risk may be starting to build following the sharp decline from the October highs, although the broader momentum picture remains bearish.
I wouldn't put too much weight on price action in early Asian trade, although the broader market backdrop points to the potential for Friday's rebound in risk appetite to extend. Nasdaq futures are trading higher, with similar gains likely in the Nikkei and KOSPI, both of which have been influential in the AI sentiment trade. Given how the broader US dollar behaved last week, that's another factor worth monitoring.
For USD/CAD, the immediate level to watch overhead is the 100-day moving average, which the price tested early on Monday before being comprehensively rejected. A recovery above that level that sticks would shift attention to 1.4080, which has acted as both support and resistance recently, alongside the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement of the move from the May 2021 low to the February 2025 high.
Beyond that, 1.4200 and 1.4294 are the next levels to watch, with the latter marking an area where the pair stalled on multiple occasions earlier this month.
Underneath, 1.3967 remains the key level, having acted as resistance on March 31 before providing support on Friday. A break beneath it would bring 1.3910 and then the 200-day moving average into focus.
While Friday's bullish pin bar warns of a potential reversal, the oscillators continue to favour short setups over longs. RSI (14) remains below 40 and, although starting to curl higher, has yet to stage a meaningful rebound. MACD has also delivered a bearish crossover and moved into negative territory, confirming that downside momentum remains dominant.
With price action and momentum sending conflicting signals, greater weight should be placed on how USD/CAD trades through the remainder of Monday, particularly around the 100-day moving average and 1.3967, for confirmation of whether Friday's bullish reversal signal has any staying power.
USD/JPY Weekly Outlook: AI earnings could overshadow the Fed and BoJ
AI sentiment has become a major driver of US Treasury yields and USD/JPY. With Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon reporting this week, central bank decisions may have competition for traders' attention.
EUR/USD forecast: All eyes on Warsh at Jackson Hole - Forex Friday
For much of this week, the EUR/USD has been edging lower with the US dollar regaining some ground after last week’s sell-off that was triggered, in part, by the bond market worries. Investors have been unwilling to bet further against the US dollar so far this week ahead of Kevin Warsh’s keynote speech at the Jackson Hole summit, due later today.
Bitcoin Forecast: BTC/USD Back to $80K Ahead of Warsh’s Jackson Hole Speech
After surging over $15,000 in the past 10 days alone, there is risk of a near-term pullback if Warsh says anything remotely hawkish at Jackson Hole - what are the levels to watch from here?

articles.title: Why the Federal Reserve matters more to crypto market than many investors realise - investingLive
articles.summary: Why the Federal Reserve matters more to crypto market than many investors realise  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Federal Reserve's policy is a key driver of the broader crypto market through its impact on liquidity, real yields, the US dollar and risk appetite. Expectations of rate cuts and easier financial conditions can support cryptocurrencies, while a hawkish repricing can trigger market-wide selloffs. However, crypto-specific catalysts and differences in fundamentals can influence the magnitude of moves.
Cryptocurrencies have different use cases and fundamentals, but the macroeconomic conditions are an important underlying driver. The Federal Reserve's policy has an enormous influence on macroeconomic conditions through liquidity, borrowing costs and risk appetite, making it a key factor for the crypto market. Because cryptocurrencies are risk assets, they tend to struggle when monetary policy tightens and benefit when policy becomes more accommodative.
By raising interest rates, the Fed increases borrowing costs for households and businesses, restraining consumption and investment. This can slow economic growth and tighten financial conditions. Conversely, rate cuts reduce borrowing costs and can support economic activity by encouraging spending and investment.
When growth is resilient and financial conditions are supportive, investors are generally more willing to allocate capital to riskier assets, including cryptocurrencies. During tightening cycles, higher borrowing costs and reduced risk appetite can trigger capital outflows from speculative assets, contributing to corrections or bear markets. During easing cycles, improving liquidity and a greater appetite for risk can support crypto rallies.
This helps explain why Bitcoin, Ethereum and many altcoins often move in the same direction during major market swings, even when their underlying fundamentals differ.
Keep in mind that policy tightening can coincide with strong growth, while rate cuts driven by recession fears can still weigh on crypto prices. So, the economic context is also an important factor to consider.
One of the most important things to know is that markets respond to expectations about the Fed's future policy path. If markets anticipate rate cuts, cryptocurrencies can rally before the Fed acts. Conversely, if investors reprice expectations toward higher rates in the future, the crypto market can drop even if the Fed leaves rates unchanged in the near-term. The key is how expectations evolve relative to what markets have already priced in.
Bitcoin, Ethereum and altcoins have different fundamentals, but they are all exposed to changes in global liquidity and risk appetite. Smaller cryptocurrencies are particularly vulnerable to tightening financial conditions because they tend to carry greater volatility and liquidity risk. Crypto-specific developments do matter, but the Fed determines the broader macroeconomic environment in which these assets trade. So, crypto-specific developments rarely change the main the trend, but they do affect the magnitude of price moves.
In conclusion, crypto traders should focus mainly on the Federal Reserve and the factors influencing future interest rate expectations rather than monitoring all the crypto-specific fundamentals.

articles.title: Asian stocks rose on expectations for Anthropic's IPO. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Asian stocks rose on expectations for Anthropic's IPO.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Asian stock markets mostly rose on October 27, as the long-awaited initial public offering (IPO) filing of Anthropic, a leading artificial intelligence (AI) company, helped improve investor sentiment.
This development comes ahead of a series of earnings reports from technology companies, seen as a test of the wave of AI investment, and central bank meetings that could impact short-term interest rate prospects.
However, the gains were mainly concentrated in South Korea and Japan, while other Asian stock markets showed mixed performance as investors prepared to receive a series of important corporate earnings reports and monetary policy decisions this week.
In its IPO filing, Anthropic, one of the world's leading AI companies, stated that revenue in the first half of the year increased by approximately 1,300% compared to the same period last year. However, the company also warned about risks related to AI security. Anthropic's IPO is seen as a crucial test of the profitability of the AI investment wave. If the stock does not receive a positive market reception, optimism for the sector could continue to weaken, as investors have begun to question the massive amount of capital poured into AI and the financial health of some companies.
Market sentiment was further boosted by Meta Platforms' plan to raise up to $95 billion through a stock offering, the company's largest equity fundraising ever.
At the close of trading on October 27, the MSCI Asia-Pacific index, excluding Japan , rose 0.9%. Earlier, the US semiconductor index gained 2.8% in overnight trading on October 26, marking its strongest single-day increase in a month.
In Japan, the stock market rebounded on October 27th, as details from Anthropic's IPO filing helped ease recent concerns about the massive investment in the AI industry. The Nikkei 225 index rose 1,078.72 points, or 1.73%, from the previous session, closing at 63,268.37 points.
You may also like
In South Korea, the Seoul stock market also closed higher, led by technology stocks. Returning optimism regarding AI, coupled with falling oil prices, boosted demand for riskier assets. Meanwhile, the won depreciated against the US dollar. At the close, the KOSPI index rose 168.87 points, or 3.09%, to 5,638.34 points. However, since the beginning of October, the index is still down 17%, reflecting investor concerns about the recent surge in AI investments.
The Sydney (Australia), Mumbai (India), and Manila (Philippines) markets also recorded gains. Conversely, the stock markets in Singapore , Wellington (New Zealand), Bangkok (Thailand), and Jakarta (Indonesia) all declined.
In mainland China, the Shanghai Composite index fell 1.33% to 3,648.3 points. Meanwhile, the Hang Seng index in Hong Kong also lost 0.8%, closing at 23,029.33 points.
In the currency market, trading activity was relatively quiet ahead of policy decisions by the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB), and the Bank of Japan (BoJ).
Economists predict that all three central banks will keep interest rates unchanged at these meetings. Therefore, market attention is focused on the statements of policymakers in order to look for signals about the outlook for interest rates in the near future.
Fed officials have signaled that the U.S. central bank will not continue raising short-term interest rates this week. However, with inflation concerns remaining central, investors believe this pause in rate hikes is unlikely to last. The market is now betting on the possibility of a Fed rate hike in December.
Geng Ngarmboonanant, Director of Macroeconomics and Policy in the Multi-Asset Investment Solutions division at JP Morgan Asset Management, questioned whether the US economy could sustain growth in a high-interest-rate environment. He stated that the answer is yes, as the US economy is expected to remain adaptable and function even under higher interest rates.

articles.title: European Gas Prices Surge to Nearly Four-Year High; Winter Energy Crisis and Inflation Fears Resurface - Sunsirs
articles.summary: European Gas Prices Surge to Nearly Four-Year High; Winter Energy Crisis and Inflation Fears Resurface  Sunsirs
articles.full_text:
SunSirs: European Gas Prices Surge to Nearly Four-Year High; Winter Energy Crisis and Inflation Fears Resurface
October 27 2026 09:23:24
European natural gas prices have spiked once again, intensifying concerns over energy supplies for the upcoming winter.
On October 23, the Dutch TTF futures—the benchmark for European natural gas—rose by as much as 3.8% during intraday trading, reaching €93.43 per megawatt-hour (MWh), the highest level since late 2022. This surge was driven by escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and market anxieties regarding potential disruptions to liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.
According to *The Wall Street Journal*, the contract has gained nearly 7% over the course of this week. Meanwhile, European natural gas storage levels remain below those seen at the same time in previous years. As the winter heating season approaches, the combination of supply uncertainty and insufficient inventory buffers has once again brought Europe’s energy security and inflation outlook into sharp focus.
Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) shows that, as of October 22, EU gas storage facilities were 74.6% full. While Europe has gradually adjusted its natural gas supply structure following the previous energy crisis, its continued reliance on the global LNG market means that developments in the Middle East, international competition for spot cargoes, and weather patterns could all impact the European economy through fluctuations in gas prices.
Insufficient Inventory Buffers
The current rise in European gas prices is not driven by a single factor. Heightened geopolitical risks have fueled market fears regarding potential LNG supply disruptions, while relatively low inventory levels have made the market more sensitive to the prospect of supply shortfalls.
*The Wall Street Journal* reported on October 23 that the market is concerned that a further escalation in tensions involving the U.S. and Iran could jeopardize LNG supplies. Supply risks in the Middle East are a major concern—not only because regional exports could be disrupted, but also because Europe may need to compete in the global market to secure additional LNG cargoes. Unlike pipeline gas, LNG can be transported by ship between different regions; however, its final destination is influenced by factors such as total supply volume, shipping conditions, and the bidding power of various buyers.
The state of gas inventories further compounds market uncertainty. According to GIE data, EU storage facilities were at 74.6% capacity as of October 22. The association’s previously released winter supply outlook noted that Europe entered the heating season with relatively low inventory levels. Coupled with uncertainties surrounding LNG supplies, this leaves the natural gas system with limited buffers to cope with demand peaks or supply disruptions.
Furthermore, Europe’s competitive position in the global LNG market is another key factor driving up natural gas prices in the region.
Following the reduction in Russian pipeline gas supplies, LNG has become a vital component of Europe’s gas supply system. While this shift has enhanced Europe’s ability to seek alternative sources, it has also made the region more vulnerable to global supply fluctuations. When risks emerge in major exporting regions, European buyers must not only account for local demand but also consider LNG procurement needs in markets like Asia, as well as the feasibility of spot cargoes arriving in Europe in a timely manner.
Countries such as the United States and Qatar are major global sources of LNG. Should the situation in the Middle East disrupt exports or shipping, Europe’s ability to secure sufficient alternative supplies will depend on the production capacity of other exporters, the reallocation of cargoes, and market pricing. Even if Europe manages to attract supplies by paying higher prices, it would likely face significantly increased energy procurement costs.
However, rising gas prices do not necessarily mean that Europe is destined for a repeat of the 2022 energy crisis.
A recent analysis by the *Financial Times* points out that while LNG exports from the Gulf region have faced disruptions, other suppliers have offset some of the losses; consequently, the overall impact on global LNG supply has been less severe than the scale of the disruption in the Gulf alone.
The analysis further suggests that European natural gas demand has declined since the 2022 energy crisis. Improvements in energy efficiency, the widespread adoption of heat pumps, the growth of renewable energy generation, and a contraction in certain industrial sectors are all reshaping Europe’s natural gas consumption patterns.
Weather is another critical variable for short-term market trends. Citing analysts at ANZ, *The Wall Street Journal* reported that recent mild weather has helped ease pressure on the European gas market; however, an expected drop in temperatures in November could drive up heating demand. For Europe, the real risk lies in the potential convergence of low inventories, supply bottlenecks, and cold weather—rather than simply gauging the likelihood of a winter shortage based solely on current inventory levels. Resurgence of Inflationary Pressures
The impact of rising natural gas prices on the European economy is propagating downstream through three primary channels: household energy costs, operational pressures on businesses, and the cost of fuel for power generation.
Data from Eurostat indicates that the inflation rate in the Eurozone climbed to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August. Energy prices, in particular, surged by 18.8% year-on-year—an increase from the 14.3% recorded in August—making them a key driver of the rebound in Eurozone inflation.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has noted that businesses are becoming increasingly sensitive to cost fluctuations. With the transmission of price changes accelerating, energy shocks are propagating more rapidly through the supply chain, thereby reinforcing the stickiness of inflation.
Energy-intensive sectors—such as chemicals, glass, ceramics, and steel—experienced production cuts or even plant closures during the 2022 energy crisis. The latest spike in natural gas prices has once again intensified the operational pressures facing these industries.
European industry associations have recently warned that if energy prices remain persistently high, some companies may be forced to cut production capacity again or relocate operations abroad—a trend that poses a long-term threat to the competitiveness of Europe’s manufacturing sector.
Meanwhile, the squeeze on household purchasing power caused by soaring energy bills cannot be overlooked. Natural gas and electricity expenditures account for a significant share of household consumption in the European Union, a burden felt most acutely by low-income families. In many European countries, electricity pricing mechanisms remain pegged to the marginal cost of natural gas; consequently, rising gas prices directly drive up wholesale electricity costs, which in turn increases electricity expenses for both households and businesses. Higher energy expenditures leave households with less disposable income for other goods and services, potentially dampening retail consumption and the recovery of the service sector—creating a negative feedback loop: "rising energy prices → contracting consumption → slowing economic growth." (Source: China Energy Net)

articles.full_text:
Dollar Firms as Central Bank Week Begins; Budget Risk Hangs Over Sterling
The dollar firmed on Tuesday as a rebound in tech stocks revived risk appetite. Traders are bracing for five central bank decisions in three days, plus a UK Budget that could reshape the outlook for gilts, Britain's government bonds, and sterling.
Dollar: Waiting on Warsh
The dollar index held near a one-week high around 102.04 as last week's rush into safe havens faded and a weaker euro lent support, Reuters reported. The yen, one of last week's best performers when worries about AI stocks drove investors to safety, slipped as risk appetite returned.
The Fed is expected to skip a hike when its two-day meeting ends Wednesday. Even so, CME's FedWatch tool, which turns futures prices into rate odds, put the chance of at least one hike by December at about 73% on Monday. US durable goods orders and consumer confidence data are due Tuesday, followed by third-quarter GDP and September PCE inflation on Thursday.
Euro: France Overshadows the ECB
France remains the euro's main weakness, and the euro has slipped to a near two-week low around 1.1165, down about 1.4% this month. The yield premium on French 10-year bonds over German debt, meaning the extra interest France pays to borrow compared with Germany, reached about 167 basis points ahead of this week's meeting, up from 92 at the ECB's September meeting, Reuters reported.
The ECB is expected to hold its deposit rate, the rate it pays banks to park cash with it, at 2.5% on Thursday. ECB President Christine Lagarde has said the fix for France's finances must come from fiscal policy at home. Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin said earlier this month that he does not think the ECB needs to intervene "as of now, given the current conditions."
Pound: Healey's First Test
Chancellor John Healey delivers his first Budget on Wednesday. The Financial Times reported that Healey will give two state-backed lenders, the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, a £20.4bn capital boost over five years. Deutsche Bank said that removes one large Budget Day risk, though it still adds to borrowing, which can push gilt yields up.
Markets treat a quarter-point Bank of England hike to 4% on November 5 as almost certain, so sterling's support depends on the Budget not shaking that view.
US Dollar Index Technical Analysis: DXY Climbs Above 102 as 102.43 Comes Into Focus
The US Dollar Index is trading near 102.09 on the 4-hour chart. Buyers defended the 101.54 support zone several times last week, helped by a rising trendline, a line connecting higher lows. DXY has now moved back above its faster moving average, a line showing the recent average price.

Three of the largest companies in tech are about to open their books in the same 48-hour window. Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon are set to release quarterly earnings between October 28 and October 29, 2026.
The Federal Reserve picked the same week to announce its next rate decision. Wall Street gets two major events in one stretch, which is a lot to absorb before Halloween.
The central question for investors is simple to state and hard to answer. Can cloud growth keep pace with the enormous sums these companies are pouring into AI infrastructure?
The schedule and the numbers
Microsoft goes first, reporting on October 28 after the market closes. That same afternoon, the Fed will announce its policy decision at 2:00 p.m. ET, followed by a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET.
Amazon follows on October 29, and Alphabet also reports within the window.
Consensus estimates set a high bar for each company. Microsoft is expected to post revenue of approximately $90.6 billion, with earnings per share of roughly $4.71 to $4.73.
Alphabet’s expected revenue sits at around $128 billion. Analysts are looking for EPS of approximately $2.94 to $3.03.
Amazon is the biggest by top line. It is anticipated to report revenue of about $202 billion, with an EPS forecast between $1.96 and $2.01.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
Cloud is where the story lives
Capital expenditure expectations for 2026 have climbed into the hundreds of billions of dollars, reflecting the ongoing race to build AI infrastructure.
Microsoft has already put a specific target on the table. The company guided Azure to 45% growth in constant currency for the upcoming quarter.
Constant currency strips out exchange-rate swings. It shows how the business grew on its own merits rather than because the dollar moved.
Analysts predict that revenue and key cloud metrics will show continued growth across all three companies. The catch is that those results will be benchmarked against prior high guidance figures like Azure’s.
Why the last few quarters matter
This earnings cycle comes after mixed reactions to the prior quarters. Demand driven by AI was strong, but it ran into concerns about rising costs and limits on capacity.
Market sentiment among analysts has framed this period as a key moment for judging whether cloud momentum can validate the ongoing capital investment. The companies face heightened scrutiny of both their spending plans and their growth strategies.
The Fed in the background
The Federal Reserve is expected to keep its target range for interest rates at 3.75% to 4.00% when it announces its decision on October 28.
Interest rates and tech valuations have a well-worn relationship. Companies valued on future earnings look less attractive when money costs more today, since those future dollars are discounted more heavily.
What this means for investors
Microsoft’s Azure figure is the cleanest single test. The company set a specific number, and the market will compare the result directly against it.
The timing adds a layer of complexity. Microsoft reports just hours after the Fed speaks, so its stock reaction could blend company news with macro sentiment in ways that are hard to untangle. Amazon and Alphabet will be read in light of both the Fed decision and Microsoft’s numbers.
Investors should watch three things closely: cloud growth rates against guidance, any changes to capex outlooks, and the Fed’s language on the path of rates.

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boomTrillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major compa...
articles.full_text:
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

articles.full_text:
In brief
- Robinhood reported record third-quarter revenue of $1.42 billion, slightly below the roughly $1.43 billion expected, and earnings of $0.51 per share versus $0.55 expected.
- Event contracts revenue rose to $173 million from $156 million in the second quarter, and crypto revenue rose to $120 million from $100 million but fell 55% from a year earlier.
- Robinhood trimmed the top of its 2026 cost guidance to a range of $2.675 billion to $2.75 billion, and shares slipped in after-hours trading.
Robinhood, the trading app where more than 28 million people keep money to buy stocks and crypto and now bet on sports and elections, reported third-quarter revenue of $1.42 billion billion on Tuesday, missing the roughly $1.43 billion Wall Street expected
Earnings came in at $0.51 per share, missing the $0.55 analysts projected and down from $0.61 a year ago. Earnings per share is profit divided by the number of shares outstanding, and it is the figure investors use to call a quarter a beat or a miss.
Robinhood is the app that brought commission-free trading to a generation of first-time investors, which makes its quarterly report one of the clearest readings of what ordinary people are doing with their money. When customers trade more, deposit more or pile into new products, the shift shows up in these numbers.
Net income was $476 million, down 14% from $556 million a year earlier and 17% from $573 million in the second quarter. The quarter included a $67 million unrealized loss, meaning a drop in value on paper, on Robinhood Ventures Fund I, which cost $0.07 per share. Adjusted earnings per share, which exclude certain items, came to $0.60, down 3% from a year ago.
Event contracts, the yes-or-no bets that pay out $1 if a game, an election or an economic report goes a certain way, brought in $173 million, up from $156 million in the second quarter, when they overtook crypto revenue for the first time. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion of them, more than seven times a year earlier.
“I believe we’re at the very beginning of a prediction market supercycle,” CEO Vlad Tenev said in December last year, when Robinhood added NFL player contracts and parlay-style combos that pay only if every outcome hits.
Crypto trading revenue rose to $120 million from $100 million in the second quarter, but remained down 55% from the $268 million Robinhood earned in the third quarter of 2025. Customers traded $50 billion in crypto during the quarter, down 38% from a year earlier, with $21 billion on the Robinhood app and $29 billion through Bitstamp, the crypto exchange it acquired
Robinhood Chain went live on July 1 as a layer-2 network, meaning a blockchain that runs on top of Ethereum to make transactions cheaper and faster. Its first weeks were driven by meme coins, joke-themed tokens, rather than the tokenized stocks it was built for, which are digital versions of company shares that trade on a blockchain.
By the end of August the chain had earned about $3.13 million in fees over 30 days, more than Ethereum and Base, which came in at $2.47 million and $2.89 million.
Hours before the report, Robinhood announced a deal with Ripple that brings RLUSD, a stablecoin (a crypto token designed to stay worth one dollar), to Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, with an in-app rollout planned later this year. RLUSD has a market value above $2.5 billion, and Ripple will also supply Robinhood’s treasury software and lending for Bitstamp traders.
Robinhood shares closed Tuesday at about $94.61 and slipped in after-hours trading- The stock is down roughly 18% this year and about 37% below its 52-week high of $150.47.
Robinhood narrowed its 2026 outlook for adjusted operating expenses and stock-based pay to $2.675 billion to $2.75 billion, trimming the top of the $2.675 billion to $2.775 billion range it set in July.

articles.title: Futures Mixed: 3 Catalysts - Fed, MSFT, GOOGL [2026] - shattered.io
articles.summary: Futures Mixed: 3 Catalysts - Fed, MSFT, GOOGL [2026]  shattered.io
articles.full_text:
U.S. stock futures traded mixed on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, while investors waited for a Federal Reserve rate decision and for Microsoft and Alphabet to report after the closing bell. Yahoo Finance told readers that Oct. 28 would be an important day for the stock market, and Investor’s Business Daily put the same story in its headline, which pairs mixed futures and five late movers with the Fed, Microsoft and Google looming.
The setup is unusual because three big catalysts land inside one trading day. The Fed announces its interest-rate decision at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Alphabet reports after the close and holds its call at 4:30 p.m. Microsoft follows with its first-quarter fiscal 2027 results and a call at 5:30 p.m. Futures sit in a holding pattern until all three finish.
For developers and engineering leaders, the day matters beyond the stock tickers. Cloud platforms and AI tooling now drive a huge share of software budgets, and both reports will show how fast customers keep spending. Our earlier look at Google Cloud’s 82% jump to $24.8 billion set the baseline that Alphabet has to defend tonight.
This analysis sticks to what the cited reports confirm. Where the record is thin, such as the exact list of five movers in the IBD headline or any after-hours price reaction, we say so and avoid filling the gap with guesses.
What the Fed Decision at 2:00 p.m. ET Means for Tech Stocks
The Federal Open Market Committee releases its decision at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time, and Chair-led remarks follow at a 2:30 p.m. press conference. The cited reports put the committee’s stated target range at 3.75% to 4.00%. Coverage describes a clear market expectation that the Fed leaves rates unchanged at this October meeting.
A hold is the base case, so the decision itself rarely moves prices. The words around it do. Traders parse the statement for changes in language about inflation, the labor market and the path of future meetings. A single reworded sentence can swing Nasdaq futures by more than the rate decision does when the outcome is already priced in.
Technology stocks react more sharply than most sectors because their valuations lean on long-dated cash flows. Higher expected rates shrink the present value of those cash flows, and lower expected rates inflate it. Cloud and software names carry that sensitivity into every Fed meeting. Chipmakers and memory suppliers share it, with an extra layer of exposure to AI capital spending.
The timing adds a twist. Because the Fed speaks at 2:00 p.m. and the two earnings reports arrive hours later, the market digests the macro signal first and the company signal second. If the press conference shifts the rate outlook, Alphabet and Microsoft report into a changed backdrop. Their guidance then lands on a market that has already repriced once.
The takeaway for readers: treat the 2:00 p.m. decision as a volatility event and the 2:30 p.m. press conference as the real information release. Anyone comparing today’s futures moves with tomorrow’s open should expect the two to differ.
Microsoft Earnings: Fiscal 2027 Opens With Azure’s 43% Bar
Microsoft reports its first-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the U.S. market close, with the earnings call scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Eastern Time. One cited report states that Azure and other cloud-services revenue grew 43% in the prior quarter. That figure sets the bar investors will hold the new quarter against.
Cloud growth at that pace carries a cost. Training and serving AI models requires data-center buildouts, chips and power, and those expenses weigh on margins even while revenue climbs. Investors want to see two things at once: Azure holding strong growth, and capital spending that does not outrun the revenue it supports.
Microsoft’s story also reaches into developer tools and enterprise software. Its agent strategy, which we covered in Nadella’s pitch on agents and 11,000 models, depends on cloud demand staying hot. Any comment on how customers consume those agent workloads on the call will draw attention from engineers as much as analysts.
The company also faces workforce and cost questions. Management commentary on headcount, operating costs and AI investment could tie those threads together tonight, since all three feed the same margin story.
Our sources do not confirm consensus estimates, guidance ranges or any after-hours move for Microsoft, so we leave those out. What the record does confirm is the schedule, the fiscal quarter and the 43% prior-quarter cloud growth figure. Everything else in tonight’s print remains unknown until the company releases it.
Alphabet Earnings: Google Cloud’s $24.8 Billion Base
Alphabet reports after the close as well, and its call starts at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time, an hour before Microsoft’s. One cited report states that Google Cloud revenue reached $24.8 billion after growing 82% in the prior quarter. A growth rate that high leaves little room for a slowdown without a visible market reaction.
The earlier call order matters. Alphabet speaks first, so its cloud and capital-spending comments reach the market before Microsoft’s team starts. If Alphabet signals that AI demand keeps outrunning capacity, investors may carry that read into Microsoft’s call. If it flags constraints, the same logic can run in the opposite direction.
Retail-focused brokers have published previews of the quarter. Admiral Markets titled its preview Alphabet Stock Before Q3 2026 Earnings: Levels and Risks, which signals how much of the pre-earnings conversation centers on technical price levels and downside scenarios. We do not reproduce its targets here because our fact sheet does not confirm them.
Google Cloud now ranks among the most closely watched lines in all of tech earnings. Developers who build on Google’s platform, from small teams shipping Kubernetes workloads to enterprises training models, keep that segment growing. Investors will listen for backlog commentary, customer concentration and how much of the growth traces to AI workloads versus classic infrastructure.
The Five Key Movers Headline: What We Can and Cannot Confirm
The IBD headline promises five key movers late in the session. The specific list of those five is not confirmed in the material available to us, and we decline to guess it. Readers who want the exact names should check the IBD market note directly once it updates.
What the cited reports do confirm is a roster of companies tied to this week’s earnings or market coverage. That roster spans technology, energy, health care, consumer goods, telecom, finance and aerospace, which explains why the week feels crowded. The reports identify these names:
- Technology and cloud: Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Intel Corporation
- Memory and chips: SK Hynix, which released third-quarter results
- Health care: Eli Lilly
- Energy: Exxon Mobil and Chevron
- Telecom and payments: Verizon Communications and Visa
- Consumer and industrial: The Coca-Cola Company and The Boeing Company
The Raleigh News & Observer ran a week-ahead piece that paired the Fed with tech and oil earnings, which fits the mix of Alphabet and Microsoft on one side and Exxon Mobil and Chevron on the other. That blend of sectors helps explain why futures stayed mixed instead of leaning one way.
Our sources do not confirm which of these companies the IBD list calls out as movers, nor how far any of them moved. We therefore treat the headline as a signal of attention, not a ranked list of winners. That distinction keeps this article accurate, and it protects readers from acting on a price move nobody has verified.
Today’s Schedule in Eastern, UTC and Berlin Time
Global readers need the schedule in their own time zones. The table below lists each confirmed event in Eastern Time and converts it for UTC and Central European Time. Clocks in the U.S. change on November 1 while Europe changed on October 25, so this week the U.S.-to-UTC gap is four hours and the Berlin gap is six.
| Event | Eastern Time | UTC | Berlin (CET) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| FOMC rate decision (target range 3.75% to 4.00%) | 2:00 p.m. | 18:00 | 19:00 | 
| Fed press conference | 2:30 p.m. | 18:30 | 19:30 | 
| U.S. market close, Alphabet and Microsoft releases follow | 4:00 p.m. | 20:00 | 21:00 | 
| Alphabet earnings call | 4:30 p.m. | 20:30 | 21:30 | 
| Microsoft earnings call (first-quarter fiscal 2027) | 5:30 p.m. | 21:30 | 22:30 | 
Engineers who like to script their own alerts can convert the same times with a few lines of Python. The snippet below uses the standard library’s zoneinfo module, so it respects daylight-saving rules without extra packages.
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
ET = ZoneInfo("America/New_York")
events = {
    "FOMC decision": datetime(2026, 10, 28, 14, 0, tzinfo=ET),
    "Fed press conference": datetime(2026, 10, 28, 14, 30, tzinfo=ET),
    "Alphabet call": datetime(2026, 10, 28, 16, 30, tzinfo=ET),
    "Microsoft call": datetime(2026, 10, 28, 17, 30, tzinfo=ET),
}
for name, when in events.items():
    utc = when.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC"))
    berlin = when.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin"))
    print(f"{name}: {when:%H:%M} ET | {utc:%H:%M} UTC | {berlin:%H:%M} Berlin")
One practical note: futures keep trading outside regular hours, so the first read on the Alphabet and Microsoft reactions will appear in after-hours futures and stock quotes. The next full-session reading comes at Thursday’s open.
Cloud Growth and AI Capex Side by Side
The strongest numbers on the confirmed list come from the cloud segments and from Meta’s spending. The table pulls together the figures that investors will use as yardsticks tonight. Every figure comes from the cited reports and covers the prior reporting period, not the quarter being announced.

articles.title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more - TechCrunch
articles.summary: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more  TechCrunchChart: Anthropic's cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company  CNBCInside Anthropic's massive — and wild — IPO prospectus  AxiosAnthropic IPO filing reveals AI security breaches, training halt  Fox NewsDon’t expect supersize profits from Anthropic soon  The Economist
articles.full_text:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions.
Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.
While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.
Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.
According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.
As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.
Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.
But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.
Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.
Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.
While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.
The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.
