articles.title: RFI offers path forward for DoD with CMMC - Federal News Network
articles.summary: RFI offers path forward for DoD with CMMC  Federal News NetworkDoD’s reasons for CMMC pause falling apart in face of RFI responses  Federal News NetworkThe battlefield has no boundaries: How the Iran war is redrawing the cyber threat map  Federal News NetworkScope And Cost: A Cybersecurity Guide For Small Defense Suppliers  Aviation WeekThe CMMC deadline paused, but the obligations didn’t  DevPro Journal
articles.full_text:
Storage Preferences
DoD’s Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification task force outlined several short- and medium-term steps to address long-time program challenges.
This is part 2 of a two-part investigation into the Defense Department’s Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) program. You can find part 1 here.
While the future of the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification is unclear, the Defense Department has a host of options to not only save face after its self-imposed, months-long pause, but also to address several of its publicly expressed concerns.
Current and former federal officials and industry experts say DoD’s reasons for pausing CMMC have little to nothing to do with the actual program, but they are all about the underlying security control requirements outlined in National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171.
And while rewriting SP 800-171 is a long process and moving away from it altogether is possible, but difficult, there are several initiatives DoD could implement over the short and medium term to address real or perceived concerns.
“Industry identified several common approaches to easing these burdens, and of the recommendations, several are feasible in the short term, while others would require more time and effort to implement, if approved,” states a summary of DoD CMMC task force findings in early September.
In the summary of responses to the CMMC request for information DoD issued in July, which Federal News Network obtained, the task force outlined three sets of reform options:
Among those that the DoD CIO could make meaningful improvements without rulemaking include addressing ambiguity in CMMC because of inconsistent implementation among assessors, primes contactors and the CMMC program management office. Another option would be to implement NIST 800-171 Revision 3, which has been on hold since DoD CIO Kirsten Davies took over in December. And they could address a long-standing complaint of inconsistent marking of controlled unclassified information (CUI) by the military services and defense agencies and by the defense industrial base (DIB).
Suggested changes that fit under category two, costly or more difficult, include extending the plan of action and milestones (POA&M) compliance requirements, creating templates and configuration settings to make acceptance testing easier and addressing reciprocity with other security compliance programs where there are competing requirements and potentially unacknowledged overlap, such as with ISO 27002.
Additionally, the task force offered five sets of recommendations, some of which mirror earlier suggestions like finalizing the move to NIST SP 800-171 Revision 3, and to begin a second revision to address the new direction from the CMMC Reform Task Force. What that new direction is wasn’t detailed in the documents.
Over a 90-day period, the task force says DoD could restart Phase 2 of CMMC with a narrower population, while working on longer-term recommendations through the rulemaking process. It could work with the CMMC Accreditation Body (Cyber AB) and the Cybersecurity Assessor and Instructor Certification Organization (CAICO) to provide more guidance to assessors and consultants and to increase consistency.
Another recommendation is to publish assessor availability statistics and continue efforts to grow the ecosystem.
And finally, the DoD CIO could expand POA&M eligibility to 270 days, which the task force recognizes would require rulemaking but could be added to current “in process” amendment.
The task force also outlined actions the DoD CIO could take over the next 6-12 months and over the next year-plus to address rulemaking ideas.
For example over the next six months, the task force recommended providing explicit assessment guidance to confirm credit for comparable and relevant requirements in ISO 27002. Another option would be to minimize the volume of CUI sent to prime contractors and assist the DIB in doing the same with subcontractors through training, marking tools, security classification guides and constraining CUI flow down by extending virtual desktop interface-type solutions or hardcopy.
DoD says the RFI respondents highlighted concerns about the inconsistency of CUI marking and the associated ambiguity or burden in determining whether and which systems should be secured.
“If published, an already planned Federal Acquisition Regulations rule would include establishment of a new standard form for clearly articulating the CUI data to be shared (and safeguarded) during the performance of a contract,” DoD wrote in the summary. “The existing draft rule has the potential to drastically reduce the burden on industry, especially small businesses, by narrowing the population that must comply with NIST 800-171. Of all the RFI recommendations, those related to improving clarity in CUI marking has the greatest potential to narrow the DIB population subject to NIST 800-171 implementation and cybersecurity related costs.”
Ove the next year, the task force recommended DoD publish approved configurations and templates, similar to security technical implementation guides (STIG) for common platforms, developing assessment criteria and rule content for machine readable evidence using OSCAL and advocating for grants, subsidies and/or tax credits.
“Many respondents requested availability of free tools, grants, subsidies or tax credits to ease the burden of cybersecurity implementation and compliance. Of these, the department could develop free tools, subject to funding availability,” DoD stated in the task force summary. “For grants, subsidies or tax credits, the department could advocate on behalf of the DIB but could not unilaterally address these recommendations.”
Federal News Network repeatedly asked DoD to comment on the RFI results, the review process and Davies’ overall feelings about CMMC, sending 15 specific questions. DoD declined to comment.
Current and former federal officials and industry experts say few of these ideas are new and many have been something DoD has considered or concepts vendors have recommended over the last five or more years.
Katie Arrington, who was performing the duties of the DoD CIO before the Senate confirmed Davies, has been a vocal supporter of CMMC and rolled it out during the first Trump administration. She said DoD could roll out CMMC and then focus on improving it.
“I believe the audit process can be streamlined and refined. But it has to start in order to refine it,” Arrington said in an interview with Federal News Network. “There are things in SP-800-171 that are past their prime. Things like better identity and access management, data labeling and tagging and using AI can help. But you have to start the program in order to refine it and make it your own. That is the part that I think Davies is missing.”
Arrington, who now is a quantum technology evangelist at IonQ, said defining what data is CUI in greater specificity is one initial step. She said developing an AI tool that DoD contracting officers could run against a solicitation to determine what is CUI would be straight forward.
At the same time, she said the department could use AI to improve the labeling and tagging of data.
Over the longer term, Arrington said DoD, which never performed a proper cost realism study, could determine what the actual costs are to comply with not just CMMC, but NIST 800-171.
“We begged the acquisition community to do a study for the last nine years, which usually happens prior to milestone A when buying weapons systems. They do a market study for how much it should cost to come up with an estimated cost. It’s not clear why they aren’t or haven’t done that,” she said. “When we make you implement NIST 800-171, how much do we think it will cost? Then we can build that cost into the program estimate.”
Arrington said for every program, not just CMMC, there would be a known security cost and that would allow companies to build those costs into their rates.
A former government official with knowledge of CMMC added DoD overlooked, or ignored, the fact that implementing SP 800-171 was cost prohibitive.
“There were indicators that this was an issue several years ago,” the source, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation, said. “When DoD initiated Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation clause 252 204-7012, a regulatory analysis was not part of the rulemaking process in 2016. In 2017, when the first Trump administration updated the rulemaking process to include the requirement to do a regulatory impact analysis to understand how much it will cost people to implement 800-171, it never got done.”
At the same time, the FAR Council CUI rule does have a regulatory impact analysis. While it’s not finalized, the source said it is not as comprehensive, especially when considering the requirements of the DIB.
The idea of loans or grants is another that has been floated around for many years.
Arrington said the Small Business Administration could easily set one up with an incentive for small firms to remain in good cyber standing.
“If the small business is working with the federal government and they stay in good standing based on a cyber audit, the government would forgive the debt after so many years,” she said. “We are losing so much of our budget in research and development and intellectual property every year. Every time ransomware takes someone down, they write it off as a loss. How much are we losing from that? Writing off a loan program would pale by comparison.”
Eric Crusius, a partner with the law firm Hunton, said a loan program or some sort of grant for third-party assessors would be an easy win for DoD.
“If folks are looking for an easy win and to save money, this would expand the DIB pretty quickly,” Crusius said. “The cost for C3PAOs would be a fraction of the Pentagon’s budget and in exchange for a more secure contracting base and one that attracts innovative companies.”
Un

articles.title: The Fed says it ignores politics. Its rate moves tell a more complicated story - CNN
articles.summary: The Fed says it ignores politics. Its rate moves tell a more complicated story  CNN
articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials agree that inflation needs to return to the central bank’s 2% annual target. Instead, the war with Iran has sent gas prices soaring, and price increases are starting to spread beyond the gas station. Last month, that prompted Fed officials to raise rates for the first time in three years to cool the economy and bring down inflation.
Yet this month, even with the inflation picture worsening, the Fed is widely expected to hold rates steady at its Wednesday meeting.
Would that still be the case if the midterms weren’t just six days away?
At his 2:30 p.m. press conference Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is likely to face questions about political pressure if the central bank does keep rates unchanged. The Fed’s independence is a cornerstone of its monetary policy decisions. However, in an election year, that independence inevitably comes under the microscope.
Outside of the pandemic, when rates were kept at near-zero levels, the Fed adjusted rates within two months of Election Day in four out of five of the most recent election years.
In September 2024, for example, the Fed slashed its benchmark interest rate by half a point just six weeks before the presidential election. That marked the start of a cutting cycle as inflation cooled and officials grew concerned about a weakening labor market.
Meanwhile, leading into the 2022 elections, the central bank pushed out two consecutive three-quarter point hikes, triple the size of the typical rate move, as it battled the worst inflation in almost four decades. And at the meeting after Election Day it announced another hike, this time a smaller half point.
In 2016, officials didn’t change rates at the two immediate meetings before Election Day and instead hiked rates by a quarter point at the subsequent meeting.
At that time, then-Philadelphia Fed President Patrick Harker supported a rate hike in September. However, he said he was opposed to hiking at the November meeting that was just six days before the presidential election.
“What I’m worried about is depending on the outcome of the election and what happens after that, if there are policies that would have distortive effects that we would have to respond to, we’ll have to respond,” Harker said in remarks in October 2016. “And I don’t know which way that will go. But it may be prudent to wait until we have resolved some of that uncertainty.”
Then-Fed Chair Janet Yellen, though, said the election did not play any role in officials’ decision-making process.
Leading up to this week’s meeting, Fed officials have signaled that they believe economic conditions don’t warrant another immediate hike and that they would rather wait for more data. That’s because raising rates too early could unnecessarily weaken the economy — for example, by prompting consumers to pull back on spending as borrowing costs rise.
That measured approach contrasts with President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates.
Elected officials, particularly presidents, tend to favor lower interest rates because that makes it cheaper for consumers and businesses to borrow. Trump, whose support has been faltering in recent months as gas prices and other costs have risen, has increased his pressure on the Fed to lower rates.
Trump tapped Warsh to succeed Fed Chair Jerome Powell after repeatedly criticizing the central bank for not aggressively cutting rates. But Warsh’s first major move as head of the central bank was a rate hike, a decision that many viewed as a sign he wasn’t going to let politics interfere with Fed policy.
Nonetheless, if the Fed does hold rates steady as expected, Warsh may have to work harder than usual to convince Americans that the political calendar played no part in its decision. (While the Fed chair has considerable power at the Fed, the position represents just one vote on a 12-person committee.)
“Tightening cannot appear to be a move against the administration, while holding cannot look like accommodation,” EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said in a note last week.
Meanwhile, Bank of America head of US economic research Aditya Bhave noted that since investors expect the Fed to hold rates steady, a hike could now catch markets off guard and trigger further volatility at an already tense time.

articles.title: European Stocks Slip as HSBC Rout Puts Banks Under Pressure Ahead of Big Tech Earnings - Tekedia
articles.summary: European Stocks Slip as HSBC Rout Puts Banks Under Pressure Ahead of Big Tech Earnings  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
European stocks fell on Tuesday as disappointing results from HSBC dragged down banking shares, while investors reduced risk ahead of a packed week of earnings from major US technology companies and interest-rate decisions from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.
The pan-European STOXX 600 slipped 0.2%, while Britain’s FTSE 100 fell 1%, largely reflecting the sharp decline in HSBC shares. The STOXX 600 banking index dropped 1.3%, with Europe’s largest lender losing around 7% after third-quarter revenue fell short of expectations, despite a 32% increase in pretax profit to $9.6 billion.
HSBC’s results highlighted the growing difficulty banks face in sustaining strong earnings as deposit competition pushes up funding costs and slower wealth-management growth constrains fee income. The reaction also illustrated how investors have become less willing to reward headline profit growth when companies fail to deliver stronger revenue or improve their outlook.
Register for the next Tekedia Mini-MBA.
Register for Tekedia AI in Business Masterclass.
Join Tekedia Capital Syndicate and co-invest in great global startups.
The broader market remained focused on the possibility of corporate earnings withstanding the economic consequences of the conflict in Iran, including higher energy costs, renewed inflation pressures and the possibility that interest rates will remain elevated for longer.
“Banks have been the winners of the latest quarter before this one, reporting record results because of high volatility and because of AI financing,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior market analyst at Swissquote Bank.
“But right now, they are coming under pressure because we do see the interest rate rise, short-term yields rising more than long-term; that’s basically eating into the income revenue,” she added.
Ozkardeskaya said she nevertheless expected banks to remain well positioned to outperform sectors more directly exposed to rising living costs.
Attention is shifting to the United States, where more than a third of S&P 500 companies are expected to report quarterly results this week. Earnings from Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet will be in the spotlight as investors assess whether the technology industry’s enormous investments in artificial intelligence are generating sufficient returns.
That has raised a question beyond how much companies are spending on AI to whether that spending can translate into durable revenue growth, improved productivity and higher profits. Major technology companies have committed billions of dollars to data centers, advanced chips and other computing infrastructure, making their capital expenditure plans a critical indicator of the industry’s direction.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said the firm remained optimistic about companies supplying the infrastructure behind AI development.
“We remain medium-term bullish on the ‘picks and shovels’ trade. We see capex cycle remaining strong and the earnings remaining robust,” Kumar said.
“However, we do admit that, as with any cycle, there would be winners and losers in the AI trade and a number of companies will not remain profitable and even go bust.”
That backdrop has increasingly come into consideration as concerns mount about the financial sustainability of the AI infrastructure boom. Continued spending by the largest technology companies could support demand for semiconductor manufacturers, data-center operators and equipment suppliers. But if customers begin to question the returns on their investments, even businesses benefiting from strong AI demand could face pressure.
Therefore, the upcoming results are expected to influence sentiment beyond the technology sector. Investors are looking for evidence that AI investments can support future earnings rather than simply inflate capital expenditure and financing requirements. Any indication that spending is slowing, or that monetization is lagging behind expectations, could challenge the valuations of companies associated with the AI trade.
The results also arrive at a sensitive moment for the industry’s financing environment. Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, disclosed a steep loss alongside rapid revenue growth in its US initial public offering filing on Monday. The company is expected to list before the end of November, making its debut another test of investor appetite for high-growth AI businesses with substantial spending requirements.
Anthropic’s planned offering and Meta Platforms’ $95 billion equity fundraising are likely to be influenced by the reception investors give the latest Big Tech results. Strong earnings and credible returns on AI investment could support demand for new equity offerings, while weaker guidance could make investors more selective about valuations and capital commitments.
Anthropic’s disclosure also helped lift Asian equities. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 0.1%, while Nasdaq futures were little changed following strong gains in the previous session.
Central Banks Hold The Key to Rate Expectations
Monetary policy is another major source of uncertainty, with the Federal Reserve, ECB and Bank of Japan all scheduled to announce decisions later this week. Economists broadly expect the three central banks to leave interest rates unchanged, shifting attention to policymakers’ comments about inflation and the path of future borrowing costs.
Fed policymakers have indicated that they are not preparing to raise short-term borrowing costs again on Wednesday. However, persistent inflation concerns have prompted investors to question how long a pause might last. Traders were pricing in a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool.
The prospect of higher rates complicates the outlook for both banks and technology companies. Banks can benefit from higher lending rates in some circumstances, but rising deposit costs and an unfavorable shift in the yield curve can erode margins. Technology companies, meanwhile, face higher financing costs and potentially lower valuations when investors demand greater returns to compensate for risk.
The euro slipped 0.1% to around $1.115, close to the low it reached in May two weeks earlier. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note was steady at 4.986%, remaining below the 5% threshold it breached in September as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds during market turbulence over AI concerns.
The rate outlook is also tied to developments in the Middle East. Ongoing talks with Tehran could influence energy prices and inflation expectations, while continued attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia have added to concerns about regional supply disruptions.
Brent crude rose 0.6% to $116.82 a barrel, while spot gold fell 0.6% to $3,992.70 an ounce.
Higher oil prices threaten to complicate central banks’ efforts to contain inflation by increasing transportation, manufacturing and household energy costs. If the resulting price pressures persist, policymakers may have less room to ease monetary conditions, even if economic growth weakens.
For equity investors, the combination of corporate earnings, AI spending and central-bank guidance creates a difficult balancing act. Strong results could support valuations, but resilient profits alone may not be enough if companies face rising costs, tighter financial conditions and uncertain returns on investment.
Tuesday’s decline in European shares reflects that tension. Investors are not abandoning the outlook for banks or AI-related businesses, but they are demanding stronger evidence that earnings can hold up as financing conditions tighten and geopolitical risks continue to influence markets.

articles.title: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign - investingLive
articles.summary: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Fitch says the US credit outlook stays broadly benign despite tighter funding, lifts 2026 and 2027 GDP forecasts to 2.1% and sees the Fed hiking to 4.25% in December. It calls AI the main growth driver and a key risk, flagging a recession scenario.
Fitch’s December call fits the view that the Fed is still on a hiking path, which supports front-end Treasury yields and the US dollar and argues against any near-term easing. The more telling signal for credit is the split it describes: investment-grade spreads near multi-year lows while CCC yields have blown out. Heavy hyperscaler issuance on top of Treasury supply raises the risk that new deals need bigger concessions even where credit quality holds up. For equities, putting a recession scenario next to AI capex keeps the spotlight on any sign that hyperscalers are scaling back spending plans.
---
I spotted the headlines from Fitch overngiht and just bringing it to investingLive now. Fitch trails behind S&P and Moody's but I doubt their analysis and conclusions would be too much different.
----
Fitch still calls US credit benign overall, but its December Fed hike call, record private credit defaults and an AI-driven recession scenario show the pressure building on the weakest borrowers.
Summary:
- Fitch expects the US credit outlook to stay broadly benign, though higher-for-longer rates and AI funding needs will test interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers.
- It raised its US GDP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 point to 2.1% each, and expects the Fed to hike to 4.25% in December and hold through 2027.
- US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months, and corporate bond issuance rose around 25%, driven partly by hyperscaler AI borrowing.
- Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while CCC yields have widened by about 480 basis points this year.
- Fitch calls AI both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. Its adverse AI equity-correction scenario would mean a US recession, with GDP falling 0.6% in 2027.
- Fitch’s private credit default rate hit a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and leveraged loan defaults are expected near the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end range.
Fitch Ratings expects the US credit outlook to remain broadly benign, even as higher-for-longer interest rates and rising AI-related funding needs put interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers under pressure, according to a Fitch Wire commentary published Tuesday alongside its fourth-quarter US credit brief.
The ratings agency has lifted its US growth forecasts for both 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 percentage point to 2.1%, pointing to resilient consumer spending and AI-driven private investment. Fixed investment is forecast to grow 4.8% this year and 4.6% next year. On policy, Fitch expects the Federal Reserve to raise its policy rate to 4.25% in December and keep it there through 2027, which it says will sustain pressure on borrowers who need to refinance at higher costs.
Funding conditions are also being shaped by heavy Treasury supply and increased borrowing by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators, to pay for AI capital spending. Fitch said US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months of 2026, while corporate bond issuance climbed around 25%. The picture across the credit spectrum is uneven. Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while yields on CCC-rated debt, the lowest rung of high yield, have widened by about 480 basis points since the start of the year.
Fitch described AI investment as both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. IT-related private investment grew around 18% year on year in the second quarter, but the agency warned that intensifying competition and cheaper open-weight models could weaken the pricing power of AI service providers and prompt a rethink of hyperscaler capex plans over the next one to three years. Under Fitch’s adverse AI equity-correction scenario, the US would fall into recession, with GDP contracting 0.6% in 2027. Its sector-level AI stress test found broad resilience, with material risks concentrated in services, data centres, and telecommunications, media and technology.
Higher rates are weighing most heavily on housing-related sectors and lower-rated borrowers. Fitch’s US private credit default rate reached a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and the agency expects leveraged loan defaults to rise toward the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end forecast range.
The commentary leaves the Fed’s December decision and the durability of AI spending as the two variables most likely to determine whether a benign outlook for credit overall holds up for its weakest borrowers.

articles.title: Rzepczynski: 5.5% Treasury Yields Are Fair Value, and Broken Bond Plumbing Will Feed the Next Trend - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Rzepczynski: 5.5% Treasury Yields Are Fair Value, and Broken Bond Plumbing Will Feed the Next Trend  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Mark Rzepczynski wants to correct a widespread misreading. A 10-year Treasury yield near 5.5% is not the market breaking — it is the market doing arithmetic. Speaking on the Systematic Investor podcast, the trend-following researcher and former institutional quant argued that anyone who started their career after 2006 has no memory of a normal rate regime, and that memory gap is why a yield near 5% feels like a crisis when it may simply be fair value.
His build-up is simple. Take the natural real rate — long-run growth plus productivity — and with Atlanta Fed GDPNow running above 3% for the third quarter, allow 2.5%-plus. Add expected inflation of about 3%, justified because inflation has sat above the 2% target for well over six years. That gets you to roughly 5.5% before any term premium. Then add the term premium, which he argues should be higher now because the stock-bond correlation has turned positive and bond volatility has risen. On that basis, a 10-year near 5.5% is close to fair.
He applies the same math to France, where the 10-year traded just above 5% — a 24-year high, up about 1.65 percentage points in yield over twelve months and roughly half a point in the prior month alone. The euro-area stress of the 1990s sat farther south than France; this time the question is inverted. His verdict:
"It's not that we have an oddity, it's that this is normal."
That framing matters because it changes what investors should worry about. The level is not the story. The holders are.
Hedge funds replaced central banks, and they sell at a 5% loss
With quantitative easing wound down, central banks are no longer the marginal buyers of government debt. Hedge funds and multi-strategy pods have taken that role through basis trades and financing, and their relationship to price is entirely different from a government's.
"The elasticity of demand for bonds from hedge funds is much greater than what you're going to find from the government, because if they're not making profits... they're going to be reducing their positions. They're going to be much more sensitive."
Rzepczynski puts a number on it: a multi-strategy pod down 5% cuts positions. Government buyers do not have a stop-loss. So when a large holder wants out, expectations can flip into either a large rally or a large selloff quickly, depending on which side of the trade the leveraged money is on. This is the plumbing behind the violent single-session moves that have become routine in Treasuries.
Private balance sheets are clean; public ones are not
Rzepczynski separates the two using the Bank for International Settlements' credit-to-GDP early-warning framework. Households and private businesses have deleveraged and now manage their balance sheets well. Public debt ratios in the US, France and other advanced economies keep rising because budgets are not under control and because interest costs now dwarf many other line items.
He expects a cycle: countercyclical deficits in a recession, primary surpluses in the recovery. The second half is not happening.
"We run deficits when we have a recession because we're going to have countercyclical fiscal policy, and then once we come out of that, then we're going to use a primary surplus. So we're not getting that. And then on top of that, you add in the cost of debt."
The concrete example is Japan. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, the host, cites Jesper Koll's estimate from the episode published that Wednesday: roughly a third of Japan's national budget now goes to debt service after the rise in Japanese rates. Rzepczynski's conclusion is blunt — the private sector learned the lesson and the public sector did not.
The safe-asset premium is disappearing at the long end
Rzepczynski connects deficits to pricing through the convenience yield: what investors pay for liquidity, depth, and the ability to park size in a safe asset. In a crisis, demand for the safe asset rises and its convenience yield widens. When the Treasury issues more and more debt, the supply of the "safe" asset grows, and the premium compresses.
"When the government such as US Treasury continues to issue more and more treasury debt, then the supply of what is perceived as the safe asset increases by more and more, and that means the convenience yield is going to be shrunk."
His read is that the convenience yield has largely vanished at the long end of the Treasury curve and survives mainly in bills — possibly one reason issuance skews short. The same marginal erosion applies to the dollar's reserve premium: still dominant, but central bank reserve managers are diversifying into a more multipolar mix, a theme Rzepczynski credits to prior guest Ken Rogoff.
In Europe the hierarchy is being rewritten. Bunds were the safe asset, with a liquid French market as the alternative. Rzepczynski asks whether France qualifies as a safe asset "by any stretch of the imagination" relative to Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece — meaning the southern rim once treated as risky may now be less risky than France.
Gold complicates the story. It ran above 5,000 earlier in 2026, fell to about 4,100 in the summer, and was back near 4,100 at the time of recording — off its highs precisely when safe-haven demand should be strongest. For a classic safe asset, that is an odd place to be.
Watch dealer capital, not just price
Rzepczynski ties the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics, awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, to how he thinks about markets. Hall worked on consumption and labor-market decisions; Woodford on interest-rate control, the natural rate, and forward guidance — ideas that shaped a generation of central bankers. The prize, in his telling, honored building macroeconomics up from individual behavior.
He wants the same treatment for markets. Rather than reading price action alone, ask who the agents are, how exchanges set rules, and how policy shapes profit-maximizing behavior. That is the lens through which he reads Perry Mehrling, the Barnard College economist and author of the "money view" course, who died unexpectedly in the days before recording. Mehrling's influence: money is one integrated global system, so follow the money through wholesale payments, dealer financing and the shadow banking system. Mehrling also wrote a biography of Fischer Black.
The practical payoff is a way to spot crisis-prone environments before the crisis, rather than labeling them after the fact. Rzepczynski's variable is intermediation capital — the capacity of banks and primary dealers to warehouse risk. When a seller wants to offload bonds, a dealer holds them until a buyer appears. If that dealer is capital-constrained, by repo-market stress or balance-sheet limits, it cannot warehouse, and the transfer from seller to buyer happens fast and disorderly. He extends the same logic to commodity dealers.
Fragmentation decouples markets — and lets trend followers take more risk
Rzepczynski frames geoeconomics — tariffs, sanctions, capital controls, industrial policy — as the micro foundations of how countries interact. The investment consequence runs through correlation. A more fragmented world decouples markets and raises diversification; a less fragmented one correlates them and lowers it. Because trend followers size risk off the correlation matrix, fragmentation is directly a risk-budget input.
Kaastrup-Larsen adds the practitioner's version:
"When markets are more divergent, the correlation between positions and holdings in these strategies tends to come down, and that actually allows us as trend followers to take a little bit more risk."
He explains the reverse too: when correlations rise, good risk managers cut back because reversal risk in the portfolio climbs. He credits an old presentation by Kathryn Kaminski on convergent versus divergent strategies.
The concrete trading implication is duplicate contracts. New York and London cocoa, New York and London coffee, US versus European natural gas, crude in different locations — if tariffs and sanctions break the old arbitrage, a manager may need to trade both legs because delivery points diverge.
Commodity prices are set by inventories, and hoarding creates the shortage
Rzepczynski's commodity framework is that the binding constraint is inventory, not production. A stockout problem arises when a producer runs out of an input and will pay almost any price to avoid shutting down — a refinery without crude, a diesel truck that cannot take gasoline, a chocolate maker with no cocoa pods and no close substitute.
The dynamic is self-reinforcing.
"Everybody wants to hoard because they don't want to be stocked out, then you create the very problem that you want to avoid."
His analogy is shoppers clearing bread and toilet paper off the shelves before a blizzard. Europe's winter gas inventories were below the five-year average at the time of recording, so his prediction is specific: if Europe gets a genuinely cold winter, energy markets go parabolic. He separates "crisis alpha with a big C" from the market-by-market version, and points to cocoa as the recent example.
Machine-learning alpha decays faster than trend following
The AI arms race that dominates most market conversations arrives only at the end of the interview, and Rzepczynski's take is counterintuitive. Surveys put machine-learning use among hedge fund managers above 90%. Researchers are now measuring alpha half-life, and the finding is that it is shrinking.
"As all these people are using this, the half-life of alpha has shortened, alpha has reduced, because everybody's crowding out the returns from strategies."
The mechanism is structural, not cyclical. Quants are trained at the same schools — Carnegie Mellon, University of Toronto — on the same techniques: transformers, boosted methods, well-known published papers. Crowding accelerates, alpha decays faster, and firms must spend more compute to find the next model. That is the red queen problem: running faster just to stay even. 13F filings show gro

articles.title: ASX pares gains as inflation figures put pressure on RBA - SMH.com.au
articles.summary: ASX pares gains as inflation figures put pressure on RBA  SMH.com.au
articles.full_text:
The Australian sharemarket has shed some of its morning gains after the release of the nation’s latest inflation figures increased pressure on the Reserve Bank to lift interest rates at its meeting next week.
Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that headline inflation jumped to 4.3 per cent in September after being at 4 per cent in August, due to a surge in petrol prices and a pick-up in the cost of building homes.
The closely watched underlying measure of inflation was 3.6 per cent. It was up slightly from the August report which had been revised down to 3.5 per cent. The bureau noted that petrol prices jumped by 9.4 per cent in September after a 14.8 per cent increase in August.
The S&P/ASX was up 38.4 points, or 0.4 per cent, to 8888.50 as of 11.52am AEDT, the bourse easing after the release of the inflation figures.
Meanwhile, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has made clear a further interest rate rise is on the agenda at the bank’s meeting next week.
Appearing before a Senate estimates hearing today, Bullock said the nation’s fundamental economic challenge was the inability of the economy to grow without putting upwards pressure on inflation.
“Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market still seems a little tighter than we previously judged,” she said in an opening statement.
Miners, banks and tech stocks powered the ASX this morning, while energy stocks declined. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.31¢.
Shares of Star Entertainment went into a trading halt ahead of a judgment by the Federal Court, which found the casino operator contravened anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws and hit it with a $260 million fine. Star argued in court last year that a fine of more than $100 million may exceed its financial means to pay.
Justice Cameron Moore was damning about Star’s conduct, and acknowledged that the casino operator may need to raise further cash to pay the fine. ”Star’s profitability is such that it is likely to need to raise money to pay any penalty,” he said.
Gold shares led the mining sector higher, with Northern Star Resources up 1.8 per cent, Evolution Mining up 3 per cent and Newmont up 1.1 per cent. Prices for the precious metal advanced as bargain hunters stepped in after it fell below a key level, while traders await the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision later this week.
“Gold is finding its feet again after briefly falling below $US4,000, with the sharp correction attracting bargain hunters and physical buyers,” said ING commodity strategist Ewa Manthey.
The two biggest miners, BHP and Rio, took a breather after their rally on Tuesday, rising 0.8 per cent and 0.6 per cent in early trade. Silver miner South32 rose 2.6 per cent, steelmaker BlueScope added 1.6 per cent and Lynas Rare Earths jumped 6.9 per cent.
Tech stocks also advanced, after renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted US stocks ahead of earnings from some of the tech giants. Software makers WiseTech, Xero and Technology One added 2.4 per cent, 1.7 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively, drone components maker Codan gained 2.3 per cent and cloud and data centre connections provider Megaport climbed 6.8 per cent.
Embattled NextDC, still recovering from its $3 billion share sell-off last week, rallied 10.7 per cent after outlining the contract conditions and financial covenants it has with its lenders and saying it was meeting those, with $8.67 billion in liquidity left at the end of September.
AI data centre landlord Goodman Group rose 2.5 per cent, leading the property sector higher.
Woolworths, the nation’s biggest supermarket chain, rose 1.1 per cent after saying its first-quarter sales rose 4.7 per cent to $19.4 billion, slightly beating market expectations, with Australian supermarket sales up 6.9 per cent. Woolies’ sell-out Ooshies campaign, which ran from mid-July and was sold out in a month, was so popular that staff were at times unable to cope with the demands of higher foot traffic and sales, chief executive Amanda Bardwell said. Rival Coles, which is releasing its first-quarter trading update on Friday, slid 0.2 per cent.
Meanwhile, the big four banks were all trading higher, bolstering the market’s early gains. CBA, the nation’s second-biggest stock, rose 1.4 per cent, Westpac added 0.9 per cent while ANZ Bank and National Australia Bank advanced 0.6 per cent.
Energy stocks were lower as oil held its two-day decline, with traders tracking the outcome of a tight Israeli election that’ll help to shape the course of the US war with Iran. West Texas Intermediate traded near $US100 a barrel after falling more than 3 per cent in the past two sessions. Brent fell below $US114. In Israel’s election, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot edged ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in exit polls, though both blocs remain short of a majority and votes were still being counted.
Local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos both slumped 2 per cent, and refiner Ampol lost 2.5 per cent.
On Wall Street overnight, renewed enthusiasm for artificial intelligence lifted equities ahead of earnings from some of the biggest tech companies and the Federal Reserve’s rate decision.
The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and pulled within 1.2 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 15 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.2 per cent.
The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks rose to another winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.
Broadcom climbed 4 per cent after announcing a $US63 billion ($89.6 billion) financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions.
Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia added 0.9 per cent and was one of the strongest forces behind Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.9 per cent and was consistently higher through the day following several days of sharp swings.
General Motors climbed 5.5 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it.
JetBlue Airways flew 19 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share in 2028.
Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far.
Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 5.5 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year.
Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market.
Boeing fell 10.7 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.1 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter.
In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged down to 4.99 per cent from 5.00 per cent late on Monday.
Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.2 per cent to $US109.41.
In other international markets, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves.

articles.title: SEBI imposes Rs 18 lakh penalty on Taurian MPS, directors and merchant banker over IPO disclosures - Moneycontrol.com
articles.summary: SEBI imposes Rs 18 lakh penalty on Taurian MPS, directors and merchant banker over IPO disclosures  Moneycontrol.com
articles.full_text:
Market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has imposed a total penalty of Rs 18 lakh on Taurian MPS Ltd, its two directors and merchant banker Gretex Corporate Services Ltd for failing to make required disclosures in the company's initial public offering (IPO) documents.
In an adjudication order passed on Tuesday, SEBI imposed a penalty of Rs 5 lakh on Taurian MPS, Rs 5 lakh jointly and severally on its directors Yashvardhan Sumit Bajla and Puja Sumit Bajla, and Rs 8 lakh on Gretex Corporate Services.
The regulator alleged that Taurian MPS failed to disclose Taurian Engineering Pvt Ltd (TEPL) as part of its promoter group and did not disclose the entity's liquidation status in the IPO offer document. SEBI held that these omissions violated the disclosure requirements under the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations.
The order said Puja Bajla's shareholding in Taurian Engineering had crossed the 20 percent threshold prescribed under the regulations for classifying an entity as part of the promoter group. Her shareholding had reached about 80 percent during the relevant period.
Taurian MPS and its directors argued that Taurian Engineering's investment in the company had been written off and its shareholding in the issuer had fallen to zero before the IPO. They also said the entity was under liquidation and its affairs were controlled by a liquidator.
SEBI rejected these arguments, stating that the promoter-group disclosure requirement could not be avoided merely because the investment had been written off or the entity was under liquidation. The noticees had also not sought an exemption under the relevant regulations.
Also read: SEBI extends deadline for debenture trustees to separate non-regulated businesses by six months
The order noted that Taurian Engineering was not under liquidation when Taurian MPS filed its draft red herring prospectus on February 28, 2025. Although the company entered the corporate insolvency resolution process in 2023, a liquidator was appointed on April 4, 2025. The liquidation followed its failure to repay Rs 3 crore, along with interest, to a financial creditor.
SEBI said the liquidation status was material information that could affect investors' assessment of the promoter group and associated risks. The regulator also examined allegations concerning Taurian Iron and Steel Pvt Ltd and Taurian Infrastructure Pvt Ltd. However, it concluded that the alleged disclosure violations relating to these two entities were not established.
SEBI held that Gretex Corporate Services had failed to exercise the required due diligence regarding the disclosure of Taurian Engineering's promoter-group status and liquidation.
The noticees argued that the IPO documents had undergone scrutiny by the National Stock Exchange and that the omissions were technical in nature. SEBI rejected the defence, saying exchange scrutiny did not absolve the issuer and merchant banker of their statutory disclosure obligations.
The noticees have been directed to pay the penalties within 45 days of receiving the order.

articles.title: Federal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections - Fox Business
articles.summary: Federal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections  Fox Business
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest interest rate decision on Wednesday with the midterm elections less than a week away.
Policymakers at the Fed say they avoid letting politics influence their monetary policy moves, and can be hesitant to hike or cut interest rates at meetings that occur ahead of the election.
Inflation has remained stubbornly high and the September consumer price index (CPI) data showed inflation rose faster than expected, with headline CPI rising 0.6% on a monthly basis and 3.7% from a year ago. The latter figure is well above the central bank's 2% inflation target.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told FOX Business in an interview that while the September inflation data was hotter than expected and raised the prospects of an October rate hike, the Fed is likely to wait to "hike again in December."
"This hotter than expected inflation data did increase the chance of an October rate hike, but it's a very high bar to increase in October, they would do it within a week of the election. I know they like to say that they're not political, but it's a high bar for October," she explained.
"Right now, this data indicates that the Fed needs to act again, but it's not a five-alarm fire. They don't have to act immediately, they could wait until December."
"The reality is, gas prices have come down a little bit since the September highs, so we would expect the October data – you know, it won't be great, but it could be a little bit cooler than what we're seeing today. And the Fed has a reasonable case to say, we're probably still gonna hike, but let's wait a few more weeks and see just how broad-based this problem really is," Long said.
The market expects the Fed to hold rates steady this week, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 90.6% probability of rates remaining at their current target range of 3.75% to 4% – up from 84.5% a week ago and 35.8% last month.
For the Fed's meeting in mid-December, the tool shows a 75.1% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike, which could mark the resumption of the rate-hiking cycle if inflation remains elevated.
"The Federal Reserve will definitely hike interest rates again, probably in December," Long said. "The big question is how many more times do they have to hike after that? And what was scary in this latest inflation data for September is to see so many areas of hot inflation: to see used car prices, airfares, recreation costs, auto repair costs, buying a used car, medical costs."
"The story really is starting to take shape that it's probably going to take a couple more hikes in 2027, and this higher-for-longer borrowing costs and mortgage rates well above 7% is going to stick around for at least a year, maybe longer," Long said.
The CME FedWatch tool shows the market is anticipating multiple rate hikes by March, with a 46.5% chance that rates will be 50 basis points higher than they are now at a range of 4.25% to 4.5%.

articles.title: Should you open a CD account before the Fed's next meeting? - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Should you open a CD account before the Fed's next meeting?  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Knowing how the Federal Reserve's monetary policy decisions impact your interest earnings over time is key to making an informed decision about where to put your money. With a potential rate hike looming, a certificate of deposit (CD) may be a good long-term option.
CDs can be a smart way to guarantee steady returns, especially if interest rates increase. When the Fed raises rates, CD rates typically tend to follow, though the timing and size of the increase can vary.
Here's why you may want to consider opening a CD before the Fed's next meeting.
What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?
A CD is a type of bank account that requires you to keep your money on deposit for a set period, known as the term. CD terms can range from a few months to several years.
In exchange for keeping your money tied up, CDs pay a fixed interest rate for the entire term. And CD rates are typically higher than what you'd get from a regular savings account. Once the CD reaches its maturity date, you can withdraw your original deposit plus any accrued interest.
Read more: Fixed rate vs. variable rate: What's the difference, and why is it important?
How the federal funds rate impacts CD rates
The federal funds rate is the target interest rate set by the Federal Reserve. It determines the rate banks charge one another to borrow funds overnight to meet reserve requirements.
The federal funds rate is expressed as a range, which is currently 3.75%–4%. Banks negotiate a specific rate between each other within that range.
The Fed uses the federal funds rate as a tool to quell inflation. When inflation is high, the Fed raises its target rate to make borrowing money more expensive, which discourages consumer spending and helps bring everyday costs down. When the economy needs a boost, the Fed might initiate a series of rate cuts to encourage more spending and borrowing.
Read more: A look at the federal funds rate over the past 50 years: How has it changed?
Changes to the federal funds rate have major implications for financial institutions and the economy at large. But these decisions also affect your bottom line.
Although the Fed's rate doesn't directly impact the interest rates set by individual banks for consumer deposit accounts and loans, they are closely correlated. When the Fed raises its rate, for example, interest rates on deposit products — including savings accounts and CDs — also tend to go up. And when it lowers its rate, deposit interest rates generally fall.
Also read: CD ladder vs. bond ladder: Which strategy is best for maximizing interest?
Should you open a CD before the next Fed meeting?
The Fed will meet again on Oct. 27-28 to decide whether to adjust the federal funds rate. In its last meeting, the committee raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75%–4%.
Markets believe the Fed will hold its benchmark interest rate steady this week. However, it's not possible to predict the Fed's next move with 100% certainty.
Read more: What time is the Fed's meeting?
If the Fed decides to raise the federal funds rate at some point this year, CD rates will soon start to increase. However, if you open a CD, you will lock in today's rates on your balance and continue earning that deposit rate.
If the rate hike is expected, there's a chance banks have already priced in the increase into today's CD rates. Waiting may not bring you a higher rate.
Even so, we can't know for sure what will happen. So, while you wait for the Fed's official announcement about how rates will change (or not), it could be a good time to evaluate where you're currently keeping your savings and consider opening a new CD.
Should the Fed decide to keep rates unchanged, it won't have a direct impact on CD rates, so now is as good a time as any to open an account and take advantage of historically high interest rates. As it stands, the best CD rates today hover around 4%.
But if the Fed does decide to lower rates, now might be your last chance to lock in today's competitive CD rates.

articles.title: The Fed’s October Meeting Starts Today. Here’s What You Need To Know - Investopedia
articles.summary: The Fed’s October Meeting Starts Today. Here’s What You Need To Know  Investopedia
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- Federal Reserve officials will likely hold interest rates steady Wednesday.
- September inflation ran at 3.7%, nearly double the Fed’s target.
- Analysts expect a December rate hike unless economic conditions shift unexpectedly.
Hotter inflation gives the Federal Reserve reason to raise interest rates again, analysts say, but officials will likely hold off at their meeting Wednesday and hike rates in December instead.
Fed officials have telegraphed this week’s pause in recent speeches, signaling little hurry to follow up their rate hike in September. That would keep the benchmark federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4%.
A surprise hike is certainly possible, analysts say, but that risks spooking markets after last week’s volatility and upcoming election uncertainty.
“With many Committee members calling for patience, we expect the Fed to avoid surprising markets and remain on hold in October,” wrote Michael Gapen, chief U.S. economist at Morgan Stanley.
There’s a strong case for rate hikes nonetheless, Gapen said, with inflation data arguing for more urgency. The Iran war’s energy shock is raising prices on gasoline, diesel and airfares, and September’s data suggested inflation pressures are broadening. The Consumer Price Index rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September, almost double the Fed’s 2% target.
Why This Matters
The Fed’s next move could affect borrowing costs on mortgages, credit cards, and other loans, even as inflation continues to squeeze household budgets. A December rate hike could keep those costs elevated for longer.
When the Fed raised rates in September, Warsh said the Fed’s standard for taking action is inflation failing to return to the Fed’s 2% target “clearly and at sufficient speed.”
That should make hiking on Wednesday a “much closer call than what the market is currently pricing,” wrote Thomas Simons, U.S. economist at Jefferies. Fed officials have put themselves in a “no-win situation,” he wrote, by talking down the need for hiking again and guiding the markets toward a pause.
“The Fed isn’t going to hike, but we’re not sure why,” Simons wrote.
Why Wait?
That is the key question that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will likely grapple with at his 2:30 p.m. ET press conference: Why wait until December to hike?
Warsh’s inflation-fighting credibility got dinged in July, when he talked tough on prices but signaled little willingness to take action. He gained it back in September, when the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023.
On Wednesday, he’ll have to thread the needle again, wrote Aditya Bhave, a Bank of America economist.
Sounding dovish may reignite questions about credibility, Bhave wrote, while sounding too hawkish on rate hikes may spook markets. He will “have an easier time at the presser if the Fed hikes than if it does not,” Bhave wrote.
The “bar is low for the market to feel that the Fed is falling behind the curve,” raising the stakes for Warsh, wrote Oscar Muñoz, head of U.S. economics at TD Securities.
“The chairman has been successful in gaining back his more hawkish credentials,” Muñoz wrote. “With that said, the act will be hard to follow for a second consecutive meeting if the Fed decides to hold rates steady.”
Policymaker Debate
The Fed decision may not be unanimous, analysts say, since officials are split on how quickly to raise interest rates.
The most likely dissenters: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari. The three voted against the Fed decision to keep rates flat in July, arguing that higher rates were needed to tamp down inflation.
Years above the Fed’s 2% inflation target “has badly strained Americans’ budgets,” requiring tighter monetary policy, Logan said in a speech this month.1
Other Fed officials have wanted to be more patient, since higher interest rates slow the economy and job market. There’s “no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information,” New York Fed President John Williams said last month.2
Those comments helped markets start to anticipate a Fed pause, since the New York Fed president’s voice is influential at the central bank.
Warsh’s stance isn’t clear. He did have a chance to shift market expectations back toward hiking in a mid-October appearance—but he opted against doing so.
“The message policymakers have left us with is that another hike will probably be needed, but that they see little urgency to deliver it in October,” wrote Larry Meyer, a former Fed governor and founder of Monetary Policy Analytics.
December Hike
The flip side of keeping rates steady in October is that a December hike is “all but locked in,” wrote TD Securities’ Muñoz, unless there’s an unexpected shock.
Warsh is unlikely to tip his hand about December, analysts say, pointing to his belief that the Fed offering guidance to markets is unhealthy. But he may still indirectly validate the markets’ expectations, Muñoz wrote.
“By not clearly pushing back against it, and doubling down on his inflation focus, he will corroborate the clear guidance provided by the rest of the committee,” he wrote.
Keeping rates on hold this week raises the risk that a larger rate hike may come in December, wrote Monetary Policy Analytics’ Meyer. It’s looking “increasingly likely that the data over the next couple of quarters will keep up the pressure on the Fed a little longer,” Meyer wrote.
Related Education
Other analysts are a bit more optimistic that inflation will cooperate. September’s data was admittedly hot, wrote Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. But it didn’t seem to cause enough alarm at the Fed for officials to guide markets back toward an October hike, he wrote, adding that “their silence speaks volumes.”
Inflation trends should peak soon, he wrote, as sluggish wage growth and a less-hot stock market will weigh on consumer spending and, in turn, prices.
“The roughly three hikes that markets anticipate over the next eight months look overdone,” Tombs wrote, anticipating the Fed will raise rates in December but then pivot back to rate cuts in the second half of 2027.

articles.title: Fed Meeting Begins Today: Will Interest Rates Go Up Again? - Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.summary: Fed Meeting Begins Today: Will Interest Rates Go Up Again?  Norada Real Estate Investments
articles.full_text:
Will interest rates go up again? Probably not this week, but a December hike looks more likely by the day. The Fed meeting begins today, Tuesday, October 27, and the decision lands on Wednesday, October 28, at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Traders using the CME FedWatch tool put the chance of a hold at about 90.6%, which would keep the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%. The odds of a quarter-point hike this week are only about 9.4%.
The bigger story is what comes next. The odds of a hike at the December 8–9 meeting have jumped to about 73%, up from roughly 42% a month ago. Inflation got hotter in September, and the Fed already raised rates once this fall. So if you're borrowing money, buying a home, or keeping cash in savings, this two-day meeting is worth a few minutes of your attention.
Below, I'll walk you through why the Fed is likely to sit tight for now, why another increase is still on the table, and what each outcome could mean for your mortgage, your credit card, and your bank account.
Fed Meeting Begins Today: Will Interest Rates Go Up Again Before Year-End?
Here's the honest answer in plain words. A pause this week is the most likely result. But the Fed is leaning toward higher rates, not lower ones, and many experts expect it to raise rates one more time before 2026 is over.
A Quick Look Back: The September Surprise
At its September meeting, the Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point, to today's range of 3.75% to 4.00%. That was the first hike in more than three years. For a long stretch before that, borrowers were hoping for cuts. September flipped the script.
Why does that matter now? Because the Fed rarely moves in giant leaps. It often raises rates, waits to see how the economy reacts, and then decides whether to go again. This week looks like one of those “wait and see” moments.
What the Market Odds Are Telling Us
Traders bet on Fed moves through futures contracts, and the CME FedWatch tool turns those bets into simple odds. Think of it like a weather forecast for interest rates. It isn't a promise, but it tells you which way the wind is blowing.
Right now, the forecast for this week is calm. Odds of a hike this week were 10.5% on Monday afternoon, down from 33.8% on October 14, according to InvestmentNews. So the fear of a surprise move this week has cooled off.
December is a different picture. The chance of a hike at that meeting has climbed from about 42% to about 73% in a month. InvestmentNews also puts the odds of at least one hike by the end of the year at more than 80%.
Why Inflation Keeps the Fed on Edge
The Fed has two big jobs: keep prices steady and keep people working. When prices rise too fast, raising rates is its main tool to cool things down.
The latest numbers aren't helping. Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the past year in September, up from 3.4% in August. That's moving in the wrong direction, and well above the Fed's long-run goal of 2%. When inflation speeds up like this, the Fed gets nervous about waiting too long.
What the Experts Expect
Most analysts see a pause this week with a strong warning attached. Here's what a few of them are saying:
- Aditya Bhave, economist at BofA Securities, told Kiplinger: “The inflation picture has gotten worse on net since the September meeting.” He thinks the case for raising rates now is real.
- Paul Eitelman, global chief strategist at Russell , told Kiplinger: “We expect a hawkish hold in October with the Fed delivering one more hike at year-end.”
- Melissa Cohn of William Raveis Mortgage pointed out to InvestmentNews: “It's a week before the election.” She expects a hold this week, and she thinks the Fed should raise rates in December if oil prices keep soaring.
A “hawkish hold” simply means the Fed keeps rates the same but signals that it's ready to raise them later. Picture a parent who doesn't take away the car keys today but makes it very clear that one more late night will do it.
The Election Factor
The midterm elections are on November 3, just days after this meeting. The Fed says it doesn't make decisions based on politics. Still, a big surprise move a week before voters head to the polls would draw a lot of heat. That's one more reason many people expect Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and his colleagues to stay put now and save any hike for December, once the votes are counted and more data is in.
How a Rate Hike Could Reach Your Mortgage
Here's a point that trips up a lot of people. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly. Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which moves on what expect from inflation and the Fed over many years.
Before the stock market opened on October 27, Kiplinger reported the 10-year yield at 4.995%, right at the doorstep of 5%. The 2-year sat at 4.735%, and the 30-year at 5.302%. Those are high levels, and they help explain why home loans still feel expensive. According to Zillow, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.23% today. You can see the full breakdown in our latest mortgage rates update.
So even if the Fed holds this week, a tough message about December could push yields, and mortgage rates, a bit higher. A softer tone could do the opposite.
What It Means for You
Here's how the two paths could play out for everyday money decisions:
- Homebuyers: If you've found the right home and the payment fits your budget, don't sit on the sidelines waiting for a big rate drop. The odds point the other way for now. Get a rate lock quote, and ask your lender how long the lock lasts.
- Homeowners with an adjustable-rate loan or a HELOC: These rates often move soon after the Fed. A December hike could raise your payment. Now is a good time to look at fixing the rate or paying down the balance.
- Credit card users: Card rates usually follow the Fed's rate closely. Paying down high-interest balances before December is one of the smartest moves you can make.
- Savers: Good news here. High-yield savings accounts and CDs keep paying solid returns while rates stay high, and another hike could nudge them up a little more.
What to Watch on Wednesday
The decision comes out at 2:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday, and the chair's press conference typically starts at 2:30 p.m. ET. Three things are worth listening for:
- The wording of the statement. Watch for any phrase that hints more increases may be needed.
- How the chair talks about inflation. If he sounds worried about September's jump, December odds could climb even higher.
- Any dissent. If one or more members vote for a hike this week, that's a strong sign the next move is up.
My Take
I don't expect rates to go up this week. But I wouldn't plan your finances around rates coming down soon, either. With inflation at 3.7% and the market leaning hard toward a December hike, the safer bet is that borrowing stays pricey through the end of the year.
That doesn't mean you should freeze. A home you can comfortably afford today is still a good home. Just build your budget around today's rates, not hoped-for ones, and keep some room for a slightly higher payment if you have a variable-rate loan. We'll be watching Wednesday's announcement closely and will share what it means for you as soon as it's out.

This rise continues to be driven by limited supply and demand from those receiving remittances from Europe.
MLC: Indicative Figures With Low Trading Volume
The freely convertible currency (MLC) is around 564 Cuban pesos on average, with a purchase rate of 526 CUP and a selling rate of 602 CUP. This value should be taken as indicative since the trading volume recorded is low. Compared to the previous session, the MLC decreased by 10 pesos (-1.7%) from 574 CUP, and over the past week, it has dropped 12 pesos (-2.1%) from 576 CUP a week ago. Over the last month, the MLC has ranged from a high of 742 CUP to a low of 457 CUP, reflecting the volatility and lack of data in this segment. Without physical presence, its use is confined to state-run stores that accept it, limiting its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rate Summary
USD to CUP exchange rate: 843 CUP. Euro to CUP exchange rate: 929 CUP. MLC to CUP exchange rate: 564 CUP (indicative value, limited data).
The Gap Between Informal and Official Exchange Rates
The official exchange rate set by the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III) remains at 749 CUP per dollar and 837 CUP per euro, significantly lower than the values prevailing in the informal currency market. The gap is 94 pesos for the dollar and 92 pesos for the euro, highlighting the divergence between the official economy and the everyday reality on the streets.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rates remain far from the informal market, failing to meet the real currency demand of the population. In the past month, the official dollar rate increased from 681 to 749 CUP, and the euro from 776 to 837 CUP, indicating a sustained devaluation of the peso even in the official channel.
In a scenario of ongoing inflation, low state salaries, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, any fluctuation in the informal market directly affects internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
Methodology
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate is an index of the Cuban informal market, created through automated analysis of thousands of currency trading posts in Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation excludes atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each transaction based on its age, and consolidates a representative value updated several times a day.

FAQs on Cuba's Informal Currency Exchange
What is the current exchange rate for the U.S. dollar in Cuba's informal market?
As of October 27, 2026, the U.S. dollar is trading at an average of 843 Cuban pesos in the informal market.
How does the euro compare to the U.S. dollar in Cuba's informal market?
The euro is trading at 929 Cuban pesos, maintaining a higher value compared to the U.S. dollar, which is at 843 CUP.

The gap exists because the official rates set by the Central Bank of Cuba do not reflect the real demand and supply dynamics present in the informal market.

articles.title: Will US Federal Reserve keep interest rates on hold for US economy? Key things investors need to know - Upstox
articles.summary: Will US Federal Reserve keep interest rates on hold for US economy? Key things investors need to know  Upstox
articles.full_text:
Market News
SUMMARY
The US Federal Reserve's FOMC is conducting its two-day policy meeting, after which the central bank will release the outcome as markets predict a rate hold in the upcoming outcome.
The US Fed's FOMC will release the outcome of the meeting through an official press release at 2:00 pm (ET) on October 28.
The United States Federal Reserve (US Fed) is set to begin its two-day October 2026 monetary policy meeting on Tuesday, October 27, as global investors now turn their attention towards the central bank’s upcoming policy outcome amid elevated inflation in the American economy.
The official schedule for the US Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) indicates that the central bank will start its policy meeting on Tuesday, October 27, and conclude on Wednesday, October 28.
After concluding the meeting, the FOMC will release the outcome of the meeting through an official press release at 2:00 pm (ET).
In the September policy outcome, the US Fed unanimously decided to raise its rates by 25 basis points (bps) for the first time in over three years to the range of 3.75% to 4% citing solid expansion pace of economic activity amid inflation risk in the country.
Earlier, the Fed officials have indicated that the central bank is in no rush to move the interest rates again before the committee decides the correct trajectory for the same, even though higher global energy prices adds pressure to households.
CME Group’s FedWatch tool indicates that the market experts predict there is a 90.6% probability of the US Federal Reserve keeping their key interest rates unchanged or on hold at the range of 3.75% to 4% in the upcoming meeting outcome.
However, the data also suggests that there is a 9.4% probability for the Federal Reserve to increase the key interest rates by 25 basis points to the range of 4% to 4.25% in the upcoming outcome schedule to be published on Wednesday.
Investors are focused on a potential rate pause rather than a back-to-back rate hike to tighten situation in the American economy.
This potential rate hold is expected to come at a time when the CPI inflation for the US economy surged to 3.7% as of September 2026, in comparison to 3.4% in the month of August 2026.
The 3.7% inflation rate remains elevated, well above the central bank’s target of 2% as the US Fed aims to contain the increase and cater to the labour market amid crude oil prices rallying in the global market.
In September 2026, the unemployment rate in the country surged to 4.2%, from earlier 4.1% levels in the 12-month period ended August 2026, according to the official Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data.
Although the unemployment rate increased in the period, non-farm payroll jobs increased by 29,000, with growth in sectors like healthcare services and hospitals, while other segments like nursing and residential care lost employment.
Reports suggest that US job growth was slower than expected, ruling out bets of a potential rate hike from the US Federal Reserve. The central bank has two major mandates: containing inflation and aiding the job market.
With jobs slowing down, elevated inflation, and upcoming US mid-term elections, the central bank will keep a close watch on the economic data to determine the trajectory of interest rates for the economy.
Although the central bank cited strong economic activity in the economy, the Fed remains concerned about the elevated uncertainty in the market due to geopolitical developments.
“Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2% goal. The Committee will deliver price stability,” the FOMC said in its September policy outcome.
With the sticky inflation situation in the American economy, the US Fed’s goal is now looking clear to balance out the rising cost of energy sources and the higher cost of imports weighing on the economy.
