articles.title: What the Fed's interest rate decision means for your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: What the Fed's interest rate decision means for your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to pause further interest rate increases on Wednesday, following September's first hike in more than three years. Based on 30-day fed funds futures prices, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee are likely to raise the benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point in December.
"The Federal Reserve's interest rate decision takes center stage this week after a hotter-than-expected September CPI report showed price pressures broadening," Ehsan Khoman, economist with the BlackRock Investment Institute, said in an analysis. "Even as we expect another hike by year-end, we don't view recent tightening as the start of a sustained hiking cycle."
What will a higher rate environment mean for your money? The federal funds rate influences not only the stock market, but also savings rates, interest charges, and, to a lesser degree, mortgage rates. Here's how to prepare for the impact on your deposits, credit, and debt.
Read more: Understanding the Fed decision: Do we want high or low interest rates?
How a Fed rate hike affects checking and savings accounts
A series of Fed rate hikes will likely slowly lift deposit earnings. However, deposit accounts are mostly for convenience, not substantial returns. So far in 2026, the gains have been meager.
Checking accounts
Your checking account churns cash flow to pay bills. The liquidity limits your earning power.
The national average interest rate on checking accounts has barely budged this year, remaining at 0.07%. A Fed short-term interest rate increase may nudge earnings incrementally higher.
Savings accounts
Interest rates on savings accounts are only marginally better, clinging to 0.38%. But savings accounts are for near-term money.
High-yield savings accounts have been more effective at paying interest. Rates are split in the 3% to 4% range.
This is one category where rate shopping and subsequent increases in the Fed rate really pay off.
Dig deeper: 10 best high-yield savings accounts
Money market accounts
If you have $10,000 or more that you want to keep on the sidelines but easy to tap when you need it, money market accounts have been convenient — but low-paying, with a national average payout of only 0.63%.
A high-yield money market account is a better option, where you may still find a rate just under 4%, but mostly in the mid-3% range.
Read more: 10 best high-yield money market accounts
What a rate hike does to CDs
CD rates have begun inching higher. The national average on a 12-month CD is 1.76%, but you can find better deals if you're willing to shop around — and move your money to the best offer.
Your minimum deposit and term will affect your rate. Fed rate hikes may ultimately sweeten CD rates.
Learn more: The best CD rates on the market
What a rate hike will mean for mortgages
And then there are mortgage rates, often the largest borrowing expense consumers face. Fed interest rate increases don't usually affect mortgage rates — the bond market often prices in hikes before monetary policy moves.
At the end of February and into early March, mortgage rates were hitting three-year lows. Then the war in the Middle East began, and rather than falling further, home loan rates reversed course and edged higher. Home loan rates have recently topped 7% (depending on the rate reporting source), mirroring the higher yields of the 10-year Treasury note.
Housing industry analysts at the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae predict that mortgage rates will remain near 7.5% through 2027.
Dig deeper: Mortgage rate predictions for the next 5 years
What a rate hike means for personal loans and student loans
Personal loans
Personal loan interest rates have risen slightly to an average of 11.9%. Advertised personal loan rates vary widely, from 6% to 9%.
The Federal Reserve influences consumer loan rates by setting the federal funds rate, which affects how much banks charge each other for overnight lending. That cost typically gets passed on to borrowers through higher or lower rates on personal, auto, and student loans.
Read more: How the Fed rate hike shapes consumer loans
Student loans
The Federal Reserve doesn't set student loan rates directly, but its federal funds rate influences the 10-year Treasury yield (which determines federal loan rates) and the prime rate (which determines private loan rates).
The federal funds rate doesn't directly determine federal student loan interest rates, but it can influence them indirectly. Congress sets the federal student loan rates based on the 10-year Treasury note, adding a fixed margin each year.
But the 10-year Treasury yield moves with investor demand, not the Fed's rate. When investors expect high inflation or strong economic growth, they demand higher yields, which can push federal student loan rates higher.
That said, if the Fed's rate hikes successfully cool inflation, Treasury yields may drop — and the following year's federal student loan rates could be lower.
Private student loans are offered by banks, credit unions, and online lenders, many of which use the prime rate as a basis for setting their interest rates. The prime rate moves alongside the Federal Reserve's rate decisions. So, when the Fed raises rates, new private loan rates usually rise, and when it cuts rates, they tend to fall.
Read more: How the Fed's rate hike will impact student loan interest rates
What happens to credit cards when the Fed raises rates
Credit card interest affects everyone — except those who pay off their balance each month. Rates have climbed from around 16% in 2021 to an average of over 22% toda
Michele Raneri, vice president and head of U.S. research at TransUnion, expects consumers to see "minimally higher" borrowing costs as variable-rate credit products reflect the Fed's interest rate hike.
"A consumer carrying the average Q2 2026 credit card balance of $6,610 at a 22% APR could see an increase of $1.38 in minimum monthly payments as those higher rates are passed on," Raneri said in a statement. "While the near-term impact on minimum monthly credit card payments may be relatively small, higher borrowing costs can add up over time, particularly for consumers carrying larger balances or making only minimum payments.
Reducing revolving debt will limit the impact of rising interest rates, she added.
Yahoo Finance tip: The best way to earn a lower credit card interest rate right away is to ask. If you make regular payments and have seen your credit score improving, it's a good time to call your credit card provider and ask for a lower interest rate.
Read more: Will your credit card APR go up? What to know after Fed rate hike.
How the Fed's interest rate policy impacts your investments
"There's an old Wall Street adage that says, 'Don't fight the Fed,'" Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at Schwab, said in an analysis. "The idea behind it was that there's often a lot of turbulence associated with Fed rate-hiking cycles."
He noted that history shows an average maximum loss of more than 10% for the S&P 500 sometime within 12 months after the start of a higher-interest-rate cycle.
"Broadly, though, we would say that the economic backdrop is still relatively favorable for the Fed to be hiking. So even if it is a hiking cycle where they do hike more than once, we think that the economy can probably hold up," he added.
Stock prices often react to the Fed's rate actions, but they are only one of many factors affecting the investing climate and stock prices. AI investments and oil-price-fueled inflation seem to be the most motivating factors for equity markets these days.
If you want to manage your investments for the current environment, monitor broader economic and corporate profit trends, as well as interest rates. If you prefer to stay conservative, fill your portfolio with high-quality stocks that have proven themselves in all economic cycles.
Then, wait patiently for long-term growth.

articles.title: UK Shop Price Inflation ‘Highest since 2024’ As Retailers Struggle to Limit Price Rises - تسنیم
articles.summary: UK Shop Price Inflation ‘Highest since 2024’ As Retailers Struggle to Limit Price Rises  تسنیم
articles.full_text:
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out, The Guardian reported.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the New Year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said, “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a liter can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said, “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are (and) not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on (Prime Minister) Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

articles.full_text:
Indian equities in a downturn: Why retail investors should stay disciplined
Improving corporate earnings, six-year-low valuations and continued mutual fund inflows feature among the factors investors are weighing amid the market downturn
Many retail equity investors are perplexed by the downturn in the Indian equity market over the last one year. Ups and downs are common in the equity market. However, when retail investors see a continuous decline without knowing where the bottom lies, they worry.
Over the past year (as of late October 2026), India's benchmark indices have seen a sharp downturn.
The BSE Sensex is down approximately 13.17% compared with the same period last year, trading in the 72,650–73,100 range (down from higher levels over the preceding 12 months).  
Also read | Specialised investment funds: What investors should know before investing
The NSE Nifty 50 is down roughly 14% year-to-date and is trading around the 22,400–22,500 level amid an extended weekly losing streak.
What is driving the market downturn?
The following key factors are driving the continued decline.
• Geopolitical and energy shocks: Tensions in West Asia and a surge in Brent crude oil prices (remaining above $100 per barrel) have strained India's import-dependent economy.
• Global yields and capital flight: Elevated US bond yields (surpassing 5%) have led to massive foreign portfolio withdrawals from emerging markets.
• Valuation pressures: High stock valuations relative to earnings growth have triggered persistent profit-booking and long-term institutional selling.
Now the question arises: how should retail investors approach their investments at this juncture?
First, they must maintain discipline and stick to their asset allocation plan. Under normal circumstances, if one has followed an asset allocation plan, one would naturally have shifted funds from fixed-income instruments and other investments into the equity portfolio.
Investors should also consider the following factors, which provide reassurance that the market may rebound one day and that equity investors may be rewarded for their patience.
Corporate earnings show resilience
In the long run, share prices reflect companies' profits. Let us analyse the sales and profit figures of companies.
For a common sample of 357 companies that have declared their September-quarter results so far, revenue grew at a nine-quarter high of 22.1% year-on-year, while net profit growth of 27.5% was faster than the 9.7% growth recorded in the June quarter.
This provides reassurance to investors that companies are performing well despite several headwinds, such as international geopolitical tensions and higher energy prices.
Valuations hit six-year low
India’s equity valuations are at their lowest levels in six years following the recent market decline, which was triggered by a range of factors, including foreign selling, a weaker rupee, higher crude oil prices and rising US bond yields.
It is a different matter that Indian equities remain more expensive than their emerging-market (EM) peers from the perspective of foreign investors. This may be relevant for foreign investors and not for domestic investors. However, this valuation gap is also relevant to Indian investors when comparing investment opportunities across asset classes and markets.  
Also read | Repo rate up, stocks down: Should equity investors worry? History offers hope
The dollar-denominated MSCI India Index trades at around 18.5 times its 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio, the lowest level since May 2020. It hit a record high of 24.54 times in September 2024, when the Sensex and Nifty reached their all-time highs.
Equity mutual funds sustain inflow
According to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), net inflows into open-ended equity mutual funds during the last one year were as follows:  
The above figures indicate continued support for the equity market from retail investors through the mutual fund route.
IPO market remains active
Initial public offerings (IPOs) indicate investors’ willingness to invest in newly listed companies. During the calendar year 2026, mainboard IPOs raised over ₹1.04–1.10 lakh crore across 81–84 or more issues.
High-profile issues, such as Reliance Jio’s massive public offering, attracted unprecedented investor demand, drawing record institutional and retail bids totaling over ₹64 lakh crore. Strong domestic mutual fund inflows, heavy retail participation through systematic investment plans (SIPs), and robust institutional appetite continue to drive the primary market boom, despite selective pricing by issuers.
Inflation and interest-rate pressures
India's retail inflation climbed to a 23-month high of 5.54% in September 2026, driven sharply by surging food and fuel prices. In response to rising price pressures, the Reserve Bank of India increased its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on 7 October 2026, marking its first-rate hike in nearly four years.
It is expected that interest rates may harden further in the coming months. As in the past, the RBI may succeed in bringing inflation down towards its target of 4%, within the permitted range.  
Also read | IRDAI insurance reforms: Lower costs may not be enough without better claims
While other countries face inflation alongside relatively modest GDP growth, India remains one of the fastest-growing major economies.
The RBI has projected real GDP growth of 7.1% for FY 2026–27, an upward revision of 40 basis points. The World Bank has also upgraded its FY 2026–27 GDP growth forecast to 7.1%, from 6.6% predicted in April.
Staying the course amid volatility
Equity investors should prepare to stay invested for long-term gains and avoid panic-driven exits. As noted earlier, maintaining discipline and sticking to your asset allocation plan are essential.

articles.title: Interest rate odds: Traders forecast a 93% chance the Fed holds in October - Kalshi News
articles.summary: Interest rate odds: Traders forecast a 93% chance the Fed holds in October  Kalshi News
articles.full_text:
Midterm races are hitting the home stretch, but on Wednesday, all eyes will be on the Federal Reserve. Kalshi traders are pricing a 93% chance that the central bank will hold steady on interest rates. Only 6% of traders are all in on a 25bps hike, while the possibility of a 25bps cut sits at just 1%.
Whether an October rate hike is imminent has divided Fed watchers this past month, with many initially expecting an increase. However, with the decision only a day away, most observers are now banking on the status quo of 3.75%–4.00% prevailing.
‘It is important to realize how fast the market changes,’ Kenneth Carow, professor of finance at Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business, told US News and World Report, noting that forecasts have fluctuated wildly. ‘This shows that even the most knowledgeable investors have a very difficult time predicting rates.’
Market sees hints in Fed honcho’s IMF talk
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, like his predecessor Jerome Powell, is focused on tightening. Inflation has been over 2% for half a decade now and with progress on that front negligible, the FOMC seems unlikely to reverse course. Soaring energy prices have been a major contributor to ballooning prices, largely caused by supply chain issues linked to the Iran war.
At the Fed’s annual Jackson Hole retreat this past August — the first for Warsh, who took the helm at the Eccles building in May — the chair called the central bank’s 2% producer PCE goal ‘a firm, fixed target,’ CNBC said.
Speaking at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok last Friday during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, Warsh praised the global trend in tightening. ‘There are no free riders,’ CNBC reports.
However, Warsh stressed that he was not signaling a decision ahead of the FOMC’s October meeting. ‘I don’t prejudge meetings,’ he told IMF Director Kristalina Georgieva during a fireside chat. ‘I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.’
Nevertheless, the Fed chief’s comments were widely taken as a sign the Fed would hit the brakes this month. ‘Warsh’s comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October,’ Goldman Sachs economists, led by Jan Hatzius, wrote in a note that was widely quoted in the press.
Warsh, for his part, is resolute. ‘It’s a new chapter at the Fed,’ he said in Bangkok, insisting he will not be engaging in previews or hint-dropping. ‘We’re not in that business anymore.’
Consensus says December hikes likely
Still, the market seems certain that rate increases will resume before the end of the year, an encore of September's 25bps increase. President Donald Trump, who has made no secret of his eagerness for cuts, seems likely to find a rate increase in his stocking on Dec. 9. Out of 100 economists polled by Reuters between Oct. 16 and 20, 94 expect the Fed to pause in October. All 100, however, anticipate a December hike.
And while the Fed is dropping no official line, Fast Company reported earlier this month that minutes released from the central bank’s most recent meeting show officials expect another increase will be necessary before 2026 comes to a close.

articles.title: Why Central Banks Should Tread Carefully - Haver Analytics
articles.summary: Why Central Banks Should Tread Carefully  Haver Analytics
articles.full_text:
The Federal Reserve, Bank of Canada, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan meet this week against a difficult backdrop. An energy shock has pushed inflation higher just as households and businesses are contending with expensive borrowing. Economic growth has proved resilient, but the question for policymakers is how secure that resilience really is. There is a strong case for caution before tightening monetary policy further.
The immediate dilemma is familiar. Central banks cannot prevent an oil price shock, but they must guard against its spreading into wages, other prices and inflation expectations. At the same time, higher energy bills reduce spending power and raise costs for businesses. Further increases in interest rates could compound that pressure, even as the effects of earlier tightening are still being felt.
For now, there is little evidence that higher energy prices are feeding into broader inflation. The foundations of demand also deserve closer scrutiny. Government borrowing, rising asset values and investment based on expectations of future returns have all supported spending. Those supports may be less durable than the headline growth figures suggest.
The danger is that policymakers mistake this spending for lasting economic strength. Until productivity gains translate into broader income growth, further tightening risks undermining both today’s demand and the revenues needed to justify tomorrow’s investment. That does not mean central banks should overlook persistent inflation. It does mean they should weigh the evidence for it against the fragility of the growth they are seeking to restrain.
The evidence on inflation Latest data for September show that core CPI inflation, which strips out food and energy, is 2.6 per cent in the United States, 2.5 per cent in the euro area and 2.4 per cent in Japan. None has moved materially higher over the past six months, and the American and Japanese measures are lower than a year ago. So far, the rise in headline US inflation to nearly 4 per cent has not been accompanied by a comparable increase in core inflation.
The cost side offers a similar picture. Unit labour costs are rising at a y/y pace of 1.5% in the United States and 2.6% in the euro area, rates close to those consistent with a 2% inflation target. Japan is different: unit labour costs are rising by 4.1 per cent and accelerating, giving the Bank of Japan reason to assess the risks differently. Elsewhere, there is limited evidence so far that the energy shock is feeding into more persistent wage and cost pressures.
There is an important qualification. Weak productivity can itself make inflation harder to contain, so the absence of a productivity boom is not sufficient reason to hold rates. Policymakers must judge whether higher energy costs are spreading into wages, services prices and longer-term expectations. If inflation becomes more persistent, further restraint may be necessary. If it does not, the case for waiting is stronger, particularly when the sources of demand are themselves vulnerable.
The growth foundations are weaker than they look Recent resilience is encouraging, but its foundations matter. An economy supported by public deficits, rising asset values and investment undertaken in anticipation of future profits may respond differently to higher rates from one in which productivity is already lifting incomes across businesses and households.
Let’s start with the consumer. Real household disposable income per head is growing by 0.6% y/y in the United States and 0.4% in the euro area. In the UK it is falling by 0.3 per cent and in Japan by 1.8 per cent. Consumption has nonetheless held up more broadly, implying a decline in saving where consumption has grown faster than disposable income.
The role of wealth In the United States, rising asset values appear to have encouraged households to spend a larger share of their income. This need not involve additional borrowing: households can also save less. But spending supported by confidence in wealth is vulnerable to a change in that confidence. Falling markets or weaker employment prospects could encourage households to rebuild saving.
The relationship is in fact quite striking in the US data. When household net worth runs ahead of its trend relationship with income, households tend to save less out of current income; when wealth falls behind, saving tends to rise. Across more than a hundred quarters the correlation is -0.77. The latest observation sits at the far right of the distribution, with net worth some 92 percentage points of disposable income above trend. Almost all of that excess is in equities.
US household net lending against the deviation of net worth from trend, quarterly, 1999 to 2026. Source: Federal Reserve Board and Oxford Economics via Haver Analytics; author calculations.
This leaves consumption more exposed to asset valuations. A fall in equity prices would reduce wealth and could encourage households to save more out of current income, adding to the pressure on demand.
The investment boom is narrow AI investment has provided another support. Spending on data centres, computing equipment and electricity infrastructure generates activity now, against the expectation of substantial returns later. As I argued last week in “AI’s costs are arriving before its benefits”, those returns ultimately depend on customers able to benefit from using the technology and willing to pay for it. The industry’s investment plans are therefore partly a claim on the future incomes of the wider economy.
What is striking is how concentrated that investment has become. Since the end of 2023, real spending on information processing equipment and software has risen by 41% while all other business investment has fallen by 1%. That category now accounts for 44% of real business investment, against 31% before the pandemic, and for roughly half the increase in real GDP over the past year. This is a concentrated capital spending cycle.
Productivity is central to the argument. If AI allows businesses to produce more efficiently, it can support profits, real incomes and further investment. But while those gains remain concentrated or uncertain, infrastructure spending can run ahead of the customer revenues needed to sustain it. Confidence in future income is supporting expenditure before that income has arrived.
Fiscal policy is already stretched Let’s look finally at fiscal policy. Government borrowing has supported incomes and employment through a succession of shocks. And that support has been valuable. But some of the spending sustaining activity depends on deficits that governments may eventually seek to reduce. Rising interest costs make the choice harder: maintaining support becomes more expensive, while withdrawing it risks weakening growth.
Growth does not require every sector to borrow more. But if households seek to save more, businesses restrain investment and governments reduce deficits together, another source of spending must offset them if demand is to hold up. Otherwise sales, employment and incomes may weaken. Financial balances help reveal where the adjustment may occur; they do not make a downturn inevitable. The vulnerability is that several important sources of spending could retreat at once.
Who has been spending, and who has been saving. Source: IMF World Economic Outlook October 2026 and Federal Reserve Board via Haver Analytics; author calculations.
The exhibits above and below illustrate how saving and spending differ across economies. China, Japan and the euro area have private sectors that save more than they invest, while government borrowing absorbs part of those surpluses. For the global outlook, the question is how domestic demand evolves across these economies as spending elsewhere slows.
Government, private and current account balances, and the same balances in US dollars. Source: IMF World Economic Outlook October 2026 via Haver Analytics; author calculations.
How tightening could expose the weakness Higher interest rates could accelerate that retreat. They raise financing costs, squeeze borrowers’ disposable incomes and can weigh on asset prices. They also affect prospective customers of the AI industry. A business facing weaker sales and expensive finance may postpone the integration, training and organisational changes needed to adopt AI. Spending on the technology could fall short just as providers need revenues to validate their investment.
The consequences could extend beyond technology. Disappointing revenues could weaken infrastructure investment and equity valuations, with further effects on employment, household wealth and consumption. Central banks would then be restraining an economy whose apparent strength had depended partly on expectations their decisions were helping to unsettle. Further tightening therefore needs a clear justification in the inflation evidence.
Resilience is not the same as durability The balance of risks will differ across economies. Fiscal restraint could reinforce monetary restraint, while stronger domestic demand or more persistent inflation elsewhere could justify a different response. The relevant test is both whether spending is pressing against productive capacity and how durable that spending is. A shared energy shock does not require an identical interest rate decision.
A more secure expansion would see productivity gains translate into stronger real incomes and profitable investment across a wider range of businesses. That would help customers afford the technology and validate the infrastructure being built to supply it. Until those gains spread, growth remains exposed to shifts in borrowing, saving and confidence in future returns. Central banks should take that fragility very seriously before tightening further.
- Andy Cates joined Haver Analytics as a Senior Economist in 2020. Andy has more than 25 years of experience forecasting the global economic outlook and in as

- US futures trade mixed ahead of Fed decision with 89.5% probability of rate hold
- HSBC shares drop 7.1% after mixed Q3 results; Cadence rises 2.53% on beat
- 10-year Treasury yield holds at 4.99% while WTI crude gains 0.54% to $102.31
- Moody's economist warns against further rate hikes citing economic risks
*this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only.
US stock futures traded mixed on Tuesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, with markets pricing an 89.5% likelihood of rates remaining unchanged.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average futures edged up 0.01%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.09% and Nasdaq 100 futures declined 0.17%. The Fed's two-day meeting began Tuesday, following a 25 bps hike in September that set the benchmark range at 3.75%-4%.
Key Corporate Earnings and Movements
Several major companies reported results or faced analyst scrutiny ahead of the open:
- Novartis AG (NYSE: NVS) rose 1.68% in premarket after reporting Q3 adjusted EPS of $2.46 on revenue of $14.52 billion, a mixed result versus estimates.
- HSBC Holdings PLC (NYSE: HSBC) fell 7.1% after posting Q3 adjusted EPS of $2.10 on revenue of $18.62 billion, also a mixed outcome against expectations.
- Cadence Design Systems Inc. (NASDAQ: CDNS) gained 2.53% following a beat on estimates, with Q3 adjusted EPS of $2.11 on revenue of $1.63 billion.
- Welltower Inc. (NYSE: WELL) climbed 0.87% after reporting Q3 Funds From Operations of $1.67 on revenue of $3.72 billion.
- Visa Inc. (NYSE: V) was up 0.25% as analysts anticipate Q4 EPS of $3.44 on revenue of $12.08 billion.

| Russell 2000 | -0.08% | 2,786.42 | +0.38% | 
What the Numbers Show
A divergence exists between equity sentiment and bond market yields. While stock futures showed modest negative pressure in tech-heavy indices, the 10-year Treasury yield stood at 4.99% and the 2-year yield at 4.72%. This near-inversion or flat yield curve structure, combined with the high probability of no rate change, suggests the market is pricing in stability rather than aggressive tightening, despite HSBC's significant 7.1% drop indicating specific sector concerns unrelated to broad macro policy.
Analyst Commentary and Economic Context
Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, advised the Fed to avoid raising rates again, citing mounting economic risks including oil prices and potential AI stock losses. He stated, "The Fed won't raise interest rates again when it meets this week, and it shouldn't."
David Morrison, Senior Market Analyst at Trade Nation, noted that attention remains on hyperscaler capital expenditures and free cash flow. He observed that Treasury yields have stabilized, with the 10-year note "hovering just shy of 5.0%."
Commodities and Global Markets
Crude Oil WTI futures rose 0.54% to $102.31 per barrel, while Brent futures gained 0.90% to $111.74. Gold Spot fell 0.20% to $3,997.22 per ounce. Bitcoin traded at $79,580, down 1% over the last 24 hours.
Asian markets were mixed, with Australia's ASX 200, South Korea's Kospi, and Japan's Nikkei 225 rising, while India's Nifty 50, China's CSI 300, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng indices fell.

articles.summary: Boeing (NYSE:BA) reports Q3 2026 in line with expectations  Barchart.com
articles.full_text:
Aerospace and defense company Boeing (NYSE:BA) met Wall Street’s revenue expectations in Q3 2026, with revenue rising 3.9% year on year to $24.19 billion. Its non-GAAP loss of $0.34 per share was 69.2% below analysts’ consensus estimates.
For more on Boeing, read our full research report, available free.
Boeing (BA) Q3 2026 highlights:
- Revenue $24.19 billion vs S&P analysts’ consensus estimates of $24.21 billion (3.9% year-on-year growth, in line)
- Adjusted EPS -$0.34 vs S&P analysts’ consensus estimates of -$0.20 (69.2% miss)
- Operating margin 1.5%, up from -20.5% in the same quarter last year
- Free cash flow margin 1.9%, similar to the same quarter last year
- Backlog $745.4 billion at quarter end, up 17.3% year on year
- Sales volumes were flat year on year
- Market capitalization $148.8 billion
"Recent milestones, including certification of the 737-7 and 737-10 and selection to design and build the Navy's sixth-generation fighter aircraft, are important steps as we continue building on our progress," said Kelly Ortberg, Boeing president and chief executive officer. "But we are not done. We remain focused on safety and quality as we redouble our efforts on Lean and disciplined execution to deliver on our commitments and build the durable performance our stakeholders expect."
Revenue growth
Reviewing a company’s long-term revenue performance reveals insights into its quality. Any business can experience short-term success, but top-performing ones sustain growth for years. Boeing’s revenue grew at a decent 8.6% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years. Its growth was slightly above the average industrials company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.
Long-term growth matters the most, but within industrials, a half-decade historical view may miss cycles, industry trends or a company capitalizing on catalysts such as a new contract win or a successful product line. Boeing’s annualized revenue growth of 13.8% over the last two years is above its five-year trend, suggesting its demand recently accelerated. The number of units sold helps explain the company’s revenue dynamics and reached 161 in the latest quarter. Over the last two years, Boeing’s units sold averaged 51.8% year-on-year growth. Unit growth outpaced revenue growth, indicating that the company’s average selling price decreased.
This quarter, Boeing grew its revenue by 3.9% year on year, and its $24.19 billion of revenue was in line with Wall Street’s consensus estimates.
Looking ahead, sell-side analysts expect revenue to grow 14.8% over the next 12 months, according to S&P, similar to its two-year rate. This is a strong growth projection for a company of its scale and indicates its newer products and services will spur better revenue performance.
Operating margin
Although Boeing was profitable at the operating level this quarter, it has generally struggled over a longer period. Its expensive cost structure has contributed to an average operating margin of negative 3.6% over the last five years. Unprofitable industrials companies warrant extra scrutiny because they can be vulnerable in a downturn.
On the positive side, Boeing’s operating margin rose by 22.2 percentage points over the last five years, as its revenue growth provided operating leverage. Still, it will take much more for the company to show consistent profitability.
In Q3, Boeing generated an operating margin of 1.5%, up 22 percentage points year on year. This increase was a positive development and shows it operated more efficiently.
Earnings per share
Revenue trends explain a company’s historical growth, but the long-term change in earnings per share (EPS) points to the profitability of that growth – for example, a company could inflate its revenue through excessive spending on advertising and promotions.
Boeing’s full-year EPS flipped from negative to positive over the last five years. This is a good sign and shows it’s at an inflection point.
As with revenue, looking at EPS over a shorter period can reveal a change in the business.
For Boeing, its two-year annual EPS growth of 60.5% was higher than its five-year trend. Accelerating earnings growth is a positive sign, especially from an already high base.
In Q3, Boeing reported adjusted EPS of negative $0.34, which rose from negative $7.47 in the same quarter last year. Despite growing year on year, the result missed analysts’ consensus estimates, but long-term adjusted EPS growth matters more than short-term movements. Over the next 12 months, Wall Street expects Boeing’s full-year EPS to shrink by 74.7% from $8.62 to $2.18, according to S&P.
Key takeaways from Boeing’s Q3 results
Boeing’s Q3 results offered few positives, making for an underwhelming quarter. Shares remained flat at $189.65 immediately after the release.
The latest quarter is only one piece of Boeing’s longer-term business quality picture. Quality, combined with valuation, can help determine whether the stock is a buy. Read the full research report here (it’s free).

articles.title: Chart of the Day: USDJPY Caught in a Trap. Tokyo Intervention and a Hawkish BoJ Loom - XTB.com
articles.summary: Chart of the Day: USDJPY Caught in a Trap. Tokyo Intervention and a Hawkish BoJ Loom  XTB.com
articles.full_text:
- USDJPY trades around 158 as investors await upcoming interest rate decisions from the Fed and the BoJ.
- Japan services producer price growth accelerates to 3.7%, supporting expectations for further Bank of Japan rate hikes.
- Japanese authorities warn that they remain ready to take decisive action against excessive yen depreciation near the 160 level.
USDJPY remains in focus ahead of key meetings of the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan. On Tuesday, October 27, the pair is trading around 158 as investors prepare for decisions that could shape its direction over the coming weeks. Markets are not currently expecting an interest rate hike from either the Fed or the BoJ. However, this does not mean that further monetary tightening is off the table.
Inflation remains a key factor. In Japan, price pressures, including rising service prices, are strengthening the case for further rate hikes. At the same time, Japanese officials are increasingly signalling that they will not stand by and allow the yen to weaken indefinitely. On the other side of the equation is the US dollar, whose outlook depends on how long inflation in the United States remains elevated.
Source: XTB Research
Key Factors Currently Driving USDJPY
Japanese Inflation Continues to Support the BoJ Rate Hike Outlook
The latest data on Japanese producer prices for services show annual growth accelerating to 3.7%. At the same time, the previous reading for August was revised lower. Despite this revision, the latest figure suggests that price pressures in the services sector remain significant.
This is an important signal for the Bank of Japan. Service prices can reflect not only energy and import costs, but also more persistent economic trends, including wage pressures and the pass through of higher costs to consumers. From the central bank's perspective, sustained inflation in this segment could support further gradual monetary policy normalisation.
However, this does not mean the BoJ must raise rates this week. Following previous policy adjustments, policymakers may want to assess their impact on the economy and financial conditions. As a result, the central bank's guidance on the future path of interest rates is becoming just as important as the decision itself.
The BoJ May Pause, but a December Hike Remains a Real Possibility
The Bank of Japan is likely to keep interest rates at 1.25% at its meeting concluding on October 30. However, this would not necessarily signal a dovish shift. The central bank could use its updated economic and inflation forecasts to indicate that monetary policy normalisation will continue and that another rate hike remains a matter of timing.
The outlook for underlying inflation is particularly important. Rising energy costs, a weak yen pushing up import prices, and persistent wage pressures all argue for continued vigilance among policymakers. The BoJ may conclude that inflation has become sufficiently entrenched in the economy to warrant further gradual monetary tightening in order to maintain price stability over the longer term.
Investors will primarily be looking for confirmation that a December rate hike remains a realistic option. Under this scenario, the policy rate could rise from 1.25% to 1.50%, although the final decision will depend on incoming data and the central bank's assessment of the Japanese economy.
The yen could benefit simply from a signal that another rate hike is approaching. Even if the BoJ leaves rates unchanged in October, more hawkish guidance could limit USDJPY's upside potential. Foreign exchange markets respond not only to current interest rates, but also to expectations about their future path.
The key question, however, is whether signals from Tokyo will prove more hawkish than the Fed's message. If both central banks leave rates unchanged, but the BoJ more clearly opens the door to a December hike, expectations for the future interest rate differential could begin to work in the yen's favour.
The Fed Is Likely to Pause, but US Inflation Remains a Risk
The Federal Reserve's upcoming meeting concludes on October 28. The market's base case is that interest rates will remain unchanged, giving policymakers time to assess inflation and economic conditions. For USDJPY, however, the important question is not simply whether the Fed holds rates steady, but also how it assesses the inflation outlook over the coming months.
Persistent price pressures in the United States could make the Fed cautious about signalling future monetary easing. If its statement is more hawkish than markets anticipate, the dollar could remain supported even without an October rate hike.
This matters because the absence of a rate increase does not automatically imply a weaker US currency. If investors conclude that US interest rates will remain elevated for longer, Treasury yields could rise, making the dollar more attractive relative to the yen.
In this scenario, the arguments for further BoJ tightening may not be sufficient to trigger a sustained decline in USDJPY. The interest rate differential between Japan and the United States continues to favour the dollar, and narrowing that gap would require clearer signals of further Japanese rate hikes or a shift in expectations for Fed policy.
Tokyo Issues Another Warning: Intervention Risk Remains Real
Another important factor is the Japanese authorities' stance on the weak yen. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reiterated on October 27 that the government is closely monitoring foreign exchange market movements and stands ready to take decisive action if necessary.
Such warnings do not amount to an announcement of imminent intervention. However, they show that Tokyo remains vigilant and that rapid, excessive yen depreciation could prompt a response from the authorities.
The 160 level remains an important reference point for investors. As the pair approaches this area, the risk of Japanese authorities stepping in to curb further yen weakness increases. However, this should not be treated as an automatic intervention threshold. The pace of the move, market conditions, and whether exchange rate movements are considered excessive also matter.
As a result, intervention risk could limit USDJPY's upside even without a clear signal from the BoJ. The warning alone could trigger a short term rebound in the yen, particularly if investors are heavily positioned for further gains in the pair.
USDJPY Ahead of Central Bank Decisions: Consolidation or Another Test of 160?
In the short term, the market is caught between two opposing forces. On one side, Japanese inflation and warnings from Tokyo increase the risk of a downside correction in USDJPY. On the other, persistent US price pressures and the interest rate differential could continue to support the dollar.
Trading around the 157 to 158 area suggests that investors are waiting for fresh catalysts. Ahead of the Fed and BoJ decisions, it is difficult to identify a clear directional bias, and the tone of the policy statements may matter more than the decisions themselves.
A more hawkish BoJ combined with a relatively cautious Fed could open the door to further yen appreciation and a move lower in USDJPY. The opposite combination, with a hawkish Fed and a cautious BoJ, would increase the risk of another test of 159 to 160, where the possibility of intervention could become an additional obstacle for dollar bulls.
Conclusion
USDJPY enters a week of important central bank decisions without a clear directional catalyst. Japanese inflation continues to support the prospect of further BoJ rate hikes, while the latest producer price data for services reinforce the view that price pressures have not been fully contained. At the same time, Tokyo is reminding markets that currency intervention remains a possibility.
The United States cannot be overlooked, however. If US inflation remains persistent, the Fed could maintain a hawkish stance, limiting USDJPY's downside potential. Over the coming days, the most important signals will therefore concern the outlook for December policy decisions rather than the expected October pause itself.
USDJPY does not need to wait for an actual BoJ rate hike to come under pressure. Confirmation that a December move remains possible could be enough to shift market expectations. However, sustained yen appreciation will also depend on the Fed's communication and the US inflation outlook. For now, downside risks are increasing, but a decisive reversal has yet to be confirmed.
Key factors for USDJPY:
- Japanese inflation: Rising service prices strengthen the case for further BoJ rate hikes.
- A hawkish BoJ pause: Holding rates at 1.25% does not rule out an increase to 1.50% in December.
- The Fed decision: Markets expect rates to remain unchanged, making the policy statement and guidance for the coming months particularly important.
- Intervention risk: Warnings from Tokyo could limit the pair's upside, especially near 160.
- US inflation: Persistent price pressures could support the dollar and limit yen appreciation.
- Base case: USDJPY could consolidate ahead of the central bank meetings, with a clearer direction emerging only after policymakers deliver their statements.

articles.title: US Fed Decision: What to expect from Warsh's October meeting - The Economic Times
articles.summary: US Fed Decision: What to expect from Warsh's October meeting  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
According to the Associated Press (AP), the Federal Open Market Committee's October 27-28 meeting comes amid rising consumer costs, elevated mortgage rates and renewed questions about the Federal Reserve's independence under Chairman Kevin Warsh, who was appointed by President Donald Trump earlier this year.
Also Read | Who are the biggest investors backing Anthropic? A look at key stakeholders
The meeting also takes place less than a week before the US midterm elections, with affordability concerns remaining a key political issue as gasoline prices rise and grocery costs stay elevated.
Mortgage rates have added to the financial strain on households. The average rate on a 30-year mortgage climbed to a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month before easing to 7.32% last week, compared with just under 6.2% a year ago. Oxford Economics estimates that this year's sharp increase has put homeownership out of reach for another 5 million households, AP reported.
Any further tightening by the Fed could increase borrowing costs and put additional pressure on prospective homebuyers.
Fed Rate Hike Unlikely Despite Persistent Inflation
Financial markets initially considered the possibility of a quarter-percentage-point rate increase after inflation data came in hotter than expected for the previous month. Such a move would have lifted the Fed's benchmark interest rate to approximately 4.1%.
However, several senior policymakers have played down the prospect of an October rate hike, and futures markets now indicate that investors see little chance of an increase from the current rate of around 3.9%.
The Fed typically raises borrowing costs to restrain spending and bring inflation under control. However, policymakers must also weigh the broader economic consequences of tighter financial conditions.
Also Read | Global Market: South Korean shares jump over 4% as AI chip rally lifts Samsung, SK Hynix
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson has pointed to the sharp rise in longer-term market interest rates, suggesting that policymakers need more time to assess financial conditions before deciding on their next move, AP reported.
Joseph LaVorgna, chief economist at SMBC Americas and a former senior Trump administration official, expects the central bank to avoid an increase immediately before the election, according to AP.
Although most economists consider a rate hike unlikely, persistent inflation could keep the possibility of tighter monetary policy on the table in the coming months.
Forward Guidance Under Scrutiny
The meeting will also test Warsh's approach to communicating monetary policy. The Fed chairman has expressed reservations about forward guidance, the practice of signalling the central bank's likely policy direction in advance.
Warsh has argued that such signals can commit policymakers to a particular course and limit their ability to respond flexibly to changing economic conditions.
However, recent remarks by senior Fed officials have given markets clues about the likely outcome of the October meeting, raising questions about whether the central bank is effectively continuing the practice under its new leadership.
Aditya Bhave, head of US economics research at Bank of America, has highlighted the uncertainty surrounding the approach, according to AP. If Warsh supports the recent messaging by other policymakers, it could raise questions about his opposition to forward guidance. If he does not, a surprise policy move could undermine the credibility of signals provided by other officials.
Nevertheless, economists broadly expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged on Wednesday.
Fed Independence Remains a Key Concern
Warsh's relationship with Trump is another issue investors will monitor closely.
At its September meeting, the Fed raised interest rates despite the president's preference for lower borrowing costs. The decision helped ease some concerns that Warsh might prioritise the White House's economic preferences over the central bank's inflation mandate.
James Knightley, chief international economist at ING, said the September decision had encouraged markets to view the Fed as continuing to exercise independent judgment, AP reported.
However, questions remain about the extent of communication between Warsh and Trump. The president has said he spoke to the chairman before the September meeting and indicated that Warsh could support a rate increase because other policymakers had publicly backed the move.
Trump has also criticised the rate-setting committee, describing it as politically motivated.
Separately, Trump has renewed efforts to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook. The Supreme Court blocked an earlier attempt to remove her in June. A successful removal would create another vacancy on the central bank's board for the president to fill.
Warsh declined to discuss his communications with Trump at the September news conference, leaving uncertainty about the nature and extent of their interactions.
Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, said questions about the chairman's independence remain unresolved, according to AP.
Inflation Outlook Could Shape December Decision
Inflation is expected to remain central to the Fed's policy deliberations after price increases exceeded economists' expectations for two consecutive months.
Rising fuel costs have added to concerns that inflation could spread across the broader economy. Diesel prices reached a record $6.53 in late September and have since eased only modestly to $6.35.
Higher diesel prices increase transportation costs for businesses, affecting the movement of groceries, vehicles and other goods. Companies could pass those additional expenses on to consumers, extending inflationary pressures beyond the energy sector.
Inflation has also remained above the Fed's 2% annual target for an extended period. According to AP, Bhave noted that the target had not been achieved for an entire calendar quarter since the final three months of 2020.
Investors will therefore pay close attention to how Warsh characterises the inflation outlook and whether he reiterates the need to bring price growth back to the central bank's target more quickly.
Any indication that policymakers remain dissatisfied with the pace of disinflation could strengthen expectations of a rate increase at the Fed's December meeting.
Possible Dissent Could Signal Support for Higher Rates
The Fed's September rate decision was unanimous, but the October meeting could produce dissenting votes as policymakers debate whether the current interest rate is sufficiently restrictive.
Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and Lorie Logan, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, are among the officials considered most likely to favour a rate increase, AP reported.
Both have expressed concerns that monetary policy may not be tight enough to slow economic activity and bring inflation under control.
According to AP, some economists believe that dissenting votes could ultimately benefit Warsh by demonstrating that support for higher interest rates remains within the rate-setting committee.
For investors, the number and direction of any dissents could offer additional insight into the balance of opinion within the Fed and the likelihood of further tightening.
With a rate hold widely anticipated, the central bank's inflation assessment, internal divisions and guidance on future policy are likely to determine how markets interpret Wednesday's decision.

articles.title: 5 things to watch from the Federal Reserve's next meeting - The Killeen Daily Herald
articles.summary: 5 things to watch from the Federal Reserve's next meeting  The Killeen Daily Herald
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal Reserve policymakers are likely to keep their key interest rate unchanged Wednesday when they finish what may seem like an uneventful meeting. But investors and economists will be looking between the lines of the central bank's statement Wednesday for clues about its next moves and where it thinks inflation is headed.
The Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting will be the fourth of Chairman Kevin Warsh's tenure, which has been marked by questions regarding his independence from President Donald Trump, who appointed him earlier this year. It also comes just six days before midterm elections that have been shaped by affordability concerns as gas prices have soared and grocery prices remain elevated.
High mortgage rates have become another elevated cost for consumers, with the average 30-year mortgage reaching a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month before slipping last week to 7.32%. A year ago, the rate was just under 6.2%. Oxford Economics estimates that the sharp increases this year has put home buying out of reach for another 5 million households. Further rate hikes by the Fed could push mortgage rates even higher.
With all those moving parts, here's what to watch for from the Fed's meeting:
Slim chance of a rate hike
After inflation came in hotter than expected last month, Wall Street investors and some economists expected the Fed to lift rates at Wednesday’s meeting by a quarter-point, to about 4.1%. The Fed is charged with combatting inflation, and typically seeks to cool spending and bring down inflation by boosting borrowing costs.
Yet several top officials on the Fed’s rate-setting committee in speeches downplayed the likelihood of a rate hike in October. Investors now see almost no chance of an increase in the Fed's rate, currently at about 3.9%, according to futures prices.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed's board of governors, noted that longer-term interest rates had shot higher in financial markets and added that, “my colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time.”
Joseph LaVorgna, chief economist at SMBC Americas and a former top Trump administration official, said that the central bank will hold back just before the election.
“The Fed doesn't want to poke the White House in the eye six days before an election,” LaVorgna said.
Forward guidance — or not
The comments from Jefferson and others raise questions about one of Warsh’s signature initiatives: His disdain for so-called “forward guidance,” a term for the clear signals about the central bank's next moves provided by previous chairs. Warsh has said that such direction commits the Fed to a specific path and limits its ability to respond to economic data.
Yet the speeches this month by top officials appeared to some economists to be very much like forward guidance — just not from the chairman.
“Either he blessed this message from them and he was on board, in which case, one would have to question the credibility of this idea that that he doesn’t like forward guidance,” said Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics research at Bank of America. “But the other possibility is that he wasn't on board."
In that case, Warsh could implement a surprise rate hike, which would “end forward guidance by showing markets that they can’t listen to the guidance anymore."
Still, most economists see the odds of a hike as quite low.
Sizing up Warsh's independence
At the Fed's last meeting in September, Warsh defied Trump's preferences and raised rates, a step that defied concerns that the new Fed chair would turn out to be, in the words of Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, “a sock puppet” for the president.
Trump had said before choosing Warsh in January of this year that he would only pick a Fed chair who would cut rates.
James Knightley, chief international economist for Netherlands-based bank ING, said that September's rate hike, in defiance of the White House, largely assuaged those concerns.
“So far I think the markets have been encouraged by what they've seen,” Knightley said.
Yet since the September meeting, Trump has renewed his efforts to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook. If he is successful, it would open up another slot on the Fed's board for Trump to fill. The Supreme Court in June blocked an earlier attempt to remove her.
Trump also said after last month's Fed meeting that he had called Warsh beforehand and told him he “might as well” vote to raise rates because other officials on the rate-setting committee had publicly called for a hike. Trump said the committee is “hostile” and “political.”
Warsh declined at last month's news conference to comment on any communications with Trump, despite news reports that he has spoken often with the president. With the scope of Warsh's communications with Trump unclear, Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, said, “I think there is still a question mark there” regarding the chairman's independence.
Warsh's characterization of inflation
Inflation has come in hotter than most economists expected for two months in a row, heightening concerns that gas price spikes could raise costs across the economy. Diesel fuel reached an all-time high of $6.53 in late September, and has only fallen to $6.35 since then.
High diesel costs raise the price of shipping all sorts of goods, including groceries, cars, and nearly everything else. Businesses could then pass on the costs to consumers, spreading inflation to more parts of the economy.
Bhave notes that inflation hasn't been at the Fed's target of a 2% annual rate for a single calendar quarter since the final three months of 2020 — nearly six years ago.
If Warsh reiterates some of what he's said before — that inflation is too high, and the Fed intends to return it to 2% in a “timelier” fashion — economists and investors will see such comments as a sign the Fed will likely hike rates at its next meeting in December.
Signs of dissent
The Fed's September decision to lift rates was unanimous. Many Fed watchers, however, expect there could be two or even three dissents among the 12 officials who vote on rates. Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and Lorie Logan, president of the Dallas Fed, are considered the most likely to vote in favor of a rate hike this week.
Both have expressed concerns that the Fed's key rate isn't high enough to slow the economy and cool inflation.
Ironically, dissents could help Warsh and the Fed, some economists say, by illustrating that there is still support for higher rates on the committee.

articles.full_text:
Summary
- PBOC CNY reference rate setting for the trading session ahead.
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.
Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.
Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.
As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.
In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet this week, when U.S. central bankers will decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to subdue inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday.
Consumer prices have surged this year, with headline inflation across the U.S. rising at a in September as energy costs jumped. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago amid signs inflation could be seeping into the broader economy. The Fed targets annual inflation of 2%.
Gasoline prices, which have hovered above $4 a gallon for the last three months, accounted for more than half the September increase in consumer prices, according to the Labor Department.
"Although the latest hot inflation readings and rise in inflation expectations will concern Fed officials, they still appear broadly intent on tightening policy at a measured pace," Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at investor advisory firm Capital Economics, said in a recent research note.
In September, the Fed raised — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — by a quarter of a percentage point — its first hike in three years, thereby raising borrowing costs across the U.S. economy. The Fed is scheduled to announce its latest interest rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The meeting comes at a crucial time, as Americans head to the polls to cast their ballots in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Many Americans have expressed frustration with the state of the economy as they contend with of gas, food, and other expenses.
Most economists and investors expect the Fed to raise rates one more time before year-end, likely at its last meeting of the year on Dec. 8-9.
According to CME Group's Fed Watch tool, which uses 30-day Fed funds futures prices to predict rate decisions, traders see an 88% probability that the Fed will hold rates steady in October and a 71% probability the Fed will raise rates in December (no meeting scheduled for November).
In quarterly projections last month, the Fed signaled that its rate-setting committee expected to raise rates later this year. At the same time, some Fed policymakers have signaled that the central bank is in no rush to lift borrowing costs.
"With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information," New York Fed President John Williams said in a speech at the University at Buffalo following the Fed's rate hike in September.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will give a press conference after this week's rate decision. Until then, investors are unlikely to get any clues from Warsh, who has argued against sharing forward guidance on rate decisions.

articles.title: The Fed Could Hike Interest Rates Again in 2026. Here's What Investors Should Do Right Now. - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: The Fed Could Hike Interest Rates Again in 2026. Here's What Investors Should Do Right Now.  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
In just a few days -- on Oct. 28, to be precise – the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee will make a decision about the federal funds rate.
Despite September's quarter-point increase, meant to curb the inflation that's clearly still lingering, interest rate futures data from exchange CME Group says there's a 90% chance the FOMC will leave the fed funds rate's current target range of 3.75% to 4% alone, with only a 10% chance the committee will raise this target range by another quarter point.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Don't think we're off the hook just yet, however.
The Fed's Open Market Committee (FOMC) has one more scheduled opportunity after the one later this month to raise interest rates in 2026. That's on Dec. 9. And as it stands, the market is betting on a rate hike then. Specifically, interest rate futures indicate there's a 76% chance of a quarter-point increase in the fed funds rate being made at that time, while there's a 9% chance the FOMC will raise its target range for this baseline interest rate by half a point, to between 4.25% and 4.5%.
The question is, of course, how might another likely rate hike affect investors? Let's have a look.
History says...
There's no getting around the fact that higher interest rates can work against stocks. Price inflation reflects strong consumer and corporate spending, but too much inflation for too long can take a toll on the economy. Raising the cost of borrowing curbs this price-increasing demand, but since it also dials back corporate profit growth, it in turn reduces stocks' perceived value. History even shows some market setbacks corresponding with rate hikes.
Just don't lose perspective on any of it. Knee-jerk bearish reactions are often short-lived; high or rising interest rates don't inherently coincide with prolonged market weakness, if there's any weakness at all.
It's certainly possible to see both at the same time. And you sometimes will. Not always, though, and not predictably enough that you should take the chance of being out of the stock market when you'd be better served by staying in.
Periods like 2004 to 2007 and 2016 to 2019 come to mind. Although the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) eventually peaked with interest rates at the ends of those stretches, the gains made in the few years leading up to those peaks were too significant to pass up even if they ended with pullbacks.

articles.title: Experts predict the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged at its October 2026 meeting. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Experts predict the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged at its October 2026 meeting.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to Goldman Sachs Investment Research, the Fed is unlikely to adjust interest rates in October, but may implement another 0.25 percentage point rate hike in December. This forecast reflects the view that policymakers need more time to assess the impact of previous adjustments on the economy and price developments.
 Meanwhile, Michael Feroli, chief economist for US markets at JPMorgan, also predicted that the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged at its October meeting. He argued that delaying a rate hike would give the agency more time to assess new economic data, although inflationary pressures could still necessitate tighter monetary policy in the near future. JPMorgan also predicted that the Fed might raise interest rates again in December.
 According to a survey of 100 economists conducted between October 16–20, 94 predicted the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, at 3.75–4.00%; all 100 respondents predicted a rate hike in December. This represents a significant shift from the previous month, when less than half predicted another rate increase later in the year.
 Persistent inflation, rising energy costs due to the conflict with Iran , and continued tariffs are putting pressure on price prospects. Meanwhile, the US economy continues to grow, forcing the Fed to weigh the need to curb inflation against the risk of undermining economic activity if it continues to raise borrowing costs.
 According to the survey, nearly 60% of experts forecast interest rates could peak within the 4.00–4.25% range, while 38 of the 92 respondents to the interest rate outlook believe the Fed may need at least two more hikes. These differences indicate that a significant degree of uncertainty remains regarding the monetary policy path in the coming months.
 The Fed is expected to announce its interest rate decision on October 28th. Investors will closely monitor the policy statement and remarks from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh for further signals regarding the possibility of a December rate hike and the policy outlook for 2027.

articles.title: What To Expect From This Week’s Federal Reserve Meeting - Investopedia
articles.summary: What To Expect From This Week’s Federal Reserve Meeting  Investopedia
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- The Federal Reserve’s policy committee is likely to keep its key interest rate flat when it meets to set monetary policy on Wednesday.
- Economists expect the Fed to raise interest rates at future meetings to combat high inflation, but say there is no rush to raise them for a second consecutive meeting following September’s rate hike.
- Higher interest rates push up borrowing costs on all kinds of loans and can dampen inflation but risk slowing down the economy.
Federal Reserve officials are widely expected to leave the central bank’s key interest rate unchanged when they meet on Wednesday, signaling patience in their fight against inflation.
Financial markets were pricing in a one-in-ten chance that policymakers on the Federal Open Market Committee will vote to raise the fed funds rate by a quarter-point when they meet Wednesday, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool, which forecasts rate movements based on fed funds futures trading data.1
In recent weeks, Fed officials have publicly discussed whether to follow up on September’s quarter-point rate hike to counter higher-than-expected inflation. Although some Fed officials have voiced concerns, others have advocated a wait-and-see approach.
A higher fed funds rate means higher borrowing costs on all kinds of loans, which could discourage spending and subdue inflation. But it could also drag on the job market and the economy overall.
The Fed is balancing its dual mandate from Congress to keep inflation low and employment high. With inflation running above the Fed’s inflation goal for a fifth year and unemployment hovering near historic lows, most experts expect the Fed to raise interest rates again in December even if they forego an October hike.
“All signs are that the Federal Reserve will need to continue lifting interest rates in the near term, yet comments from a few key officials suggest they’re unlikely to do so at the October policy meeting,” Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a commentary.
What This Means For The Economy
If the Fed pauses its rate hike campaign in October, it would allow officials more time to assess how much the Iran war’s fuel price hikes are pushing up inflation before taking action again.
Recent comments from two key FOMC members—Fed Governor Michelle Bowman and John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York—suggested they didn’t favor rate hikes at back-to-back meetings.
The recent Fed remarks indicated that most officials will support hiking rates by a quarter point at every other meeting, which would mean the next two rate hikes will take place in December and March, David Mericle, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a commentary.
Related Education
Aside from the interest rate decision, the main point of interest from the Fed meeting Wednesday will be Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference. If he sticks to form, however, he will avoid giving hints about future monetary policy decisions. Unlike previous Fed chairs, Warsh has stuck to a policy of not giving “forward guidance” to financial markets.
Still, Warsh’s words, however cryptic, could offer some clues.
“Chair Warsh is unlikely to offer any direct forward guidance in his press conference, but we expect he will implicitly endorse a December rate hike,” Ruchir Sharma, an economist at Nomura, wrote in a commentary. “His characterization of recent inflation data and market financial conditions could provide some clues around the threshold for additional tightening in 2027.”
